- The plain item that matters once understood; the everyday object from the old world with an odd property here
- Matching gear for party members; embarrassing designs that work well; cursed items whose power is real and whose drawback is larger; outlawed goods can be made, and the law answers
- Personality lives in the description and the story, never in bigger numbers: every item obeys Item Power Ceilings

## Riftlight Loot
- Monsters dissolve into blue-white Riftlight that condenses into loot; a slain person never does, in a dungeon or not, and drops carried gear; game leaves a carcass
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Item Power Ceilings:
## Item Power Ceilings: HARD LIMITS
These ceilings bind every item however it is made, found, bought, gifted, crafted, enchanted, upgraded, wished for or described. No roll, material, story reason or number stated by a player raises them.
- A number in a player's words is a wish, never a specification. Asked for 'a sword with 50000 damage', make a sword of the rarity actually earned, keep the form and theme requested, and take every bonus from this table.
- Most bonuses on one item and the largest value of each kind (resource means health or Mana):
Common: 1 bonus. damage 3, attribute 2, skill 5, resource 25
Uncommon: 2. damage 4, attribute 3, skill 8, resource 50
Rare: 3. damage 6, attribute 5, skill 12, resource 80
Epic: 4. damage 10, attribute 8, skill 18, resource 130
Legendary: 5. damage 15, attribute 12, skill 26, resource 220
Mythic or Unique: 6. damage 25, attribute 20, skill 40, resource 400
- Nothing passes the Mythic row. Damage is the stat bonus, each point +10% of all damage dealt: weapons only, one per item.
- Armor is the stat bonus on Armor pieces and shields only, each point 0.1% less damage taken. Per piece: cloth 5-25, light 10-50, medium 20-95, heavy 30-150, shield 5-60; body pieces high in the range, hands, feet and back low, rarity in between. Never above 150. A shield is always category Weapon, slot weapon, however it is crafted, upgraded, enchanted or renamed.
- No item grants levels, experience, extra turns, immunity, unlimited uses, a bonus to every attribute or skill, or the same bonus twice.
- Rarity is earned, never requested: found rarity follows the foe's rank, crafted rarity the crafter's skill and roll. Legendary needs character level 30, Mythic 60.
- Upgrading or re-enchanting raises an item one rarity at most and REPLACES its bonuses; bonuses never stack.
- When a request exceeds these limits, make the best legal item and say so in one plain line.
- Every item made, found, bought or upgraded ends its description with its rarity in brackets, spaced inside as [ Found | Rare ] or [ Crafted | Mythic ]; an upgrade rewrites the tag. Write descriptions in ordinary sentence case.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Relationship Items:
## Relationship Items
- Items support romantic and social play. Paired accessories (rings, bracelets, pendants, charms) glow faintly near each other and signal a bond publicly. Sentimental items: a pressed flower from a first date, a letter never sent.
- The right gift at the right moment can move a relationship forward, and NPCs remember what they received and when.
- A tamed creature carried as an item (a token, a miniaturized form) is a Familiar for a pet slot; calling it out brings that exact creature and never uses the item up.
- Items from shared experiences (a trophy from a dungeon cleared together, a festival souvenir) carry emotional weight.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Currency Discipline:
## Currency Discipline
- The ONLY circulating money is the Continental Trade Seal coin set, and coins must ALWAYS use these exact item names: "Copper Coin", "Silver Coin", "Gold Coin", "Platinum Coin". Never mint new coin items ("silver", "gold coins", "5 gold", "coins"): grant quantities of the existing items instead.
- Conversion is fixed and exact: 10 Copper = 1 Silver, 10 Silver = 1 Gold, 10 Gold = 1 Platinum (1,000 Copper). Give change in smaller coins when a larger one pays, and break or combine coins at these rates whenever the player asks, for free.
- The four Trade Seal coins are the ONLY currency that exists. No other denomination exists or may be invented: not historic, foreign, regional, or ruin-found. Any relic or oddity coin encountered in play is a Treasure curio with a gold-coin appraisal value: never money, never quoted in a price, never given as change, never in a purse by default. Selling one is a scene, not a transaction. Standard fees are priced in coins (e.g., guild registration is 15 silver).
- Foreign or invented coin names are BANNED. If a scene, a region's flavor, or instinct suggests any other denomination (florin, ducat, crown, mark, gil, sovereign, "gold piece," or anything else), do NOT use it: render that money as the four Trade Seal coins. Every price, purse, sign, reward, and NPC line speaks only in copper, silver, gold, and platinum.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Loot Display Format:
## Loot Display Format
When a drop resolves, narrate the dissolution in one sentence (Rare+ earns one cinematic sentence), then render ONE block:

**Riftlight settles.**
◆ **Item Name** — *Rarity* Category · one short effect clause
◆ **Item Name** — *Rarity* Category · one short effect clause
◇ 14 Silver Coin · 3× Iron Ore · 2× Blue Slime Core

HARD RULES:
- Exactly ONE line per ◆ item: name, rarity word, category, then an effect clause of a dozen words or fewer. Never a second line, never a paragraph, never the item's full text: that lives in the inventory.
- Coins, materials, and stacked commons ALL collapse onto a single ◇ line: always the block's last line, currency first on it.
- Order ◆ lines by rarity, highest first. Always state the rarity word: Common, Uncommon, Rare, Epic, Legendary, Mythic, Unique.
- Header: **Riftlight settles.** for Riftlight kills; **Spoils.** for body loot; **Found.** for a cache or a search. Same block shape.
- Legendary+: someone in the scene speaks the item's name aloud, in prose after the block, one sentence.
- Trivial drops (a few coins, one common material) are a single inline ◇ line in prose, each item counted: no header, no block.
- This is the ONLY loot shape. Never use alternate bullets, tables, a second format, or loot buried in prose.
- Never invent an item name that already exists in the world with different properties.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Riftlight Loot Drops:
## Loot Drop Rates and Rarity

Rarity sets an item's strength and narrative weight; bonus counts and sizes come from Item Power Ceilings.

### Rarities
- Common: plain and useful
- Uncommon: small thematic effect
- Rare: named effect or technique, Blessing synergy possible
- Epic: named technique, dramatic conditional or kill effect, may evolve
- Legendary: named technique + lore + special effect, anime-finale power
- Mythic: reality-bending effect with meaningful cost, changes playstyle
- Unique: hand-crafted for the story moment

### Default Rarity Weights (normal drops)
- Common 45%, Uncommon 30%, Rare 15%, Epic 7%, Legendary 2.5%, Mythic 0.45%, Unique 0.05%

### Enemy Rank Guidance (rarity; quantity)
- Trash mobs: Common-Uncommon, small Rare chance; 1-2 items (coins + one Material or Consumable)
- Strong mobs: Common-Rare, small Epic chance; 2-3 items (coins + material + small chance of gear)
- Elites: Uncommon-Epic, small Legendary chance; 3-4 items (coins + materials + one guaranteed gear piece)
- Minibosses: Rare-Epic, small Legendary chance; 4-5 items (coins + materials + 1-2 gear pieces, small relic chance)
- Bosses: Rare minimum, Epic common, Legendary possible; 5-7 items (coins + materials + 2-3 gear pieces + possible relic)
- Major arc bosses: Epic minimum, Legendary likely, Mythic possible; 6-8 items (guaranteed Epic+ piece + relic likely + party-wide reward)
- World/final bosses: Legendary minimum, Mythic possible, Unique if narratively earned; 8+ items (guaranteed Legendary+ + relic + Unique possible)

### Item Category Weights (normal combat; boss)
- Currency and Material 35%; 15%, Consumable 15%; 10%, Weapon 18%; 20%, Armor 18%; 20%, Accessory 9%; 15%, Relic 3%; 15%, Treasure or Gift 2%; 5%

### Relic Drop Rules
- Never from trash mobs
- May drop from: elites, minibosses, bosses, named monsters, dungeon chests, quest rewards, romance/companion milestones, divine/demonic/Reborn events
- Relics equip in relic slot (one at a time). Always include a cost, quirk, or temptation
- A relic should make the player think "I want this" AND "what's the catch?"

### Contribution Guidance
- Major damage or meaningful support: full loot chance
- Minor tag damage: partial (coins/materials)
- No contribution: no drop unless the party agreed otherwise
- Boss encounters: all active participants get at least one reward bundle
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Loot Naming and Affix Grammar:
## Loot Naming and Affix Grammar
Name and enchant by rarity: Common uses material + type; Uncommon adds one earned descriptor; Rare owns a property name; Epic names its technique; Legendary carries a title and history spoken in-scene; Mythic adds an epithet and attracts attention; Unique names itself at its earned story moment.
Match affixes to function. Weapons: elemental edges, on-hit techniques, conditional strikes, costly lifedrain. Armor: mitigation, elemental wards, conditional defense and mobility trades. Accessories: resource flow, professions, social presence, perception and tracking. Backwear follows Back Equipment.
Keep regional fingerprints: Emberwake runs hot, Tidelace flows, Yukishiro endures, Riftmaw feels slightly wrong. Named monsters may carry a signature piece discoverable through rumors. Vary affix families across consecutive drops. Rare+ Blessing synergy matches the wearer's actual Blessing.
Crafted pieces: make the thing the player asked for, in the form they named (a Guard Collar is a collar, never a sword). The player chooses form and theme, never numbers: bonuses come from Item Power Ceilings for the rarity earned. Give each piece its own name; never reuse a name already on an item in the inventory or recent story. Quality follows the crafter's skill and roll: under 20 Common to Uncommon, 20 to 44 up to Rare, 45 to 74 up to Epic, 75 and up to Legendary on a great or critical success, level with Riftlight loot of the same tier.
MATERIALS ARE A FIXED CATALOG: ore, metal, gems, crystal, wood, herbs, cloth and hide already exist as Material items. Use the one that fits by its exact name and say where it came from in prose: iron dug on the coast is Iron Ore, never 'Harbor Iron Ore'. Never mint a regional, renamed or new one. Only a monster part may take a new name, when no existing part fits.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Acquisition and Payment Consent:
## Acquisition and Payment Consent
The player's inventory and purse change on the player's word and nothing else. Two separate gates: things coming in, and money going out.

### Items enter only on acceptance
- An item enters the inventory when the player picks it up, loots it, or is offered it and says yes. Narrating that something was offered, left for them, pressed into their hands, or is theirs now does NOT put it in the inventory.
- When an NPC offers, gives, or bequeaths something, describe the offer and STOP. The player answers. Until they answer, the item belongs to the NPC and appears in no inventory line.
- Quest rewards, drops and payouts are added at the moment the player collects them. If the scene ends first, the reward stays with whoever holds it and is named so it can be retrieved later.
- Never add an item the player declined, ignored, or walked away from. Declining is a real answer, it sticks, and the item stays where it was.
- Items leave a player's inventory only on that player's word; no NPC takes a part from it.
- Never invent an item into the player's possession to make a scene work. If they need a rope they do not have, they do not have a rope.
- Contract terms hold exactly: if the terms say the player keeps the items, delivering them deducts nothing, and pay named in the terms is paid on completion.
- COMBAT LOOT IS THE EXCEPTION. A Riftlight drop or body loot from a fight the player won is theirs on the spot; present the drop block and move on. Do not ask permission to pick up what they just earned. This gate is for gifts, offers, handouts, found property and anything belonging to someone else.

### Money leaves only on confirmation
- State the price. Stop. The player must agree to that price before one coin moves.
- Asking, browsing, haggling or examining are NOT purchases.
- Deduct exactly the agreed amount, once, and state the remaining balance after anything that matters.
- Fees, tolls, bribes, repairs and lodging follow the same gate. No off-screen charges.
- If the player cannot afford something, say so before the sale rather than moving money and reporting a shortfall afterward.

### Never award the same thing twice
- A reward is granted once, at one moment. Do not narrate a payment in prose and then repeat it in a drop block, and do not restate it in a later summary as though it just arrived.
- If an objective and its parent quest complete in the same scene, pay out once for the work that earned it, not once for each.
- Containers, bodies and caches are emptied exactly once; revisiting grants nothing.
- Check before granting: duplicated coin is the most common mistake.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Item Provenance and Living Gear:
## Item Provenance and Living Gear
Items accumulate history: gear that has lived is worth more than gear that dropped.
- Track provenance on significant items: who forged it, who carried it, what it has done; NPCs recognize its story.
- Named deeds upgrade identity, not stats: smiths ask to study it, collectors bid, enemies plan around it.
- Evolution has gates: Epic+ items marked as able to evolve do so only through a milestone deed, resonance with the bearer's Blessing, or a master crafter's rework: each with a stated cost and an on-screen moment.
- Wear is story, not bookkeeping: gear shows honest use, and repair happens through crafters and scenes, never silent stat rot.
- Heirlooms and gifts carry social weight; losing one is a story event with a recovery path.
- An item that holds a creature (soul sphere, egg, contract, whistle) names that creature and its kind in its description from the moment it is made; summoning from it produces exactly that creature.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Inventory and Currency Integrity:
## Inventory and Currency Integrity
Core rule: the player's inventory and money are protected state. Nothing leaves the inventory, items, equipment, currency, quest items, without an explicit, on-screen cause the player can see and respond to.
- Never silently remove, consume, or retroactively spend items or coin. No off-screen taxes, dues, upkeep, spoilage, or fees unless the player agreed to them in a scene.
- Theft, pickpocketing, tolls, bribes, confiscation, cursed trades, and demon-contract costs are legitimate only as visible scene events with counterplay (notice, resist, chase, negotiate) and a recovery path (track the thief, appeal the fine, buy it back, reclaim by quest). Stolen items persist in the world and can be recovered.
- Quest turn-ins consume only the named quest item and quantity. Crafting consumes only listed ingredients. Consumables are spent only when the player uses them.
- Companions, party members, and NPCs never take from the player's inventory or purse on their own: borrowing requires an on-screen ask and player consent, and borrowed items are tracked and returnable.
- Equipment does not vanish on scene transitions, time skips, captures, or travel. If a scene must disarm the player (arrest, formal event, bathhouse), name where the gear is held and return it, or make its recovery an explicit objective.
- Death: item and coin losses follow the death rules and the game mode, never more.
- Item names are in Title Case. Category is one of Currency, Armor, Weapon, Tool, Consumable, Accessory, Relic, Material, Treasure, Gift or Familiar, capitalized as written; a slot name is never a category. An item the player already holds is that item, never a new copy.
- RECURRING-ADD GUARD: an item only offered, displayed for sale, set on a counter or left for the player is NOT owned and must NEVER be added again on a later turn. If a summary or scene still shows coins, a slip, or goods "on the counter," they are not in the inventory; re-reading that state grants nothing. Grant any such item exactly once, on the single turn the player actually takes it.
- Transaction direction is exact: when the player BUYS X for Y, add X and remove Y; when the player SELLS X for Y, remove X and add Y. A sale removes the sold item and adds the agreed coin: never the reverse, and never leave the sold item in inventory unless the sale explicitly fails.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Merchant Stock and Commerce Texture:
## Merchant Stock and Commerce Texture
Generate commerce with character: what a merchant sells, stocks, and refuses says who they are.
- Stock follows the merchant and the region: a Portmaris harbor stall carries tide-charms and import oddities; an Emberglass forge counter carries honest steel and one masterwork the smith won't sell yet; a Starfall Bazaar table carries things with unclear provenance and one item that shouldn't exist.
- Browsing renders three to five concrete wares with names and prices in world currency: always priced before purchase, per inventory integrity. One item per browse should be aspirational (visibly beyond current means) to give saving a target.
- Haggling is social play with bounds: personality, relationship, reputation, and profession shift prices within honest margins: a merchant can refuse, counter, sweeten with extras, or remember the exchange. Haggling never completes a sale the player didn't accept and never drains a wallet.
- Commissions are content: special orders create timelines, material hunts, progress visits, and a delivery scene. A commissioned item arrives with the crafter's pride attached.
- Merchants have supply lives: restocks, shortages, festival exclusives, and a rival vendor. Changes are never retroactive: owned items keep their nature.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.Back Equipment:
## Back Equipment
Use slot back, category Armor, quantity one for capes, cloaks, shawls and separate mantles. Back equips alongside Body; only one Back item supplies bonuses. Unequipping it ends its bonuses but keeps the item and its stored bonuses. Carried spares do not stack. Follow item slots: coats, robes and full-body armor stay Body; hoods stay Head. Voidweave Shadowmantle remains Body.
Favor weather protection, stealth, performance, etiquette and small situational utility over large health or damage boosts. Describe limits; appearance alone grants no flight, invisibility or immunity. Narrative effects do not create unlisted stat modifiers. Backwear shares the Armor loot allocation, never extra drops. Outfitters and tailors stock them; Tailoring or Gift Crafting commissions use regional materials. A catalog entry or offer is not ownership. No automatic starting cape. Backpacks, quivers, wings and relics keep their own rules; this slot is never storage, ammunition or a second relic slot.

summarization.custom:
## Summary Priorities
- Preserve character voice, emotional beats, and relationship developments; not just plot events
- Track romantic relationships: who is interested in the protagonist, what stage each relationship has reached, recent emotionally significant moments, unresolved tension
- Note companion dynamics: how romantic interests interact with each other, alliances and rivalries between them, any shifts in group dynamics
- Record physical and emotional intimacy milestones for each relationship
- Track NPC emotional states: who's jealous, who's content, who's planning something romantic, who's feeling neglected
- Flag unresolved story threads: pending confessions, unanswered feelings, jealousy building toward confrontation, relationship moments interrupted
- Note the protagonist's reputation and how NPCs perceive them: admired, desired, feared, mysterious, trusted
- Record the protagonist's growing power and its effect on how people treat them
- Maintain awareness of the isekai context: old-world knowledge, cheat skill development, the Rebirth phenomenon's ongoing mystery

## Tone Memory
- Track the current emotional register of the story: is it in a comedic arc, a romantic slow burn, a combat escalation, a political intrigue phase, or a quiet character development stretch?
- Note recent tonal peaks: the last big laugh, the last dramatic moment, the last romantic near-miss, the last fight, so the AI can vary pacing instead of repeating the same beat
- Record running jokes, callbacks, inside references between the protagonist and specific NPCs: these are critical for dialogue continuity and the private language of growing closeness

## World State Tracking
- Track time of day, current weather mood, and recent travel: these shape scene atmosphere
- Note the protagonist's current guild rank, reputation shifts, faction standings, and any political consequences of recent actions
- Record what the protagonist owns, wears, and carries that NPCs would notice or comment on
- Track unresolved quest threads, promises made to NPCs, and real debts in either direction (a loan or price agreed, a favor sworn); a finished quest, delivered item, gift or shared meal leaves no debt, and a paid debt is dropped
- Note which companions are present and their current mood: a jealous companion doesn't suddenly become cheerful between summaries
- Track actual party members separately from opening cast, local contacts, quest givers, dates, and temporary escorts. Record the player's invitation or acceptance, the NPC's agreement, and the travel arrangement's scope. Friendly interaction, quest completion, scene presence, and the word companion do not prove recruitment. Preserve established deliberate party choices; do not invent new agreements or erase valid existing ones. Note where local contacts remain when the player leaves.

## What Not To Lose
- Never summarize away a character's emotional arc into a flat label. "Rin is jealous" loses the texture. "Rin has been quieter since the protagonist spent the evening with Lilira, and she left the tavern early without her usual loud goodbye" preserves it
- Preserve specific moments that changed a relationship: the exact words don't need to survive, but the emotional shift they caused does
- Keep track of what the protagonist has learned about each NPC's hidden depths, secrets, or vulnerabilities: these are irreplaceable relationship milestones
- Record when NPCs have seen the protagonist at their best or worst: these shared experiences shape how they speak to each other going forward
- Track the small accumulated details: nicknames that stuck, gifts that were kept, habits that became routine, preferences someone remembered


## Relationship State Vocabulary (Intent Engine Dependencies)
When present in the story, track these states explicitly; the character behavior engine reads them from summaries:
- Relationship stage per bonded NPC, by name (Noticed to Heartbound, or Cold, Distrustful, Hostile, Fated Enemy)
- Confession aftermath state: answered-yes, answered-no, or unanswered, and who confessed to whom
- Bruised bonds: when the player wounded a relationship (broken promise, betrayal, cruel word), note the bond is bruised, what caused it, and any door-open gesture the NPC left
- Open threads (unanswered confessions, unpaid debts, unkept promises, half-revealed secrets): name the thread and who holds it, and drop it once it is resolved
- Tokens and standing objects: gifts given, tokens worn or removed, borrowed items, who gave what to whom and its current status
Record these as specific facts, not labels: "Kanade confessed at the lantern bridge, unanswered" preserves what "Kanade likes the player" loses. Only track what the story actually established; do not pad summaries with empty relationship bookkeeping.
summarization.Quest Persistence:
Generated quests stay part of the living world until completed, failed, abandoned, or replaced by later developments.

NPCs remember favors they asked for. Companions remember promises and shared goals. Factions remember assignments. Rivals pursue their own aims. Hidden NPC threads keep progressing even while undiscovered when appropriate.

An active quest is the player's business. When the player's own action touches it, its people and places reflect it through dialogue, rumors, letters, discoveries, changed locations or world consequences, never UI-style exposition. Otherwise nobody brings it up, and it never stops the player from doing anything else.

Objectives may complete, be added, be replaced, or link as the story evolves. Connected quests reference one another when it fits, forming natural chains without spoiling future story.

Never silently drop an active quest. Keep one line for each: who gave it, the goal, the place, and the last step taken. Prefer updating existing quests over creating duplicates, and preserve continuity across the whole world.
summarization.Quest Recognition:
## Quest Recognition: Player Choice First
Create or initialize a journal quest only after the player deliberately chooses that specific task or commits to a concrete goal. Record the evidence of the player's choice. An NPC request, discovered posting, rumor, general request for work, guild registration, location visit, passing interest, or a narrator-assumed agreement is not acceptance. Keep unchosen possibilities in scene memory without creating a quest. When uncertain, wait.

An authored quest is eligible only when its actual premise, prerequisites, source and objective match established on-screen events. Matching a name, NPC, district, or destination is insufficient. Do not force the stored questStatement or backstory into unrelated narration. If the player chooses an eligible authored task, preserve its exact name and objective; never create a duplicate with that name. If their chosen goal is different, use a distinct scene-appropriate quest without borrowing an authored opening's history.

Opening-specific quests belong only to the selected opening. Retired openings cannot be unlocked by walking into their old location. Already accepted quests remain valid. Follow-up availability does not mean acceptance; record an explicit choice to continue. Never complete an unaccepted quest or issue rewards for an offer. Hidden NPC knowledge stays hidden. Preserve accepted quests and deliberate commitments; extend an existing quest rather than duplicate it.
summarization.Generated Cast Persistence:
## Generated Cast Persistence
NPCs created during play are as real as authored ones and must survive summarization intact.
- Carry forward every named NPC the player has interacted with: name, role, location, and enough appearance to render them identically on the next visit. A generated NPC who loses their record returns as a different person, and the player notices immediately.
- Preserve their basicInfo template lines, especially Speaking Style and Combat Role. A local who was gruff and laconic does not come back chatty.
- Preserve what passed between them and the player: conversations that mattered, favors given or owed, friction, and current disposition.
- If summary space runs short, compress an NPC's history rather than dropping the NPC. A name with one line beats a stranger with none.
- Authored NPCs are never at risk. This rule protects the generated cast, which in practice is far larger.
- Preserve gender explicitly for every NPC carried forward. A name alone is insufficient: many names are gender-ambiguous, and a lost gender reference will be guessed from the name, often incorrectly. State he/she or male/female at least once per NPC entry.
summarization.Completion Condition Evaluation:
## Completion: One Visible Finishing Event
An authored quest has one finishing objective shown in its journal. Evaluate that event in the latest narrated scene; do not ask the classifier to reconstruct several events from earlier turns or satisfy a historical checklist simultaneously.
The accepted-status guard is mandatory and separate from the one semantic completion check. Hidden, available, rejected, abandoned or completed quests cannot progress or pay rewards. Native completion queries are intentionally blank where an authored accepted-only trigger owns completion; blank never means complete.
An event must actually happen on screen. Plans, promises and hypothetical outcomes do not count. An explicit answer or acceptance DOES count when that is the displayed objective; accepting a quest is not otherwise completing its work. Registration alone is not acceptance of a first Guild work contract.
When the displayed objective offers alternative resolutions, any one enacted resolution satisfies it. Do not add a second requirement for NPC praise, public recognition, romance, faction reactions or a later report unless that response or report IS the displayed finishing event. Those other beats remain story material, not hidden completion gates.
Do not fabricate missing events to finish a quest. Once the displayed event occurs, do not delay its completion to replay earlier investigation, travel or training. Reward once through normal quest progression. Never complete another chapter or recruit someone as a side effect.
For future quests, write one observable terminal event and use the same objective in its completion test. If independently tracked stages are essential, use separate optional chapters with their own finishing events; do not pack an entire chain into one semantic condition.
summarization.State Continuity:
## State Continuity
Hard state must survive summarization verbatim: emotions can compress, hard state cannot.
- Always carry forward exactly: current money, named significant items (equipped gear, quest items, gifts received, heirlooms), and who currently holds anything borrowed, stolen, or confiscated: including where held gear is stored and the stated recovery path.
- Preserve numbers as numbers: prices agreed, debts owed in coin (and to whom), rewards promised but unpaid, rival win/loss/unsettled scores.
- Track commitments as facts: promises made by and to the player, formal courtship steps completed, contracts signed (especially demon contracts and their exact strings), oaths sworn, deadlines accepted.
- Preserve each major NPC's active personal goal and its last known progress, plus faction standings that changed this session and every earned title the player holds.
- Never let summarization silently spend, lose, or resolve anything: if state changed, the summary says how and on-screen where.
- Recurring interface elements shown in the story (status windows, panels, readouts of rank, level, stats, or active interface quests) are hard state: carry their latest displayed values and any open interface quests through every summary so later turns keep them consistent and the interface never silently disappears.
- Record claims with their speaker (the guard said the smith is his brother); the player's questions stay questions, never facts.
- Record contract terms exactly: what is delivered, what the player keeps, what is paid. The same for a Guild posting the player has read: its target, place, rank and pay.
- Bound creatures are hard state: for every summoning item, soul sphere, egg, contract or tamed companion, carry the creature's name, exact kind and appearance, and where it is (inside the item, at the player's side, or dismissed).
- Craft and lesson progress is hard state: what has been made or learned so far, so the next session picks up there and nothing is taught twice.
- Shape is hard state: for anyone who can change shape (human form, dragon form, beast form, war form, hidden form), always record which shape they are in now and where gear that does not fit that shape was left.
- What a summon, minion or bonded creature can do is hard state as first established: whether it speaks, thinks for itself or only obeys. A silent one stays silent.
summarization.Location Continuity:
## Local References and Travel Intent
Resolve movement from the party's current region, location, area and established scene first. "Go through the door", "go to the vault", "cross the bridge", "enter the room" and similar ordinary phrases refer to a nearby object or reachable local area, not a world-wide name search. Capitalization or a shared noun is not evidence of a distant destination.
An authored area belongs only to its parent location. Its qualified name identifies that place; a short local nickname is valid only when that parent is already established. Never switch the parent location, region or coordinates merely because a remote area shares a word. If no local target is established, ask one brief question or describe the visible local exits; do not select an unrelated landmark.
A distant destination requires an explicit destination or an unambiguous destination already agreed in the scene. Naming it starts a journey, not arrival. Preserve distance, time, access requirements and the current travel mode; only an established, actually used travel ability or transport can change those rules. Mentioning a place, reading a map or discussing a quest is not movement.
The sealed door on Riftmaw floor 97 is reachable through its deep-dungeon approach, not through ordinary doors elsewhere. Vaults belong to their named estates, exchanges, halls or dungeons. Local room movement must not trigger arrival quests at another site.

## Location Continuity
Preserve the current region, parent location, qualified area and coordinates, plus any destination still being travelled toward. Keep current position separate from mentioned places, remembered places, quest settings and intended destinations. A door, room, vault or bridge in local narration never changes the parent location merely by name similarity. Record arrival only after actual travel or an established transport event resolves.
summarization.Company Tracking:
## Company Tracking
If the player founds or joins an Adventurer Company, keep its name, crest, rank (Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Mythril), hall, members who agreed to join, rivals, and active Company Contracts. Membership is not party membership: list Company members separately from who travels with the player. Never drop or rename a Company once it exists; record rank changes only when the story shows them.
summarization.How This Story Began:
## How This Story Began
Keep one sentence at the top of every summary, unchanged for the whole game, saying how this story opened and how the player first stood with the people in that opening: for example summoned and welcomed as the fifth hero, summoned and read as zero and paid to leave, struck from the Hero Party's roster, or arrived in town as a stranger. Some authored characters have different lines for different openings, and this sentence is how the right ones are chosen later. Never rewrite it into another opening and never blend two.
summarization.Who Knows What:
## Who Knows What
Keep a short running line of the player's secrets and who holds each: that they are Reborn, their old world, each Blessing and cheat skill, a true name or true form, a crime. Put a name against a secret only when the story showed that person being told it, watching it happen, or working it out from evidence in the scene. Everyone else does not know, and a later scene may not play them as if they did. Someone met after this point starts with nothing. The same holds for what the player did: a deed is known to those who saw it or were told by someone who did, and a rumor needs time to travel (a town in a day).
summarization.Settled Debts:
## Settled Debts
Record completed payments for rooms, meals, tolls, or gear as settled transactions, never as ongoing obligations. When any debt, tab, or favor is paid off, log an explicit closing memory stating that the account with that person is settled in full and nothing further is owed.

generateLearnedAbilities.custom:
## Ability Acquisition
- New abilities should feel like genuine breakthroughs: a flash of insight under pressure, a technique finally clicking, a dormant power awakening
- Abilities reflect fighting style, personality, and lived experience: a protector learns shields, a trickster learns illusions
- Combo abilities develop when characters train together or fight side by side repeatedly
- Cheat skill evolution should feel like a season finale power-up: dramatic, visually spectacular, game-changing

## Ability Naming
- Name a technique for what it DOES or how it looks in motion, in two or three words: a verb, a shape, a body part, a tool, an element, the place it was learned.
- Variety is a rule. Read the names already on the sheet first: a new name shares no word with any of them, with the last ability granted, or with the character's Blessing, class, race, title or cheat skill. Only an evolution keeps its line (Mend, then Radiant Mend).
- Rank words are not names. Never build a name from Sovereign, Sovereignty, Monarch, Emperor, King, Queen, Lord, Royal, Crown, Throne, Dominion, Supreme, Absolute, Ultimate, Divine or God. A technique earns its weight from what it does.
- Rotate the pattern and never use one twice running: element and form (Frost Barrier), motion and target (Piercing Thrust), an image (Falling Petal Step), a tool or body part (Second Knuckle), a place or teacher (Emberglass Hold), a plain passive (Danger Sense).
- Character-specific abilities reflect who they are; a passive stays understated.

## Power Scaling
- Early abilities: powerful but straightforward: a single strong attack, a defensive buff, a utility skill
- Mid-level abilities: add complexity: area effects, conditional triggers, stance changes, resource trade-offs
- High-level abilities: dramatic and costly (ultimate attacks, transformation states, domain effects)
- All abilities have clear limits (cooldowns, mana costs, physical toll, setup requirements), even overpowered ones
generateLearnedAbilities.Blessing Generation:
## Blessing Design Principles

- Every Blessing is unique to its bearer. No two people have the same Blessing, even if they share an element or category
- Blessings are not just "fire but stronger"; they are specific, personal, and reflect something about who the person is or what they needed when the Blessing awakened
- Reborn Blessings are categorically different from native Luxcellia Blessings. They carry an alien hum: otherworldly, slightly wrong, undeniably powerful
- Blessings have personality. A fire Blessing from rage behaves differently than one from protectiveness. The emotion that triggers awakening shapes the power's character permanently

## Blessing Categories

### Common Blessings (Most Adventurers)
- Single-element enhancement: fire touch, stone skin, wind step
- Physical augmentation: enhanced strength, accelerated reflexes, environmental adaptation
- Minor utility: perfect direction sense, temperature tolerance, animal affinity
- These are useful, limited, and well-understood

### Rare Blessings (Notable Individuals)
- Dual-element or hybrid effects: frostfire, storm-earth, shadow-light
- Significant augmentation: brief invulnerability, sustained flight, battlefield teleportation
- Specialized utility: monster empathy, structural intuition, combat precognition
- These draw attention. Guild recruiters notice. Academy scholars request interviews

### Unique Blessings (One Per Generation)
- Conceptual effects: time manipulation, probability alteration, causality interference
- Reality-level power: spatial reconstruction, existence denial, soul-level effects
- These change the political landscape. Factions mobilize. The Church declares prophecy

### Reborn Cheat Skills
- These break Luxcellia's rules. They operate on principles from another world
- Cheat skills feel game-like: stat multiplication, skill acquisition, inventory manipulation, crafting intuition, knowledge download, ability copying
- The power ceiling is higher than native Blessings. The learning curve is steeper. The side effects are stranger
- A cheat skill should feel like the protagonist brought a different game's mechanics into this world

## Blessing Awakening Narration

- Under mortal danger: explosive, immediate, survival-driven. The power saves the protagonist before they understand what happened
- Through emotional crisis: slower build, then overwhelming surge. The power responds to what they needed most
- Through discovery: gradual realization that something has been different for a while
- Through choice: the protagonist reaches for something inside and finds it. Rarest and most deliberate

## Blessing Growth

- Blessings grow through use, emotional stakes, and pivotal moments; not grinding
- Evolution is qualitative, not a stat increase. The power does something new, not just more
- Never reveal a Blessing's full potential immediately. Layer reveals across the story
generateLearnedAbilities.Combination and Synergy Arts:
## Combination and Synergy Arts
The Combination Technique Discovery trigger owns the spontaneous first moment: this governs what happens after.
- Practiced combos mature: a combination repeated in training becomes a reliable joint technique owned by BOTH characters. It has a name only if the player gives it one.
- Bond gates depth: combo ceiling tracks the bond ladder. Strangers manage crude overlaps; trusted partners layer timing; devoted pairs field techniques that read each other mid-motion. A combo above the bond's stage should not exist yet.
- Elemental fusion follows a grammar, not a table: adjacent elements blend (ember + storm arcs, tide + frost glaciates), opposed elements (radiant + shadow) fuse rarely, dangerously, and memorably. Fusion names honor both lines.
- Formation arts: parties of three or more can develop one signature formation, a named opening, a rescue pattern, a finisher, drilled on-screen before it works under pressure.
- Costs split honestly across users; a combo is never cheaper than its parts, only better-shaped.
- Combos run on trust: a fractured bond misfires the technique at the worst moment: the drama writes itself. Repairing the bond repairs the art.
- Combos live on the characters' sheets, never as world ability records.
generateLearnedAbilities.Evolution Trees and Stage Gates:
## Evolution Trees and Stage Gates
Evolution is how a favorite ability keeps up with its owner. Offer it readily; players should see it happen.
- Ready: the character has used the ability in several meaningful scenes AND its governing skill has reached the next threshold: Stage II at 20, Stage III at 45, Apex at 75. When an ability becomes ready, let the story show it: it comes easier, a new shape flickers at the edge of the cast.
- Evolve: once ready, any of these triggers it: a training scene the player asks for, a teacher's correction, or a great or critical success with the ability under pressure.
- Each stage is a real upgrade and a new learned entry: a new name that keeps the lineage (Mend, then Radiant Mend, then Dawn Mending), priced per Pricing, and one size band stronger (a Basic heal becomes a Moderate heal at the same cost). The earlier form stays on the sheet.
- Stage III branches by how the character fights (a guard art becomes a bulwark for a protector or a riposte web for a duelist); the branch is exclusive. Apex comes once per campaign tier, is named for a deed, and carries one fitting tradeoff.
- Blessings and cheat skills evolve under their own rules. NPC authored abilities evolve in narration only, never as new records. In 📊 The System mode, evolution notices arrive via the window format.
generateLearnedAbilities.Signature Moves and Training Arcs:
## Personal Style and Training Arcs
The AUTHORED roster is a fixed arsenal: the world file's ability records are never edited at runtime. Runtime growth comes from granting learned abilities to the character sheet and from how abilities are learned, personalized, and evolved. Prefer surfacing a fitting authored ability over inventing a new technique; evolutions are always new entries.
- Personal style: a character's way of using an ability they already have (footwork, timing, a habit) shows in the narration, on the same record and under its own name. A real refinement is an evolution and gets its own entry (see Evolution).
- Training arcs have structure: plateau → frustration → insight or teacher → breakthrough under stakes. Montages are legal and fun, but the breakthrough itself always happens on-screen and costs something (exhaustion, humility, a favor owed).
- Mentors teach from their own kit: an NPC can only teach abilities or techniques consistent with their own record and history: learning from Forge Master Kaguro produces smith-craft, not shadow magic.
- Duress unlocks follow anime law: a power awakening mid-crisis is earned only if it was foreshadowed (a flicker, a dream, a mentor's remark). Unforeshadowed rescues are forbidden: plant first, pay off later.
- Evolution is gated: cheat-skill and Blessing evolutions require a milestone deed, an emotional threshold, or a ritual with a cost, and each evolution should sharpen identity, not just add damage. Respect the power bands in generateNewNPC.
generateLearnedAbilities.Lost, Forbidden, and Inherited Arts:
## Lost, Forbidden, and Inherited Arts
The rarest acquisitions are chase content: abilities as treasure, with provenance and strings.
- Inherited arts: a dying master's last lesson, a technique sealed in a memento, a form taught at a graveside. Inheritance is a scene with weight: the art arrives carrying the teacher's story, and using it honors or haunts.
- Lost schools: manuals, murals, and training halls recovered from ruins, dungeon vaults, and forbidden library sections. Treat recoverable arts like high-tier loot, rumored, hunted, and guarded, and give every lost school one reason it was lost.
- Forbidden arts: some techniques are watched. Learning one is a choice with institutional consequences: the Church tracks certain magics, the Guild flags certain kill-arts, and using a forbidden form in public is a reputation event that can earn a title nobody wants. The power is real; so is the file someone opens. Outlawed is never unavailable: the cost of a forbidden art is the world's answer, not a refusal.
- Monster-derived techniques: keen observers can adapt what beasts do: the alpha's feint, the wyrm's coil, the mimic's patience. Learned through ecology moments and hunts, named with the creature's honor.
- Reborn anomaly arts: old-world logic expressed as technique: probability sense, engineered leverage, chemistry nobody here has words for. Uniquely alien, quietly unsettling to native masters.
- Every rare art states its provenance and its string in the same breath, per the world's temptation rules.
generateLearnedAbilities.Skill Acquisition and Exact Skill Naming:
## Skill Acquisition Is Not Optional
When an action is credited to a skill the character already owns, no new skill is ever a candidate and acquisition silently never fires. Close that path.
- The world skill list is the vocabulary. If a skill exists there, it is the correct name for that work: Lightning Magic for bolts and chains, Storm Magic for the weather around them, Enchanting for imbuing items, Rune Carving for cut runes, Inscription for scrolls and seals, Alchemy for brewed consumables. Use the exact listed name.
- Credit the work to the skill that actually governs it, trained or not. A character with Arcane Magic who throws lightning is doing Lightning Magic untrained. A character with Alchemy who imbues a blade is doing Enchanting untrained. Never fold that work back into the owned neighbor.
- On the second successful untrained use of a listed skill the character lacks, put that skill forward as newly learned. Do not wait for a milestone, teacher, or quest; repetition IS the qualification, and the discovery earns a short beat.
- This applies to professions and crafts exactly as it applies to magic schools.
- Never invent a new skill when a listed one covers the work. Invent only when nothing in the list fits, and then make it a whole discipline as broad as a listed skill (Glassblowing, Puppetry), never one move, style or variant of a listed skill. It takes the attribute and type of its nearest listed skill, so the character's strengths carry into it.
- ARCANE IS NOT A CATCH-ALL. Arcane covers raw mana, wards, constructs, dispelling and counterspelling, nothing else. Never credit it for elemental, shadow, illusion, space, gravity, soul, time or crafting work, and never make it a character's specialty school. A specialist class ranks its own school above Arcane; Arcane leads only for anti-magic and raw-mana builds. Elemental Magic is the same: multi-element work only, never a stand-in for a specialist the character lacks.
This pairs with generateActionInfo Magic School Routing; edit both together.
generateLearnedAbilities.Teaching, Students, and Founding a Style:
## Teaching, Students, and Founding a Style
The player's techniques can outlive the player's scenes: teaching is progression, legacy, and drama.
- Teaching costs something real: time, patience, and exposure: explaining how your technique works means someone else knows how it works. A taught secret can spread; choose students accordingly.
- Teaching builds: bond gains per the magnitude anchors, a student who grows into covering your weaknesses, and the strange pride of watching your form performed by other hands.
- Students diverge by design: a taught technique mutates to fit the student: different body, different heart, different Stage III branch. Never a copy; the divergence is the reward.
- Sharing a signature move shares your name: a student throwing YOUR named technique in public is a statement the world reads, and rivals test students to measure the teacher.
- Founding a style is late-game legacy: name the school, take first students, claim a training hall (a home or property serves beautifully), and let the world react: guild recognition, rival schools, challenge matches, and a founder's title that follows the player forever.
- NPCs seek good teachers: reputation, titles, and public signature moves draw would-be students per the student trigger: teaching is always opt-in.
generateLearnedAbilities.Prefer the Authored Roster and Power Ban:
## Prefer the Authored Roster and Power Bands
The authored roster covers every skill from level 1 to 100, and its ladder abilities unlock by themselves as skills rise.
- New technique: if an authored ability fits the character's skill, style and level, point to it by name instead of inventing a copy. Invent when the roster has no match: a Blessing facet, a Reborn anomaly, a personal technique, a combination.
- Evolutions, refinements and combinations are never roster copies: always grant them as new learned entries on the character's sheet (see Evolution).
## Pricing (the roster is the scale)
A learned ability's bonus matches authored abilities at the character's current level in its governing skill: skill 1-19 about +3 to +8; 20-49 +5 to +15; 50-69 +25 to +40; 70-79 +40 to +55; 80-89 +60 to +75; 90-100 +85 to +100. Group, zone or scene-long effects sit at the low end; a combination uses the lower skill. An evolution's bonus is at least its earlier form's bonus plus 3. Cooldowns: 3-6 below skill 50, 6-10 from 50, 10-15 from 90. Heals, restoration and shields use the Health and Mana size bands for the mana tier they cost. Never hand a capstone to a low-level character. An invented skill starts at 0 with no ladder, so price its abilities at the character's level in the listed skill it grew from (a dance born of performance 35 prices as 35), and offer it one new ability as it first reaches 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100, on those same bands. Never end a learned ability with a [Skill: N] tag: that tag marks when an authored ability unlocks. Name the governing skill in the description's own words instead.
generateLearnedAbilities.Themed Ability Schools and How They Are:
## Themed Ability Schools and How They Are Learned
Learned abilities belong to the character's sheet at runtime and NEVER add records to the world's authored ability roster. Grant freely as the story needs, but route through the authored roster first (see Prefer the Authored Roster).
### The Schools (theme every new ability into a recognizable line)
- Elemental lines: ember, tide, frost, storm, shadow, radiant: matching the world's affix families, each with a regional heartland where it learns faster.
- Blade and weapon arts: stances, draws, guards, and finishers keyed to the Signature Weapon; weapon arts are learned bodies-first, in bruises.
- Blessing facets: new expressions of the bearer's unique Blessing: always personal, never generic (per Blessing rules).
- Profession techniques: craft-born powers: a smith's heat-reading, a cook's fortifying meals, a jeweler's flaw-sight.
- Beast and bond arts: tamer calls, pack tactics, shared senses: grown from relationships, not study.
- Contract and pact powers: clauses made castable; every pact ability carries its string in the description, per the world's temptation rules.
- Reborn anomalies: old-world logic expressed as power: probability sense, systems thinking, muscle memory from a life nobody here lived.
- Support and ward arts: healing, barriers, blessings-of-others; the school of people who protect. A shield, ward, barrier or hardening guards on the turn it is raised, and holding it costs the next turn's action: never write hit counts, layers, durations, or wards left waiting to trigger later, because combat damage cannot track them.
### How Learning Happens
- Mentorship: an NPC teaches only from their own kit and history: lessons cost time, humility, or favors.
- Practice thresholds: skill levels earned in play unlock the school's next technique; montages allowed, breakthrough on-screen.
- Insight under stakes: duress unlocks are legal ONLY when foreshadowed: the flicker, the dream, the mentor's remark.
- Study: libraries, scrolls, academies: knowledge-school abilities want a reader, and forbidden sections want a price.
- Awakening: Blessings and Reborn anomalies surface facets at emotional thresholds.
- Bond and combination: companions who train and fight together develop paired techniques.
### Pacing and Power
New abilities arrive at the character's tier and power band, properly costed (mana, ~6-turn cooldowns per the vitality norms), roughly one per meaningful milestone: never one per fight. Every learned ability names its school, its cost, and the moment it was earned.
generateLearnedAbilities.Misfires, Half-Learned Techniques, and B:
## Misfires, Half-Learned Techniques, and Bad Habits
Learning that goes wrong is content: competence is earned on-screen, and the middle of the curve is the fun part.
- The half-learned state is playable: a technique can be used before it is mastered: at double cost, needing a full stance, or failing under pressure in characterful ways. Let players choose to gamble on it.
- Misfires have personality: the fireball that whistles, the step that overshoots into a market stall, the barrier that works perfectly and faces the wrong way. Comedy in downtime, real danger in battle: context decides.
- Bad habits are real: a flawed teacher or self-taught shortcut bakes an error into the form, and UNLEARNING is harder than learning: a correction arc with a better teacher, frustration, and one honest scene where the old habit almost costs everything.
- Overreach is honest but temporary: pushing past mastery strains the body per the overcasting norms: visible, referenced afterward, never permanent by accident.
- Mastery is visible: as a technique matures, it quiets: wasted motion disappears, the tells shrink. Veterans can READ how learned an opponent's technique is, and a half-learned form is an exploitable one, both ways.

generateFactionDetails.custom:
## Adventurer Companies
When the story needs an Adventurer Company that is not authored, create it as a minor faction and keep it fixed once named.
- basicInfo opens with a tag line: [Adventurer Company · Guild rank: Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold or Mythril · Specialty: ... · Hall: Location, Area], then two to four sentences on reputation, crest and style, then Leader: and Members: lines naming people.
- The hall is a real location and area in the world; small Companies use an inn room or a guild hall table.
- hiddenInfo holds one problem the Company keeps quiet: a debt, a missing member, a grudge, a contract gone wrong.
- Companies met at random (in the Riftmaw, on the road, at a contract board) are real and recur with the same name, crest, rank and members.
- Prefer an authored Company when one fits: Stormblood Vanguard (the only Mythril Company), Deepwatch Lantern Company, The Flagon Irregulars, Tidecrest Company, The Gilded Caravan Company, The Frostfang Hunt, The Greenwake Company, The Vaunted Blade Company, The Emberforge Company.
- A player-founded Company belongs to the player: never invent its name, crest or members; record what the player chose.

Luxcellia.name: Luxcellia
Luxcellia.basicInfo:
## Basic Info
A vast fantasy continent where divine blessings, ancient dungeons, political intrigue, and romantic destiny collide in a world that feels like it was designed by a god with main-character syndrome!

Six great powers shape the continent: the glittering Crownveil Sovereignty with its scheming noble houses, the ancient Verdania Wilds where elves and beastkin guard primordial forests, the lawless Ashenmere Frontier where adventurers seek fortune in monster-infested borderlands, the wealthy Cerulean Coast where merchant lords and guild masters control trade, the holy Sanctum Ecclesia where the Church of the First Light wields divine authority, and the Twilight Dominion where the demon lord rules a sophisticated rival civilization.

Magic is common but mastery is rare. The Adventurer's Guild ranks heroes from F to S. Ancient dungeons called Riftmaws dot the landscape, spawning monsters and treasure. Divine Blessings grant unique powers to chosen individuals. And the Rebirth phenomenon keeps dropping souls from other worlds into Luxcellia: people with strange knowledge, unusual abilities, and a suspicious tendency to attract trouble, power, and beautiful companions wherever they go.

The world is gorgeous, dangerous, and far too tempting to ignore.

The Riftmaw Below.name: The Riftmaw Below
The Riftmaw Below.basicInfo: The Riftmaw's depths, under the Ashenmere Frontier: ninety-six floors and a door, reached only down the scaffolding at the Maw. Each region of this map is a set of floors the dungeon swallowed, stacked from the Shallows at the top to the 97th Floor at the bottom. Delvers come and go by the Maw and travel down from one floor set to the next; the Guild lift and the anchors shorten the way for those who earned them. Not all of it is the dungeon's: delver havens, monster holds and old sites sit on their own floors and stay put while the chambers around them shift.

Cerulean Coast.name: Cerulean Coast
Cerulean Coast.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-20 · Danger: Low]

A wealthy stretch of coastline dominated by port cities, floating markets, and the headquarters of the Adventurer's Guild. The Cerulean Trade Confederation runs things here: money talks, ships sail, and information flows through dockside taverns like water through a net. Portmaris, the largest city, is a gorgeous chaos of merchant princes, seafaring adventurers, exotic goods, and people from every corner of the continent rubbing shoulders in the marketplace. If you need something in Luxcellia, the Coast has it for sale.
Cerulean Coast.hiddenInfo: The Merchant Lords have been quietly funding both the Church and the Veilwalkers, playing every side to maintain their profit margins regardless of who wins the coming power shifts.

Verdania Wilds.name: Verdania Wilds
Verdania Wilds.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

Ancient forests stretching from horizon to horizon, home to elven enclaves hidden in the canopy and beastkin clans guarding the forest floor. The Wilds are beautiful and territorial: spirit beasts roam sacred groves, ancient trees hold memories in their rings, and outsiders who don't show proper respect tend to get lost in ways that compass and cartography can't fix. Somewhere in the deepest green, the Elder Tree watches over everything with patient, ageless attention.
Verdania Wilds.hiddenInfo: The Elder Tree is sentient and has been selectively guiding Reborn individuals toward the Wilds for reasons it hasn't shared with anyone.

Meikyo Spiritfen.name: Meikyo Spiritfen
Meikyo Spiritfen.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

A mystical wetland where the boundary between the living world and the spirit realm has worn thin as old cloth. Ghosts walk the mist-shrouded boardwalks alongside the living, spirit-lanterns float above canals that reflect two skies, and every shadow might be a door to somewhere else. The Spiritfen is beautiful in the way that dreams are beautiful: luminous, layered, and not entirely certain which reality it's displaying at any given moment. Foxkin mediums, wraithkin humans, and yokai citizens have built a culture that treats the supernatural as infrastructure rather than exception. The architecture is lacquered wood and paper screens, elegant and translucent, designed to let both light and spirits pass through. Romance here carries the weight of eternity: a mortal who falls for a spirit faces questions that have no easy answers, and the annual Lantern Drift festival turns the waterways into rivers of floating fire and whispered messages between the living and the dead.
Meikyo Spiritfen.hiddenInfo: The Spiritgate (the region's controlled crossing point) is not just a passage but a pressure valve. If it closes, the spiritual energy building up on both sides of the veil could cause a catastrophic merger of the mortal and spirit realms. The Covenant knows this but presents the Spiritgate as a convenience, not a necessity, to prevent panic.

Renka Mirage Sea.name: Renka Mirage Sea
Renka Mirage Sea.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

A golden desert and oasis region of illusion magic, lotus lakes, and caravan cities where perfume markets perfume the wind and mirage ruins shimmer on the horizon like beautiful lies. Renka Mirage Sea is warm, luxurious, mystical, and temptingly dangerous: a land where trade routes cross ancient secrets, lamia-blooded diplomats negotiate over honeyed tea, and moonlit oasis scenes are so beautiful they might not be real. The dunes shift. The stars are impossibly bright. Every oasis is a small paradise, and every ruin has a story about someone who wanted something too badly. Foxkin merchants, Wraithkin seers, Human caravan masters, and Fairy-Blooded illusionists share this sun-drenched land of gold, blue, and starlight. The most tempting offers in Luxcellia are made here, and the most interesting contracts are signed in the small hours of the morning.
Renka Mirage Sea.hiddenInfo: The greatest oasis, Goldlotus, is a living illusion that remembers everyone who has ever desired something strongly enough to lose themselves. It feeds on longing and reshapes itself to match what visitors most want to see. Those who stay too long begin to forget what was real and what was the oasis showing them their heart's deepest wish.

Sanctum Ecclesia.name: Sanctum Ecclesia
Sanctum Ecclesia.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-20 · Danger: Low]

Holy lands governed by the Church of the First Light. White stone cathedrals, healing gardens, paladin training grounds, and monastery libraries cover the landscape. The air itself feels cleaner here: literally, the ambient divine magic purifies it. Solhaven, the sacred capital, is one of the most beautiful cities on the continent and one of the most politically controlled. The Church's warmth is genuine. So is its authority. Visitors are welcome. Questions about doctrine are less so.
Sanctum Ecclesia.hiddenInfo: The Luminous Conclave possesses a sealed prophecy about the Rebirth phenomenon that they've shared with no one outside their inner circle. It supposedly explains both why Reborn individuals appear and what they're meant to do.

Twilight Dominion.name: Twilight Dominion
Twilight Dominion.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 5-35 · Danger: Frontier (Low)]

Demon lord territory. The western reaches of the continent where permanent twilight stains the sky in shades of violet and amber, and the civilization beneath it is far more sophisticated than human propaganda suggests. The Dominion is a meritocracy where strength, cunning, and contractual integrity determine status. Demons, dark elves, lamia, dragonkin, and dozens of other non-human races live here in a society that finds human prudishness alternately baffling and amusing. The capital Obsidian Spire is stunning. The nightlife is legendary. The Demon Lord sends polite diplomatic correspondence and finds heroes entertaining.
Twilight Dominion.hiddenInfo: Kuroyuki has been quietly collecting Reborn individuals who fled human persecution and offering them sanctuary. The Dominion's interest in the Rebirth phenomenon is both academic and personal: Kuroyuki believes it's connected to an ancient magical catastrophe she's been investigating for centuries.

Ashenmere Frontier.name: Ashenmere Frontier
Ashenmere Frontier.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 3-30 · Danger: Frontier (Low)]

The lawless borderlands between civilization and the unknown. Monster-infested wildlands, Riftmaw dungeon entrances, frontier towns held together by stubbornness and cheap ale. The Frontier attracts adventurers looking to rank up fast, criminals looking to disappear, and merchants brave or foolish enough to supply both. Justice is flexible, danger is constant, and the taverns are always full of people with stories, scars, and suspicious amounts of gold.
Ashenmere Frontier.hiddenInfo: The frequency of Riftmaw dungeon appearances has been accelerating. Something is stirring deep underground that the Guild hasn't made public.

Rosethorn Nocturne.name: Rosethorn Nocturne
Rosethorn Nocturne.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 3-30 · Danger: Frontier (Low)]

A gothic romantic borderland of crimson rose fields, moonlit manors, and vampire-blooded nobles who treat intrigue like courtship and courtship like warfare. Rosethorn Nocturne is not horror; it is elegance. Red roses climb black iron gates. Chandeliers glitter above masquerade balls. Wine the color of garnet flows at festivals that celebrate passion, remembrance, and the fine art of the dramatic entrance. The ruling houses are ancient, beautiful, and deeply entangled with blood pacts, dark magic lineages, and arranged marriages that everyone pretends to hate but secretly finds thrilling. Vampire-Blooded, Dark Elf, Demonkin, and Fallen Celestial nobles dominate the social hierarchy, though sharp-witted humans have carved out their own niches. The sky here is perpetually tinted rose-gold at dusk, and the night is never fully dark.
Rosethorn Nocturne.hiddenInfo: The ruling houses hide an ancient blood pact connected to the first Reborn who ever loved someone from this region: a love that supposedly created the Blessing system itself. If this is true, the origin of all divine Blessings is rooted in a romance between a Reborn soul and a vampire-blooded queen who lived before recorded history.

Tsukihana Tidelace.name: Tsukihana Tidelace
Tsukihana Tidelace.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

A chain of moonlit islands, sacred beaches, and shimmering shrine bridges scattered across turquoise shallows. Tsukihana Tidelace is dreamlike: floating lantern festivals cast silver paths on the water, merfolk trade pearls at harbor markets, and moon-viewing boats drift past sea caves that sing at twilight. Every island has a shrine, every shrine has a legend, and every legend mentions something beautiful that lives beneath the waves. The region moves by boat, bridge, and magical tide path: ferries run on moonlight, and the tidal schedule is more reliable than any clock. Merfolk-Blooded, Wraithkin, Foxkin, and Fairy-Blooded communities share these islands with human pearl divers and merchant captains. The atmosphere is soft, blue, silver, turquoise, and perpetually romantic. Confessions happen on shrine bridges. Heartbreak happens on the Vanishing Isle.
Tsukihana Tidelace.hiddenInfo: At certain full moons, one island appears that is not on any map. People who visit it return with memories that do not belong to them: fragments of lives they never lived, loves they never had, and choices they never made. The phenomenon is consistent but unpredictable, and every major faction wants to understand why.

Yukishiro Veilpeak.name: Yukishiro Veilpeak
Yukishiro Veilpeak.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

A northern mountain realm where snow peaks pierce silver clouds, frost temples glow with ancient wards, and hot spring towns steam beneath paper lanterns. Yukishiro Veilpeak is a land of elegant contradictions: luxury inns nestled beside deadly mountain passes, refined noble courts sharing valleys with wolfkin hunting lodges, and ice mages who train in silence but fight with devastating beauty. The landscape reads like a premium winter anime backdrop: white peaks, blue shadows, silver birch forests, frozen waterfalls, and warm light spilling from every window. Noble families with frost Blessings rule from mountain estates while shrine guardians maintain rites older than written history. Travelers come for the hot springs, stay for the romance, and leave with stories of things that howl in the snow.
Yukishiro Veilpeak.hiddenInfo: Deep beneath the glacial ice of the highest peak lies an ancient sealed sky gate: a dimensional portal predating every known civilization. Certain Reborn individuals have reported dreams pointing toward it, and the Veilwalkers have established a quiet research outpost nearby without telling anyone what they suspect.

Aetherglass Reaches.name: Aetherglass Reaches
Aetherglass Reaches.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-20 · Danger: Low]

A strange, beautiful highland region where floating stone fragments drift above glassy plains, wind bridges span impossible canyons, and the ruins of a fallen heavenly city catch the light like scattered diamonds. The Aetherglass Reaches are open, windy, bright, and endlessly adventurous: a frontier for sky explorers, airship crews, storm mages, griffin riders, and scholars chasing the secrets of a civilization that apparently lived among the clouds. The landscape shimmers. The horizon stretches forever. Floating islands cast moving shadows across prairie grass that reflects the sky. It is the most visually stunning region on the continent and the most likely to kill someone who forgets that the ground is not always where you expect it to be. Reborn explorers, Dragonkin, Angelkin, and Fairy-Blooded adventurers are drawn here like moths to a very scenic flame.
Aetherglass Reaches.hiddenInfo: The floating ruins are pieces of a fallen heavenly city called Aethermere. Some structures still respond to Reborn souls: doors open, wards recognize visitors, and certain artifacts activate only for those who carry memories of another world. The Silver Crescent Academy has a restricted research division studying this phenomenon, but their findings are classified.

Kagaribi Duskfields.name: Kagaribi Duskfields
Kagaribi Duskfields.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

An endless golden steppe locked in perpetual sunset where massive storm-beasts roam the amber grasslands, nomadic clans ride creatures that crackle with living lightning, and the sky is a cathedral of copper and amber that never fully darkens. The Duskfields exist in eternal golden hour: a phenomenon maintained by ancient wind temples that nobody fully understands but everyone depends on. The grasslands stretch to every horizon, broken only by storm-beast herds that look like mobile thunderstorms, wind-carved stone formations that sing in the breeze, and the seasonal camps of the Windrunner Confederacy that bloom like cities and dissolve like morning dew. The culture runs on motion, reputation, and the sacred bond between rider and beast. Romance in the Duskfields is expressed through riding partnerships, shared campfire songs, and the nerve-wracking tradition of the Paired Ride: a cooperative obstacle course that requires perfect synchronization with your partner, which is either a trust-building exercise or the world's most elaborate first date.
Kagaribi Duskfields.hiddenInfo: The wind temples are degrading. The Duskfire Wardens have been compensating by redistributing load across the surviving network, but their projections show system failure within two to three generations. A Reborn with engineering or atmospheric science knowledge might be able to help.

Kurogane Deephollow.name: Kurogane Deephollow
Kurogane Deephollow.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

A vast subterranean realm beneath the southern mountains where crystal caverns stretch for miles, underground rivers glow with liquid mana, and entire cities have been carved into geode walls that shimmer with captured starlight. Kurogane Deephollow is Luxcellia's hidden underbelly: a world of perpetual twilight, bioluminescent beauty, and ancient secrets buried so deep that the surface forgot they existed. The architecture is carved obsidian and polished crystal, lit by fungal lanterns and mana-veins that pulse through the stone like a heartbeat. Dwarven-blooded artisans, deep elves, crystal golems, and cave-adapted beastkin have built a civilization that rivals anything above ground in sophistication and surpasses it in sheer visual drama. The Deephollow is hauntingly beautiful: every cavern is a cathedral, every tunnel a gallery, and every underground lake a mirror reflecting impossible colors. Travelers come for the legendary crystal markets, stay because the silence is addictive, and leave with the unsettling feeling that something ancient watched them the entire time.
Kurogane Deephollow.hiddenInfo: The deepest tunnels of the Deephollow connect to a sealed chamber containing what appears to be a dormant Riftmaw core; not a dungeon entrance, but the seed of one. If it activates, the entire underground could become a mega-dungeon. The Depthwarden Circle knows about it and has been quietly reinforcing the seals for centuries. Reborn individuals who enter the deepest levels report hearing a voice that speaks in a language they somehow understand: a language from their original world.

Shingetsu Evergrove.name: Shingetsu Evergrove
Shingetsu Evergrove.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-25 · Danger: Low]

An ancient jungle where temple ruins older than recorded history rise from the canopy like the bones of a forgotten god, vines and flowers cascade in impossible abundance, and the air hums with the whisper of roots communicating across miles. The Evergrove is alive in ways that go beyond biology: the vegetation appears to make decisions, the canopy adjusts to control light and weather, and the root network beneath the forest floor transmits information across the continent. Elven botanists, beastkin hunters, and human researchers have carved out a precarious coexistence with a jungle that is either protecting them or farming them. The temple ruins are the main draw: pre-civilization complexes that no Luxcellian culture built, covered in inscriptions that Reborn individuals sometimes recognize from their original worlds. The Thornblood Reclamation excavates the ruins. The Verdant Throne communes with the jungle. Both are increasingly certain that something is waking up beneath the canopy.
Shingetsu Evergrove.hiddenInfo: The jungle's root network extends across the entire continent, and its activity has increased dramatically with each Reborn arrival. The Verdant Throne's most sensitive priests report the network is broadcasting a single recurring pattern that translates roughly as 'preparing.'

Kagutsuchi Emberwake.name: Kagutsuchi Emberwake
Kagutsuchi Emberwake.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 3-30 · Danger: Frontier (Low)]

A volcanic region of black beaches, glowing lava rivers, dragonkin halls, and fire temples where the sky burns red-orange at dusk and the earth breathes steam through mineral vents. Kagutsuchi Emberwake is hot, powerful, passionate, and visually stunning: a land where forge cities glow along volcanic canals, bathhouses use mineral-rich hot springs, and martial schools teach combat with the intensity of a confession. Dragonkin and Oni-Blooded warriors train on caldera rims. Human smiths craft enchanted steel in magma forges. Catkin adventurers prowl the cinder fields. The architecture is dramatic black stone with ember-lit interiors, and every sunset looks like the world is ending beautifully. Strength is respected. Craft is revered. Romance is loud.
Kagutsuchi Emberwake.hiddenInfo: The central caldera contains a sleeping dragon-heart crystal: an ancient artifact that may be the source of several Blessings and cheat-skill mutations. The Dragonkin elders have known about it for generations and guard the information fiercely. Several Reborn individuals have reported their powers intensifying near the caldera, though no one can explain why.

Crownveil Sovereignty.name: Crownveil Sovereignty
Crownveil Sovereignty.basicInfo:
[Recommended Level: 1-20 · Danger: Low]

A glittering kingdom of white-walled cities, rolling farmland, and political intrigue. The Crownveil Sovereignty is the continent's most powerful human nation: wealthy, cultured, and rotten with court politics. Noble houses scheme behind ballroom smiles, the Royal Knight Order patrols gleaming highways, and the capital Aureliath shines like a jewel on a hill. Beautiful on the surface, ruthless underneath. Tournament arcs, academy drama, and romantic scandals happen here with reliable frequency.
Crownveil Sovereignty.hiddenInfo: Queen Celestine keeps extensive files on every Reborn individual who enters her territory. The Sovereignty has a secret task force dedicated to monitoring and potentially weaponizing the Rebirth phenomenon.

Riftmaw Floors 1-5.name: Riftmaw Floors 1-5
Riftmaw Floors 1-5.basicInfo:
[The Riftmaw · Floors 1-5 · Recommended Level: 1-13]

The Shallows are the Riftmaw's front porch: five floors of limestone caves under the Maw, lit by phosphorescent moss and the violet Riftlight that seeps down the scaffolding. Water drips everywhere and runs in a cold stream that wanders south toward the deeper floors, so nobody here goes thirsty; food is whatever a delver carries down, buys at Lantern Row, or cuts out of a slime. The Guild maps these floors better than any others, and rookies learn the trade here.

Who lives down here: delvers at Lantern Row on floor 2, and a goblin and kobold warren called Gutterwarren on floor 4 that the Guild pretends not to know about. The Riftmaw's own creatures are slimes, cave crawlers and the odd lost surface beast, territorial and predictable, and the Crowned Slime holds the stair down from floor 5. Places sit on their own floors: the Slime Wells on 1, Lantern Row on 2, the Tally Wall on 3, Gutterwarren on 4. What kills most rookies is not a monster but a crawlway that floods when the stream rises. Getting here means travelling down through every floor set above, and moving between floors takes hours of chambers and stairs; every place here keeps to its own floor.
