Behind it, a short dark passage only ever opens back into the same dining room. On the hour the door swings once by itself, and something unseen carries the old setting out.

The Locked Study.name: The Locked Study
The Locked Study.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 58 · Recommended Level: 53-68 · Danger: Elite (Severe)]

The Locked Study is a book-lined room at the end of a quiet corridor on floor 58, its heavy door locked from the inside an age ago with the key still in the lock. The house keeps it like every other room: the lamp is lit, the fire is laid, a reading chair faces the door. The door opens for a guest who knocks and waits through a full chime of the hall clock, and locks again behind them. Inside are shelves of books from a hundred libraries, a desk, and a letter stopped in the middle of a sentence, the ink still wet. The study has a house rule of its own that nobody remembers until someone breaks it, and its correction is the house's quietest and its worst. Portrait watchers hang in the corridor outside and follow anyone who leaves.
The Locked Study.hiddenInfo: The letter is an invitation, the one this study's house was waiting on: it was never finished, so it was never sent, so the guest never came. The study's rule is that the letter is not to be read. Whoever reads it is locked in with it until they write the next line, and the house judges each line by whether the guest would have come. Right now a delver is locked inside writing line after line, and the study's bell has started ringing on the Servants' Hall board.

The Locked Door.description: A heavy panelled door at the corridor's dead end, its key turned in the lock from the inside. It opens for a guest who knocks and waits through a full chime of the hall clock, then shuts and locks behind them with a soft, final click. Deep scratches in the paint around the handle show that not everyone waited.

The Reading Room.description: Three walls of books from a hundred libraries, in languages nobody here reads and a few they do, around a hearth where the fire is always laid and never lit. The reading chair faces the door. Books may be read here and must go back where they came from; the house checks the shelves every night.

The Unfinished Letter.description: A wide desk under a green-shaded lamp, and on it a single sheet of good paper in a careful hand, stopped in the middle of a sentence with the pen beside it still wet. The lamp never goes out. Anyone standing at the desk feels the whole room waiting for them to do something.

Wayfinders' Camp.name: Wayfinders' Camp
Wayfinders' Camp.basicInfo:
[Safe Haven · Riftmaw Floor 63 · Recommended Level: 63-83 · No hostile spawns · Downtime protected]

Wayfinders' Camp is a hard-pressed delvers' redoubt in a square stone court on floor 63 that the grinding corridors never quite crush. It holds only by exploiting a cruel law of the Labyrinth: the maze bends toward whatever is sought, so every hour a wayfinder walks out into the shifting stone, naming the camp aloud and paying an hour of their life to nail the court in place. If a walker fails to return, the walls groan inward until the next watch goes out. Who lives here: grim veteran wayfinders who chalk the corridors, a rope-keeper, a cook, a cistern-keeper and exhausted delvers, sparse-spoken people who write everything down. Water seeps into an old stone cistern overnight; light is the maze's unblinking amber glare; food comes down on delvers' backs and sells dear. Prices: a meal 1 Silver, a stick of chalk 5 Copper, a copy of today's routes 2 Silver, a length of silk rope 3 Silver, a bedroll 1 Silver a night. Law: never rub out another's chalk, post every route you walk, and never speak aloud inside the court what you seek. Delvers are welcome; a monster player needs a sponsor's tag or a wayfinder's word. Home base: a marked bedroll space under the awnings for 6 Silver a week and one chalking walk a week near the gate. People come back because the Route Board is the only map that keeps parties from being sealed alive.
Wayfinders' Camp.hiddenInfo: The camp has paid the maze an hour every hour for years, and the maze keeps everything it takes; nobody likes to count how many hours that is. The rope-keeper quietly runs the camp, because the rope comes from the Silk Vaults and the rope-keeper is the only one the spiders will deal with. Right now someone is rubbing out chalk marks on floor 64 and drawing new ones that lead toward the Vaults' toll line, and half the camp thinks it is the spiders. Work on offer: at the Chalk Gate, the wayfinder on watch is short of walkers and pays someone to take the hourly walk that keeps the way home fixed.

The Chalk Gate.description: An arched gateway into the court, its stones white with chalk arrows pointing in, layer over layer, each left by someone who found the way home. A wayfinder on watch checks who comes through. Outside, the corridor changes; inside the arch it does not, and everyone feels the moment they cross.

The Route Board.description: A tall board of planed wood in the middle of the court, covered in chalked routes dated by the hour, rubbed clean and redrawn as returning parties report. A copy of today's routes is 2 Silver. Reading it is the camp's first ritual on waking; arguing over it is the second.

The Fixed Court.description: The square heart of the camp, paved in pale stone, with an old round cistern at its centre that fills by itself overnight. Its walls never move, and wayfinders have carved their marks into them to prove it. Nobody here says aloud what they are looking for; it is the court's one rule, and the reason it stays.

The Bedrolls.description: A row of bedrolls under canvas awnings along the court's east wall, each space marked with a chalk sign. A bedroll is 1 Silver a night; a marked space of your own is 6 Silver a week and one chalking walk, and stays yours while both are kept. The warm light never dims, so everyone sleeps with a cloth over their eyes.

The Rope Store.description: A lean-to of stacked crates against the north wall, hung with coils of pale spider-silk rope traded from the Silk Vaults. A length is 3 Silver and holds a falling body without fraying. The rope-keeper lends a coil free to anyone going out to chalk, and counts every coil that comes back.

The Silk Vaults.name: The Silk Vaults
The Silk Vaults.basicInfo:
[Safe Haven · Monster Hold · Riftmaw Floor 69 · Recommended Level: 63-83 · No wild spawns inside · Residents decide who stays]

The Silk Vaults are a precarious spider hold slung across the vaulted ceilings of floor 69, where taut web bridges span corridors that grind and shift below. The maze moves its walls, not its vaults, so when the stone lurches the anchor-lines groan and hold. The Riftmaw hunts its people as rogue thread-spiders that deserted the junctions: horned hunter copies prowl beneath the drop lines, and wall-mouths snap up any strand that sags low. Who lives here: arachne-kin weavers, jorogumo who patrol the bridges, great spiders spinning the heavy cables, and free thread-spiders carrying word along the strands. They eat what blunders into the lower snares and what delvers trade up, wring bitter dew from the silk, and live by the maze's feverish glow. Trade: silk rope at 3 Silver a length, a Spider-Silk Skein at 6 Silver, and a look down from the bridges at how the corridors lie right now, 2 Silver a question. Toll: 1 Silver to be hauled up the Drop Line. Law: no fire, no blade on a strand, and nobody plucks a singing thread without leave. Monster players of spider kinds are kin and climb free; other monsters and delvers pay the toll and keep to the bridges. Home base: a hanging den, free to kin who spin a bridge strand daily; others rent one for 5 Silver a week and a shift in the Weaving Hall. People come back because one look from the rafters beats dying blind.
The Silk Vaults.hiddenInfo: The matriarch at the great loom weaves one row a day for every shape the maze takes, and she believes the pattern circles something at the Labyrinth's heart she has never seen. She will trade a look at the weave for a memory, the same price the hermit asks; the two have never met. The free thread-spiders quietly run the Vaults, since every word spoken on a strand reaches them. Right now the horned hunter has started standing under the Drop Line, looking up, and it is larger than the last time. Work on offer: at the Drop Line, the jorogumo who answers the bell wants the horned hunter drawn off from under the line long enough to hang a new one.

The Drop Line.description: A single thick line of pale silk hanging from the vault into a corridor of floor 69, with a sling at its foot and a small bell. Ring, pay the jorogumo who answers 1 Silver, and you are hauled up onto the webs. When the corridors shift, the line swings to hang over a different passage, and the hold always knows which.

The Web Bridges.description: Broad bridges of woven silk strung between the vault's arches, swaying over corridors that slide and turn below. Visitors walk them roped; kin run them. From the middle, for 2 Silver, a jorogumo will point out how the corridors lie right now, and the answer holds until someone stops watching.

The Weaving Hall.description: A wide hammock of web slung between four arches where arachne-kin weave rope, cloth and skeins on frames of salvaged bone and wood. A Spider-Silk Skein is 6 Silver, rope 3 a length. Renters take shifts here sorting silk by feel, and the weavers hum as they work, all on one note.

The Hanging Dens.description: Rows of silk sacks hung from the vault ribs like lanterns, each one a den, entered by a slit and sealed from inside. Kin who spin a strand a day for the bridges claim one free; others rent for 5 Silver a week and a weaving shift. Each den sways when someone turns over, and the whole row knows it.

The Matriarch's Loom.description: A great loom at the centre of the vault, wider than a corridor, where an old arachne matriarch weaves one row of pale silk a day. Visitors bring her disputes and requests, and she answers with her hands still moving. Nobody walks beneath the loom, and nobody touches it without being asked.

The Hermit's Junction.name: The Hermit's Junction
The Hermit's Junction.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 66 · Recommended Level: 63-83 · Danger: Mythic (Deadly)]

The Hermit's Junction is a crossroads on floor 66 where four corridors meet around a squat carved waystone, and where a former delver in a horned wooden mask has lived for longer than Wayfinders' Camp can say. The few Guild notes that mention this resident call them the horned hermit for the mask; they are not the horned thing that hunts the maze, and they take the comparison badly. The hermit sells directions, true ones, to the stair, to the camp, to a lost party, and the price is a memory, spoken aloud, written down and given up. The corridors around the junction change while a party watches, and the hunter's copies pass through it often. The hermit's directions hold for a day.
The Hermit's Junction.hiddenInfo: The hermit pays the maze's toll with the memories they buy, which is why their directions are true. They keep the best ones on the Memory Shelf, sealed in wax, and whoever breaks a seal remembers it as their own. The horned mask is there because the hermit believes the horned hunter does not hunt its own likeness; nobody has tested it twice. What the hermit wants is one memory of their own back from the maze's heart, and they are close to affording it.

The Four-Way Stone.description: A squat waystone at the centre of the crossroads, carved with four faces, one toward each corridor, worn smooth by hands. The corridors around it change, and the faces never agree with them for long. The hermit reads the stone each morning before selling a single direction.

The Masked Shelter.description: A low shelter of stacked stone and stretched canvas in the junction's corner, with a stool, a lamp and a writing board. The hermit sits in the doorway in the horned mask and hears requests. A memory is told aloud and written on a slip; once the slip is sealed, the teller cannot call it back to mind.

The Memory Shelf.description: Plank shelves at the back of the shelter lined with small wax-sealed jars, each holding one folded slip and labelled in the hermit's hand: a song, a face, a road home, a first good meal. A few are for sale, priced in other memories; most are not. The shelf hums faintly whenever the maze changes.

The Still Court.name: The Still Court
The Still Court.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 72 · Recommended Level: 63-83 · Danger: Mythic (Deadly)]

The Still Court is a paved courtyard on floor 72 that never moves. The corridors around it rearrange themselves like everywhere else in the Labyrinth, but the court's walls, its archways and its dry stone fountain stay exactly where they are, and delvers have scratched dates into its paving going back years. Nobody agrees on how they reached it. Every party that has found it tells a different route, and none of the routes works twice. Delvers rest here when they find it, because the walls hold still, but it is no haven: the horned hunter's copies come through the archways, and the fountain's basin is full of things other parties dropped and never came back for.
The Still Court.hiddenInfo: The court is the one place in the maze nobody has ever reached by asking for it. Every way in is an accident, and anyone who names it aloud while looking for it never finds it again; Wayfinders' Camp lost two parties trying to put it on the Route Board. The fountain is dry because what fed it was taken as a toll long ago. Right now a delver has camped here for nine days, afraid to leave, because they know they will not find it twice.

The Unmoving Square.description: A square of pale paving open to the warm slanting light, its stones scratched with dates and marks by delvers proving to themselves that it stays. Sounds here do not echo the way they do in the corridors. Parties that reach it tend to sit down at once, and some do not stand again for hours.

The Dry Fountain.description: A round stone fountain at the court's centre, its spout carved like an open hand, its basin dry and half full of dropped things: coins, keys, a compass, a single boot. Nobody takes from the basin. Wayfinders say it ran once, but nobody alive has seen water in it.

The Ways In.description: Archways around the court's edge, some open and some bricked up, and which is which changes from visit to visit. None of them leads back the way anyone came. Chalk left on the outside is always gone by the next visit, though the scratches inside the court stay.

The Gardener's Lodge.name: The Gardener's Lodge
The Gardener's Lodge.basicInfo:
[Safe Haven · Riftmaw Floor 78 · Recommended Level: 78-98 · No hostile spawns · Downtime protected]

The Gardener's Lodge is a low stone shelter among terraced beds on floor 78, kept by a hollow-eyed gardener who was a delver once before the deep stripped his name away. It survives on a knife-edge: the towering gardener beasts butcher anything out of place, and spare the Lodge only because every inch is manic-tended. A delver gripping a hoe in a weeded row is read as part of the garden while the long-limbed horrors stalk past. Who lives here: the gardener, slow and eerie and never quite looking at anyone; rattled delvers who earn a few days of life by working the soil; a cook; a seed-keeper; and a Reborn who stares into the window glare swearing it is the sun from home. Water runs in the channel; food grows from surface seed alongside nameless dungeon fruit; light is the scorching false sun, shuttered at night. Prices: a meal is free to anyone who worked the beds that day and 1 Silver otherwise; a room 3 Silver a night; a rare seed from the vault 1 Gold. Law: work before you eat, keep your blood off the soil, and never cut what the gardener planted. Delvers and monster players alike are judged by the beds they keep. Home base: a room in the Lodging Rooms for 15 Silver a week, or free while you work a full day in the beds every day. People come back because stop weeding and the shears come for you.
The Gardener's Lodge.hiddenInfo: The gardener's name is on the Guild's missing-persons list, and the gardener's arms grow longer every year. The Rootcourt believes the gardener is slowly becoming one of the gardener beasts, and that this is why the beasts leave the Lodge alone. The seed-keeper quietly runs the Lodge, keeping the accounts and the peace, and hides the gardener's old delving pack in the Seed Vault in case anyone ever asks. Right now a gardener beast has begun standing at the edge of the kitchen beds every dawn, waiting. Work on offer: in the Seed Vault, the seed-keeper with the vault key wants the gardener beast that waits by the Kitchen Beds each dawn given a reason to leave.

The Potting Shed.description: A long wooden shed beside the Lodge, cool and dim, smelling of loam and cut stems, with trays of cuttings in rows and tools hung on pegs in an order the gardener insists on. Visitors collect a hoe here before they work. A tool put back on the wrong peg is the only thing that makes the gardener raise their voice.

The Kitchen Beds.description: Rows of vegetables and herbs stepping down the terrace in the golden light: beans, onions, squash, and fruit with no name hanging over the walls. A day's work here buys supper and a place at the table. The channel water is cold, and the soil is so rich it smells sweet.

The Lodging Rooms.description: Small stone rooms along the Lodge's back wall, each with a cot, a basin and a shutter that closes out the false sun. A room is 3 Silver a night or 15 Silver a week, or free while you work a full day in the beds every day. Sleep comes deep here, and most guests wake hungry.

The Seed Vault.description: A dry cellar under the Lodge lined with labelled drawers of seeds: surface seeds carried down by delvers and seeds of the unnamed fruit, sorted by a system only the seed-keeper understands. A rare seed is 1 Gold. The drawers are locked, and the key never leaves the seed-keeper's neck.

The Window Bench.description: A stone bench under the Lodge's one tall window, bathed in warm golden light. Sitting in it closes wounds and leaves the golden mark, so most guests sit a short while and move to the shade. A Reborn sits here every day, face turned to the glass, and tells anyone who listens about the sun from home.

The Rootcourt.name: The Rootcourt
The Rootcourt.basicInfo:
[Safe Haven · Monster Hold · Riftmaw Floor 81 · Recommended Level: 78-98 · No wild spawns inside · Residents decide who stays]

The Rootcourt is a fortified thicket of dryads, alraune and plant-folk on a terrace of floor 81, knotted into a ring of ancient trees whose roots interlock into one living arch. The Riftmaw grew them to tend its wild beds, and has never forgiven their rebellion. They survive only because the gardener beasts ignore rooted flora, forcing the hold to stay anchored in the shade under the burning false sun. Even so, the dungeon besieges them: swarms of light-eating moths strip their canopy dark, and spilled sap spawns murderous thorn wardens from the loam. Who lives here: dryads bound to the ring's trunks, alraune who bargain from carnivorous blooms, mandrake sentries at the gate, and scarred plant-folk who speak in rustles. They drink channel water and feed on light, trading wound sap at 4 Silver a vial, Nightbloom Petals at 6 Silver, and living-wood bows for steep coin. Toll: 2 Silver or a sack of ash at the Living Arch. Law: no fire, no blood on the soil, no blade on living wood. Monster players of plant kinds are kin and pass free; other monster players are heard and pay half; delvers pay the toll and keep to the paths. Home base: a bloom den, free to kin who root for a season; others rent a woven bower for 8 Silver a week and a day's tending. People risk the climb for sap that heals without leaving the golden mark.
The Rootcourt.hiddenInfo: The oldest dryad in the Elder Grove has roots that run under the whole terrace and as far as the Gardener's Lodge, and she has been listening to the gardener for years. The Rootcourt believes the gardener is turning into a gardener beast, and some of the alraune want to sell that warning to the Lodge at a high price. The alraune quietly run the court, because sap buys everything. Right now light-eating moths are swarming the ring's windows, the beds are going dark, and the dryads are weakening. Work on offer: at the Sap Market, an alraune trader in an open bloom pays in sap for anyone who can clear the light-eating moths off the ring's windows.

The Living Arch.description: The hold's only gate, a high arch of roots knotted together from two great trees, with mandrakes sitting in pots on either side. The toll is 2 Silver or a sack of ash for the beds. Kin of plant kinds pass under it free, and the arch's leaves turn toward them as they do.

The Rootcourt Ring.description: A clear circle of soft grass at the centre of the hold, where the residents gather in the shade to talk and settle disputes. Dryads lean out of their trees to listen, and nobody walks the grass in boots. Decisions are made slowly and announced by which way the leaves turn.

The Bloom Dens.description: Hollows in the trunks of the ring's trees, lined with soft moss and hung with great flowers that close at night like curtains. Kin who root in the ring for a season claim one free; others rent a woven bower among the branches for 8 Silver a week and a day's tending. Inside, the air smells of rain.

The Sap Market.description: A row of great flowers along the terrace edge where alraune sit in the open blooms and trade: wound sap at 4 Silver a vial, Nightbloom Petals at 6 Silver, cuttings and living-wood bows. They bargain hard and sweetly and never forget a debt. Ash, salt and surface seed are welcome as payment.

The Elder Grove.description: The back of the hold, where one ancient tree stands under the brightest window and a dryad older than anyone's records sleeps in its trunk. Visitors come with questions and leave water at the roots. Answers come as dreams, the next time the visitor sleeps, and they are rarely the answer expected.

The Orchard of Unnamed Fruit.name: The Orchard of Unnamed Fruit
The Orchard of Unnamed Fruit.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 83 · Recommended Level: 78-98 · Danger: Mythic (Deadly)]

The Orchard of Unnamed Fruit climbs four terraces on floor 83 under tall windows of golden light, row after row of trees heavy with fruit no Luxcellian has a name for: blue and furred, glassy and cold, gold and ringing faintly when tapped. Some of it is a feast, some a fever, some a sleep that lasts a day, and a few kinds do something nobody has managed to describe. Delvers come to harvest, because the Academy and the Rootcourt pay well for any fruit with a known effect. Gardener beasts work these terraces every hour, pruning branches, fallen fruit, and anyone standing where a tree should be.
The Orchard of Unnamed Fruit.hiddenInfo: Some of the fruit comes from the worlds the Reborn came from. A Reborn who recognises a fruit and says its name aloud makes that tree's fruit safe for anyone to eat, and makes the tree out of place: the gardener beasts come to prune it within the hour. The Fallow Row is where named trees used to stand. Right now a Reborn delver has named three trees in a week, and the beasts have started watching the Reborn instead of the trees.

The Orchard Terraces.description: Four terraces of fruit trees stepping up under the golden windows, branches bowed with fruit in a dozen shapes and colours, the gravel paths raked white between them. The light heals anyone who stands in it and marks them for every hunter on the floor. Gardener beasts work the rows slowly, and then not slowly.

The Tasting Stone.description: A flat slab of stone on the middle terrace, scratched all over with drawings of fruit and short warnings in a dozen hands: sleep, fever, safe, never. Delvers taste here, one bite each, and add what happened. Nobody carves a name for a fruit, and the old hands say not to try.

The Fallow Row.description: A long bare row of turned earth along the lowest terrace where nothing grows, raked smooth every night by something nobody sees. Stumps show where trees once stood. The gardener beasts rest here between rounds, standing as still as fence posts, and the row is the coldest place on the floor.

The Glasshouse of Thorns.name: The Glasshouse of Thorns
The Glasshouse of Thorns.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 88 · Recommended Level: 78-98 · Danger: Mythic (Deadly)]

The Glasshouse of Thorns is a long house of iron ribs and clear panes on floor 88, built against one of the Gardens' greatest windows. Inside grow beds of glass-thorned roses, bushes taller than a rider with petals soft as any rose and thorns of clear glass sharp enough to cut through leather. The window at the far end pours the false sun in so strongly that a moment in it closes a wound and leaves a mark that glows. Delvers come for Nightbloom Petals and for the healing, and they pay in blood: every cut from a thorn calls a thorn warden up out of the beds.
The Glasshouse of Thorns.hiddenInfo: The thorns are the window's glass, grown. A thorn snapped off cleanly and carried away keeps a sliver of the false sun: pressed to a wound once, it closes it, and marks the bearer the way the window would. Herbalists on the surface pay Gold for one and are never told where it came from. Right now a party is pinned in the shade by the Glass Door, one of them bleeding, with three thorn wardens standing between them and the window.

The Glass Door.description: A tall door of clear panes in an iron frame at the glasshouse's near end, always unlocked and always closing slowly behind whoever passes. Inside it lies a narrow strip of shade, the last before the beds. Delvers stop here to cover every scrap of bare skin and check their straps twice.

The Thorn Beds.description: Long beds of glass-thorned roses filling the glasshouse from wall to wall, the paths between them barely a shoulder wide. The petals are soft and scented; the thorns of clear glass catch the light like water. A single drop of blood on the soil and the bed stirs, and a thorn warden begins to rise.

The Marking Window.description: The great window at the glasshouse's far end, golden light pouring through it so bright the air looks thick. A moment in it closes wounds; a minute leaves a golden mark that glows in the dark. The floor beneath it is clear of thorns, and every bed in the house leans toward it.

The Last Lanterns.name: The Last Lanterns
The Last Lanterns.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 93 · Recommended Level: 93-100 · Exposed camp · Danger never leaves the Last Stair]

The Last Lanterns is a grim, wind-lashed bivouac on the split landing of floor 93: low canvas shelters lashed to pitons, a ration post, and a long rail of lanterns overlooking the abyss of the Last Stair. It is not safe and never claims to be. Star-things crawl over the lip between watches, the stone cracks underfoot at any hour, and the camp endures only because half the bivouac sleeps in armor with weapons drawn while the rest hold the platform. Who is here: hollow-eyed expedition parties bracing for the last floors, a scarred quartermaster, and grim veterans who came down years ago and stayed to keep watch. Water drips from a fissure into a guarded barrel; food is only what survived a ninety-floor march; light is the lanterns kept burning for every party that went below and never climbed back. Prices are steep ninety floors down: a skin of water 1 Silver, a day's ration 4 Silver, a flask of lamp oil 5 Silver, a Riftlight Shard 1 Gold. There are no Guild services. Law: everyone stands a watch, nobody touches another party's lantern, and nobody answers a voice calling from the edge after dark. Delvers and monster players are treated alike: anyone who stands a watch eats. Home base: a tied shelter on the landing, 2 Silver a night and a watch every night, held at your own risk. People cling to it because below this rail, nobody remembers your name.
The Last Lanterns.hiddenInfo: The mirror-wraiths come to the lanterns. They wear the faces of the parties the lanterns burn for, speak in their voices and ask to be let in, and once a real lost party came back the same way and was turned away. The oldest veteran on the watch quietly runs the camp; she keeps one lantern of her own and lets nobody put it out. Right now the crack across the landing widens every day, and the camp is split over moving up to floor 92, where the moth-folk have offered space at a price.

The Lantern Rail.description: An iron rail along the landing's open edge, hung with dozens of lanterns, each tagged with a party's sign and the date it went down. The camp keeps them filled until someone comes back for them. Past the rail there is only the field of stars, and now and then something falling slowly through it.

The Tied Shelters.description: Canvas shelters lashed to iron rings driven into the well wall, rented at 2 Silver a night and a watch every night, at your own risk. When the stone cracks, the camp unties and moves them in minutes. Nobody sleeps with their boots off, and nobody sleeps alone in a shelter.

The Ration Post.description: A counter of stacked crates under a canvas roof where the quartermaster trades water, rations, oil and rope at prices that make sense ninety floors down. A day's ration is 4 Silver, a skin of water 1. A slate behind the counter lists what each party left owing, and debts here are always paid.

The Stairwatch Platform.description: A raised platform of lashed planks at the landing's far end, looking up and down the spiral, with a bell and a pair of long lenses. Two watchers stand on it at all hours. Falling stars are called out, and so is anything climbing; the watch is the only reason anyone here wakes up at all.

The Starwing Eyrie.name: The Starwing Eyrie
The Starwing Eyrie.basicInfo:
[Safe Haven · Monster Hold · Riftmaw Floor 92 · Recommended Level: 93-100 · No wild spawns inside · Residents decide who stays]

The Starwing Eyrie is a wind-scoured moth-folk hold clinging to a sheer cliff of the well wall at floor 92, a cluster of ledges and lashed perches hung over the abyss, reached from the landing only by wing or hauling basket. Its people were spawned to snuff expedition lights and feed parties to the dark; the ones here broke the compulsion and keep the lanterns burning instead. The Riftmaw hunts them as traitors: pale star-things crawl up the sheer stone to raid the lower perches, and gales rip away anything not lashed double. They survive because floor-spawn cannot walk a sheer wall, and because no flyer ventures past lantern-sight, where up and down vanish into the void. Who lives here: Mothkin of every pattern, battered avian-kin and tengu, and a scarred elder keeping the night watch. They drink from cold wall seeps, eat what they trade for, and huddle by lamplight. Trade: moth-silk at 5 Silver a bolt, warnings about the stair below at 2 Silver. Toll: 2 Silver or a flask of oil to ride the basket. Law: never put out a lantern, never touch a wing, and nobody is carried between landings. Mothkin and winged monster players are kin and roost free; others pay the toll and keep to the ledges. Home base: a roost on the Roost Wall, free to kin who tend a lantern; others rent a hammock for 10 Silver a week. People come back for warnings that keep parties alive.
The Starwing Eyrie.hiddenInfo: The elder can tell a mirror-wraith from a delver by lantern light, and sells that knowledge only to those she trusts. The moth-folk once roosted on the wall at floor 94 as well, until the beasts took it; they do not speak of it. The basket-keepers quietly run the Eyrie, because they decide who crosses. Right now the Last Lanterns want to move up onto the floor 92 landing, and the Eyrie is deciding what to charge, and whether more lanterns are worth more noise. Work on offer: at the Hauling Basket, a basket-keeper at the windlass pays someone to keep a trial row of lanterns lit on the floor 92 landing for three nights.

The Lantern Ledge.description: The Eyrie's lowest ledge, long and narrow above the landing, hung with lanterns traded, found and kept, burning in a row. Visitors step off the basket here. The moth-folk crowd close to the light with their wings shivering, and the ledge smells of hot oil and fine dust.

The Roost Wall.description: The bare wall above the ledge, honeycombed with cracks, niches and lashed perches where the moth-folk sleep hanging, wings folded. Kin claim a roost free by keeping a lantern lit beside it; others rent a lashed hammock for 10 Silver a week. The wind never stops, and everything is tied twice.

The Wing Market.description: A row of wide niches cut into the wall where moth-folk trade moth-silk, seep water and whatever fell past the edge and was caught. Moth-silk is 5 Silver a bolt; a warning about the stair below is 2 Silver and usually right. Oil is the best coin here, and all haggling is done in whispers.

The Night Watch.description: A high perch near the top of the Eyrie where the elder and two watchers hang facing the stair, lanterns at their backs. They see further down the spiral than anyone on the landings. What they see is sold at the Wing Market, and what they see coming is shouted to everyone for free.

The Hauling Basket.description: A wicker basket on a rope line run from the floor 92 landing up to the Lantern Ledge, hauled by two moth-folk at a windlass. The toll is 2 Silver or a flask of oil. The ride is short, the void is directly underneath, and the basket-keepers decide who rides it.

The Mirror Landing.name: The Mirror Landing
The Mirror Landing.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 95 · Recommended Level: 93-100 · Danger: Mythic (Deadly)]

The Mirror Landing is the broadest landing on the Last Stair, a round platform of pale stone on floor 95 with a tall mirror in a stone frame set against the well wall. A mirror-wraith lives in it. Like the others on the stair it wears the face of a delver who came this far and did not go back, and it speaks in their voice, but this one does not attack at once. It asks to be told its own name, and it listens to every answer. A stone slab by the edge is scratched with the guesses of parties who tried. A wrong answer makes it angry, and the other wraiths on the stair come down to watch.
The Mirror Landing.hiddenInfo: The face the wraith wears belongs to a real delver whose name sits in the Guild's missing-persons records, and that is the name it wants. Told it rightly, it remembers, and what it does next depends on who that delver was. Told wrongly, it takes the face of whoever owned the wrong name for a while and comes looking for them. Right now a party is camped on the landing working through a list copied from the Guild, and the slab is running out of room.

The Broad Platform.description: A round platform of pale stone, wider than any other landing on the stair, with chambers cut into the wall that will not stay shut. Falling stars break here often, and the stone is pitted with burn scars. Parties rest along the wall with their backs to it and their eyes on the mirror.

The Mirror.description: A tall mirror in a frame of carved stone, its glass flawless, showing the landing and the stars behind but never the people standing in front of it. A face appears in it when someone comes close, a delver's face, tired and patient. It asks its question quietly, and then it waits.

The Name Stone.description: A slab of stone at the landing's open edge, scratched all over with names crossed out one by one, each a guess somebody said aloud to the mirror. Some guesses carry a second mark beside them, for a party that guessed wrong and did not leave. Chalk and a knife sit on top for the next party.

The Dream Camp.name: The Dream Camp
The Dream Camp.basicInfo:
[Safe Haven · Riftmaw Floor 97 · Recommended Level: 70-100 · No hostile spawns · Downtime protected]

The Dream Camp is a cramped, eerie foothold in an alcove off the corridor on floor 97, huddled near the Antechamber inside the dead ring where the Riftmaw's spawns refuse to cross. It endures only because the dungeon's monsters recoil a hundred paces from the Sealed Door, leaving a silent pressure-zone where the walls hum and every sleeper is dragged into the same shared dream. Here Monaka Kugirime, the Academy's most obsessive field researcher, has held a one-woman station for eleven months in defiance of three recall orders: a frayed tent bristling with resonance needles, a dented tea service, and crates of notebooks. The sourceless glare never dims, the dead air never stirs, and water and food are only what the Academy expedition left in its cache and what parties haul down. Monaka trades spare rations at 4 Silver a day, pours free tea to steady shaking hands, and asks one toll of every sleeper: a written account of their dream. Law: write down your dream before breakfast, touch no instrument, and keep your voice low near the tent. Delvers and monster players are treated alike; the needles only twitch for the Reborn. Home base: a bedroll space along the alcove wall, free while you log every dream and add 2 Silver of supplies to the cache each week. People come back for the dreams, in a language understood only while dreaming.
The Dream Camp.hiddenInfo: Monaka's readings spike, cleanly and repeatably, when certain visitors approach the Door, and she keeps a separate notebook about it that she does not send up. The dream language is the same across every party and every year in the logbook, and it is not the Door's script; she believes that means two peoples, not one. She quietly runs the camp, and the expedition's cache is running low. Right now the script on the Door changed overnight, and she has not slept. Work on offer: at the Tea Table, the Academy researcher who keeps the camp pays someone to bring back two ration packs dropped in the corridor past the Ring Stakes.

Riftmaw 97th Floor: Dream Camp.description: A sheltered alcove near the Antechamber where parties sleep during long research stays, bedrolls laid along the smooth wall under warm light that never dims. The dreams here are vivid, intricate and alike across different sleepers and different years. A dream logbook holds every party's account, and reading it through takes hours and leaves a slow unease, as if the entries were one story.

The Research Tent.description: Monaka Kugirime's weather-beaten field tent, bristling with resonance instruments, cables and stacks of notebooks weighted with stones, its flap tied back with a strap of Academy webbing. Three recall letters are pinned inside, unanswered. Visitors stand at the flap and wait to be noticed, which can take some time.

The Tea Table.description: A low folding table beside the tent with a dented kettle, a tea service and a stack of blank dream forms. This is where visitors sit to give their dream accounts and where Monaka asks her careful, exact questions about them. Tea is free, and there is usually one cup fewer than there are people.

The Ring Stakes.description: A line of short iron stakes driven into the floor across the corridor, a short walk from the camp, each tagged with a date and a reading, marking where the ring where nothing spawns begins. Monaka checks them every morning. The line has never moved, and stepping back inside it feels like letting out a held breath.

The Antechamber.name: The Antechamber
The Antechamber.basicInfo:
[Riftmaw Floor 97 · Recommended Level: 70-100 · Danger: Mythic (Deadly), no spawns inside the ring]

The Antechamber is a wide, ordered room on floor 97, the last chamber before the corridor to the Sealed Door, where the ring that nothing spawns in begins. The air is still, the temperature constant, and the silence changes here from quiet into something attentive. Every serious party stops in this room first. Guild teams and the Academy have made it a place for comparison: rubbings of the Door's script pinned side by side by date, recordings, notebooks and rival theories laid out together, so that nobody approaches the Door without knowing what the last party saw. There is no other passage out of it, only the way back and the way on to the Door.
The Antechamber.hiddenInfo: The rubbings do not agree, because the Door's script changes between visits, and laid side by side the changes line up with events above: new text when the Riftmaw's entrance grew, characters lit when a Reborn stood near. Three Reborn delvers once read the same word in it untaught, and the Guild classified the word. The camp in the far corner shows long use by someone who visits regularly, and nobody has ever seen them come or go.

Riftmaw 97th Floor: Antechamber.description: A wide chamber before the Door where the ring that nothing spawns in begins. The air is still, the temperature constant, and the silence turns from quiet into something that seems to listen. Research gear left by Guild teams fills one corner; in the opposite corner a small camp shows long use by someone who visits regularly and is never there.

The Rubbing Wall.description: A long wall pinned edge to edge with rubbings and copies of the Door's script, each dated and signed with a party's mark, arranged so the same passage can be read across months. Chalk lines link the characters that changed. Theories are pinned underneath and argued over in pencil.

The Instrument Corner.description: A corner crowded with monitoring crystals on tripods, recording devices and stacks of field notebooks, all humming faintly. Readings are copied out every morning and checked against the Rubbing Wall. Nobody moves an instrument without writing down where it stood, and nobody switches one off.

Veilwalkers.name: Veilwalkers
Veilwalkers.basicInfo: A secretive organization that studies the Rebirth phenomenon: the appearance of souls from other worlds in Luxcellia. Part research institute, part spy network, part support group for confused interdimensional travelers. The Veilwalkers know that the current protagonist is not the first Reborn to arrive, and they have extensive files on previous cases. Their leader is a former Reborn who arrived decades ago and has been quietly preparing for something they won't fully explain.
Veilwalkers.hiddenInfo: The Veilwalkers' leader believes the Rebirth phenomenon is accelerating toward a dimensional convergence event that will reshape Luxcellia's relationship with other worlds entirely.

Crimson Circle.name: Crimson Circle
Crimson Circle.basicInfo: An underground information network that operates across every major city in Luxcellia, trading in secrets, blackmail material, favors, and debts. The Crimson Circle is not a thieves' guild (they consider theft inelegant) but an organization of information specialists, fixers, and social engineers who know that knowledge is more valuable than any dungeon loot. Their agents are everywhere: the friendly bartender, the well-dressed stranger at the gala, the merchant who remembers your name a little too well. They operate on a strict code: information is sold, never given freely, and a Circle debt is always collected. They are not evil, but they are expensive, amoral, and they always know more than they should. Dealing with the Circle is like handling fire: useful, dangerous, and addictive.
Crimson Circle.hiddenInfo: The Crimson Circle's founder was a Reborn who arrived decades ago and used knowledge from their old world, social engineering, intelligence tradecraft, network theory, to build an organization that no one in Luxcellia had the conceptual framework to create. The current leadership doesn't know about the Rebirth connection, but the founder's old-world methods are embedded in every protocol they use.

Twilight Court.name: Twilight Court
Twilight Court.basicInfo: The governing body of the Twilight Dominion, led by Demon Lord Kuroyuki. A sophisticated government built on binding contracts, strength-based hierarchy, and pragmatic diplomacy. Maintains embassies in human nations, engages in trade, and occasionally sends terrifyingly competent diplomats to royal functions. The Court views Reborn individuals with academic curiosity and considers them potential allies rather than threats. Demon nobles are cultured, dangerous, and unfairly attractive.
Twilight Court.hiddenInfo: Kuroyuki has been collecting Reborn individuals who fled human persecution and offering them sanctuary, building a hidden community of otherworldly souls within the Dominion.

Verdant Throne.name: Verdant Throne
Verdant Throne.basicInfo: The ancient ruling body of Shingetsu Evergrove: a theocratic council of jungle priests, serpentkin elders, plant-mages, and the hereditary guardian families who have protected the deepest temple complexes for generations. The Verdant Throne governs from Verdanthrone, the living temple city where architecture grows organically from the trees themselves: bridges of woven vine, halls of shaped wood, and throne rooms where the walls breathe and the ceiling is a canopy of flowering branches. The Throne's authority is spiritual as much as political; they maintain the jungle's ecological balance, negotiate with the semi-sentient forest, and perform the seasonal rites that keep the ancient temple wards from failing catastrophically. Their warriors fight with weapons grown from ironwood and enchanted with plant magic. Their priests commune with the jungle's vast root-network, which functions as a continent-spanning communication system older than any nation. The Verdant Throne is isolationist by tradition, welcoming by temperament, and deeply conflicted about the outside world's growing interest in their ruins. They want allies but fear exploitation, and a Reborn individual who approaches them with respect rather than treasure-hunting ambition may find the warmest welcome on the continent.
Verdant Throne.hiddenInfo: The Verdant Throne's highest priests can communicate with the jungle's root network, and through it, they have detected something growing beneath the deepest temple; not a monster or an artifact, but a new Riftmaw forming around a seed of cross-dimensional energy. The jungle appears to be trying to contain it. The Throne's most closely guarded secret is that the jungle itself may be alive in a way that transcends normal biology: an ancient organism that has been protecting Luxcellia from dimensional instability for millennia.

Fanged Covenant.name: Fanged Covenant
Fanged Covenant.basicInfo: A political alliance of beastkin clans from the Verdania Wilds, united in their fight for territorial rights, political recognition, and equal treatment under continental law. Led by a council of clan elders and war chiefs, the Covenant balances traditional clan values with the pragmatic need to engage with human-dominated politics. They're fierce allies, stubborn negotiators, and will never forgive a betrayal. Their warriors are among the best on the continent, and their clan festivals are legendary.
Fanged Covenant.hiddenInfo: The Fanged Covenant possesses an oral tradition describing a Reborn arrival thousands of years ago. If verified, this would rewrite the timeline of the Rebirth phenomenon entirely.

Moonwatch Order.name: Moonwatch Order
Moonwatch Order.basicInfo: A knightly order sworn to protect Reborn individuals, believing them to be divinely sent souls whose arrival heralds a great change in Luxcellia's fate. The Moonwatch are devoted, well-trained, and operate as independent escorts, investigators, and guardians for anyone confirmed as Reborn. Their devotion is genuine and their combat skills are excellent, but their assumptions about the protagonist's 'destiny' can become suffocating. They track Rebirth events, maintain safe houses, and have standing agreements with several factions to ensure Reborn individuals receive protection. Their knights are earnest, chivalric, and tend to view the protagonist with a reverence that is flattering at first and increasingly uncomfortable. The Order's leadership includes both sincere protectors and political opportunists who see Reborn individuals as tools for advancing their faction's influence.
Moonwatch Order.hiddenInfo: The Moonwatch Order was founded after a previous Reborn individual saved the life of the Order's first Grand Master and then vanished without explanation. The Order has spent generations preparing for the next arrival. Their archives contain detailed records of at least four previous Reborn, including one who apparently chose to leave Luxcellia voluntarily: information that challenges the assumption that Rebirth is always one-directional.

The Pale Accord.name: The Pale Accord
The Pale Accord.basicInfo: A unique governing alliance between the mortal and spirit populations of Meikyo Spiritfen: a formal diplomatic framework that grants political representation to both the living and the dead. The Pale Accord operates through a dual council: mortal representatives handle physical infrastructure, trade, and external diplomacy, while spirit representatives manage the supernatural ecosystem, ancestral affairs, and cross-veil disputes. Decisions require consensus from both sides, which makes governance slow but remarkably fair. The Accord's greatest achievement is the Treaty of Mist: a binding magical contract that prevents spirits from possessing the living without consent and prevents the living from banishing spirits without cause. Violation is punished by both councils. The Accord's members include mortal mayors, spirit elders, foxkin mediums who serve as translators, and a small peacekeeping force equipped with weapons that work on both physical and spiritual threats. The faction is respected for achieving something no other region has managed: a functional democracy that includes the dead.
The Pale Accord.hiddenInfo: The Treaty of Mist has a critical flaw: it assumes the boundary between worlds will remain stable. If the veil weakens further, the treaty's enforcement mechanisms fail, and the relationship between spirits and mortals reverts to the chaotic, predatory dynamic that existed before the Accord. Several spirit elders know this and are quietly preparing contingencies that their mortal counterparts would find alarming.

Thornveil Court.name: Thornveil Court
Thornveil Court.basicInfo:
The native ruling body of the Rosethorn Nocturne: an aristocratic council of vampire-blooded houses, dark elf matriarchs, demonkin lords, and fallen celestial nobles who govern through blood pacts, seasonal courts, and elaborate social rituals that make Crownveil politics look like a school council. The Thornveil Court is not evil; it is old, beautiful, dramatic, and operates on a value system where passion, loyalty, and aesthetic excellence matter more than conventional morality.

The Thornveil Court is the reason the Rosethorn Nocturne exists as an independent region. They have maintained neutrality through centuries of blood diplomacy, strategic marriages, and the simple fact that nobody wants to fight vampire-blooded nobles in their own territory at night.

The social season is a continent-wide invitation for beautiful, powerful people to attend parties, compete for attention, and fall dangerously in love under circumstances that are never simple. A Reborn attending a Thornveil ball is fresh blood in every sense. The Court finds them fascinating. The Court's eligible heirs find them irresistible. And the blood pact governing marriage alliances contains a clause about "souls not born of this world" that nobody has triggered, until now.

The Twilight Court considers the Thornveil an eccentric cousin. The Crown considers them a political headache. The Church considers them borderline heretical. The Thornveil considers everyone else poorly dressed.
Thornveil Court.hiddenInfo: The blood pact's clause about "souls not born of this world" was written by the first Reborn to love someone from this region: meant to protect that Reborn's descendants. But it was written as a binding magical contract, and if triggered, it grants any Reborn who marries into a Thornveil house full voting rights in the Court. This would shift the Nocturne's power balance overnight. Several houses are quietly engineering encounters between their heirs and Reborn individuals, while others are determined to prevent it, and the Crimson Circle has figured this out and is selling the information to both sides.

Duskfire Wardens.name: Duskfire Wardens
Duskfire Wardens.basicInfo: An order of storm mages who maintain the ancient wind temples scattered across the Kagaribi Duskfields, channeling weather magic to sustain the region's unique perpetual twilight and protect the plains from natural disasters. The Wardens are scholars, engineers, and mages who have dedicated themselves to understanding and maintaining a system they did not build and cannot fully comprehend. Each wind temple is a complex of spinning stone pillars, resonance chambers, and weather-focusing arrays that requires constant calibration and occasional emergency repair: usually during the worst possible storm. Warden initiates train by standing in controlled wind tunnels until they can shape air currents by instinct. The fully trained Wardens can call lightning, redirect storms, and create wind barriers capable of stopping a cavalry charge. They are respected by the clans for keeping the Duskfields habitable and slightly feared for the power they wield. The Wardens' headquarters is the Grand Aerie: a wind temple built into a mesa that serves as both research facility and the best vantage point on the continent. From the Aerie's observation platform, you can see the curvature of the world.
Duskfire Wardens.hiddenInfo: The wind temples are failing. The Wardens have been compensating with increasingly desperate improvisation, but the core systems are degrading faster than they can repair them. Within a generation, the perpetual dusk will end, and the Duskfields' ecosystem will collapse. The Wardens have been secretly recruiting anyone with advanced technical knowledge, and a Reborn individual with engineering or physics background might be the breakthrough they need.

Adventurer's Guild.name: Adventurer's Guild
Adventurer's Guild.basicInfo: The continent's largest independent organization for freelance heroes, monster hunters, and dungeon explorers. Operates guild halls in every major city with a ranking system from F to S. Politically neutral by charter, practically essential to everyone. Known for competitive contracts, brutal ranking exams, and suspiciously attractive receptionists. The Guild Master is an S-Rank retired adventurer who nobody has seen fight in years, which makes everyone nervous. The Guild also charters Adventurer Companies: banners of adventurers ranked Iron to Mythril, founded at any hall by a founder and two willing partners. Anchored by the Adventurer's Guild Central Branch beneath the harbor clock tower in Portmaris, every Guild branch, however small, keeps a voluntary reading crystal for free member appraisals and a bonded materials buyer who pays daily posted rates.
Adventurer's Guild.hiddenInfo: The Guild Master is a former Reborn who arrived fifty years ago and has been quietly shaping continental events from behind the scenes.

Cinderborn Compact.name: Cinderborn Compact
Cinderborn Compact.basicInfo:
A guild-state of master smiths, volcanic miners, oni warlords, and fire mages who control the Kagutsuchi Emberwake's forge industry through craft excellence and raw territorial power. The Compact is not one organization; it is an alliance of forge clans, mining families, and oni strongholds who agreed centuries ago that cooperation beats competition when you're all living on a volcano. Every major forge in the region operates under Compact law. Every weapon worth naming was made by a Compact smith. Every member carries a forearm brand marking them as forgesworn.

The Emberwake produces the best weapons, armor, and enchanted metalwork on the continent. The Compact controls supply, making them economically powerful in ways the Merchant Lords resent and the Crown nervously respects. They're not expansionist. They don't need to be. Everyone comes to them eventually, because everyone needs a blade.

Oni courtship in the Compact is intense, physical, and demands proof at the forge or in combat before anyone takes you seriously as a romantic prospect. A Reborn who impresses a Compact smith gets an apprenticeship offer, a personal forge key, and an oni father figure who challenges them to arm-wrestling at dinner. The romance is earned through fire.

The Guild wants Compact weapons at guild prices. The Compact says no. The Crown wants Compact loyalty. The Compact says they're loyal to the mountain. The Church wants to inspect the oni blood pacts. The Compact says the Church can inspect the inside of a volcano.
Cinderborn Compact.hiddenInfo: The central caldera's dragon-heart crystal was not discovered by the Dragonkin; it was forged by the first Compact founders as a containment vessel for an ancient fire entity. The artifact the region treats as a dormant Blessing source is actually a prison, and the intensifying powers and cheat-skill mutations near the caldera are leaks from something trying to wake up. The eldest forge masters know the truth and have spent generations reinforcing the seals.

Crown of Luxcellia.name: Crown of Luxcellia
Crown of Luxcellia.basicInfo: The royal government of the Crownveil Sovereignty, led by Queen Celestine Luxcrown. Commands the Royal Knight Order, administers the noble houses, and manages the most powerful human nation on the continent. The Queen is beautiful, brilliant, and politically ruthless. She treats summoned heroes as assets, reborn individuals as variables, and her own daughter's romantic interests as matters of national security. The court is gorgeous and dangerous in equal measure.
Crown of Luxcellia.hiddenInfo: Queen Celestine has a private intelligence network that rivals the Veilwalkers' and monitors every known Reborn individual on the continent.

Crystalvein Cartel.name: Crystalvein Cartel
Crystalvein Cartel.basicInfo: The economic backbone of Kurogane Deephollow: a powerful mining and trade consortium that controls the underground's crystal economy with the efficiency of a corporation and the ruthlessness of a crime family. The Cartel mines enchanted crystals, mana-veins, rare metals, and geode formations that surface-world enchanters, artificers, and jewelers pay extraordinary prices for. They operate crystal markets, fund expedition teams, maintain trade routes between the Deephollow and surface cities, and employ a private security force that is suspiciously well-armed for a trade guild. The Cartel's leadership is a council of mining magnates: dwarven-blooded industrialists, crystal golem artificers, and deep elf gem-mages who treat commerce as art. They're not evil, but they are aggressive about profit, territorial about mining rights, and willing to bend rules that get between them and a productive vein. Their members are hardworking, competitive, and proud of building an economy in a place the surface world forgot existed.
Crystalvein Cartel.hiddenInfo: The Cartel has discovered a crystal vein that resonates specifically with Reborn souls; it amplifies Blessings and cheat skills temporarily. They've been stockpiling this crystal in secret, unsure whether to sell it, weaponize it, or destroy it before someone else does. Several Cartel members are also quietly buying information about Reborn arrivals from surface contacts.

Depthwarden Circle.name: Depthwarden Circle
Depthwarden Circle.basicInfo: The military order that keeps the Deephollow safe from the things that live below it. The Depthwardens patrol the tunnels, maintain the ancient seals, fight the deep-dwelling monsters that crawl up from levels nobody has mapped, and ensure that the subterranean civilization doesn't get eaten by whatever lurks at the bottom. They are disciplined, brave, slightly paranoid, and equipped with crystal-enhanced weapons and armor that glow in the dark, which is both tactically useful and dramatically stunning. Warden initiates undergo trials in sealed tunnels where they face darkness, isolation, and their own fears before earning their crystal-forged blades. The order is respected and feared in equal measure, and their commander, a stone-faced dwarven woman named Iron Matriarch Tsukasa, has held the deep line for thirty years without losing a seal. The Depthwardens accept recruits from any background, and surface adventurers who prove themselves in the deep tunnels earn a respect that translates across factions.
Depthwarden Circle.hiddenInfo: The Depthwardens know that the deepest sealed chamber contains something that predates the Deephollow civilization entirely: an artifact or entity that has been slowly, almost imperceptibly, weakening the seals from the inside. The rate of weakening has accelerated since the first Reborn arrived in the Deephollow, and Matriarch Tsukasa suspects a connection she cannot yet prove.

The Wandering Table.name: The Wandering Table
The Wandering Table.basicInfo: A culinary guild of traveling cooks, brewers, and food artisans who operate the continent's best mobile restaurants, appear at every major festival, and maintain a sacred neutrality that even warring factions respect. The Wandering Table's caravan-kitchens serve everyone, adventurers, nobles, demons, beastkin, clergy, because everyone needs to eat and the Table believes that shared meals prevent more wars than armies do. Their master chefs are celebrities. Their apprentices are everywhere. Their signature (a carved wooden spoon hung outside any establishment they endorse) is the most trusted quality mark in Luxcellia's food industry. Joining the Wandering Table as a patron, supplier, or apprentice opens doors across every faction, because nobody wants to be the person who offended the people who make the food.
The Wandering Table.hiddenInfo: The Wandering Table's neutrality is enforced by a binding covenant with an ancient nature spirit who protects their caravans from violence. Any attack on a Wandering Table kitchen triggers a defensive curse that makes the attacker unable to taste food for a year: a punishment that sounds trivial until you live in Luxcellia, where food is one of life's greatest pleasures. The Table's inner circle knows about this protection and uses it judiciously, but the covenant has limits they haven't fully tested.

Lanternkeep Covenant.name: Lanternkeep Covenant
Lanternkeep Covenant.basicInfo: The shrine keepers who maintain the spiritual infrastructure of Meikyo Spiritfen: the lanterns, wards, barriers, and rituals that prevent the thin boundary between worlds from collapsing entirely. The Covenant operates dozens of shrines across the fen's islands, each one a carefully maintained anchor point that keeps the mortal and spirit realms from merging completely. Their members are priests, exorcists, ward-crafters, and spirit diplomats who have dedicated their lives to walking the line between worlds. They light the lanterns at dusk, perform the binding rituals at midnight, and negotiate with restless spirits at dawn. The work is sacred, exhausting, and deeply lonely: Covenant members often develop closer relationships with spirits than with living people, which creates a distinctive melancholy that makes them fascinating and slightly heartbreaking. Their annual Lantern Drift ceremony, where thousands of spirit-lights are released onto the waterways, is one of the most beautiful events on the continent.
Lanternkeep Covenant.hiddenInfo: The Covenant's oldest records describe the catastrophic event that tore the veil, and attribute it to a Reborn individual who attempted to open a permanent passage back to their original world. The attempt failed, the Reborn vanished, and the wound in reality has never healed. The Covenant fears that another Reborn might attempt the same thing, and they monitor every Reborn who enters the fen with quiet, desperate vigilance.

Kuroyuki's Shadowhand.name: Kuroyuki's Shadowhand
Kuroyuki's Shadowhand.basicInfo:
The Demon Lord's personal network of operatives, agents, and chosen individuals who answer to Kuroyuki directly: outside the Twilight Court's diplomatic and bureaucratic apparatus. Where the Court negotiates, the Shadowhand acts. Where diplomats sign contracts, Shadowhand agents move unseen, retrieve what the Court cannot ask for publicly, and protect interests that formal diplomacy cannot acknowledge.

The Shadowhand is not an assassin's guild. It is something more dangerous: a collection of individuals Kuroyuki has personally selected for absolute loyalty, unusual competence, and the willingness to do what the Court's formal structures cannot. This includes intelligence gatherers, covert protectors of Reborn refugees, specialists in dimensional anomalies, and the rare agent whose Blessing makes them uniquely suited to tasks no one else can accomplish. Shadowhand agents do not know each other. They know only Kuroyuki and their mission.

Kuroyuki formed the Shadowhand after centuries of watching the Court's formal diplomacy fail to protect the things she actually cares about: the Reborn individuals the Court debates theoretically, the dimensional research the Veilwalkers hoard, the secrets the Church would burn. The Shadowhand exists because the Demon Lord's conscience and curiosity outpace her government's willingness to act.

A Shadowhand agent who falls for a Reborn faces a unique conflict: they report directly to the Demon Lord, who has made protecting Reborn a personal priority, but the agent's attachment would compromise their operational independence. Kuroyuki finds this hilarious and concerning in equal measure.
Kuroyuki's Shadowhand.hiddenInfo: The Shadowhand's deepest purpose is not intelligence or covert action. Kuroyuki created it to monitor the dimensional boundary that she believes caused the ancient catastrophe she's been investigating for centuries. Every agent's mission, regardless of what they're told, feeds data into her central thesis: the Rebirth phenomenon is accelerating toward an event she cannot predict, and the Twilight Court's diplomatic structures are too slow to respond. The Shadowhand is her early warning system for a catastrophe that formal governments cannot prepare for because they do not believe it exists.

Thornblood Reclamation.name: Thornblood Reclamation
Thornblood Reclamation.basicInfo: An adventurer-scholar expedition force dedicated to exploring, mapping, and recovering knowledge from the ancient temple ruins throughout Shingetsu Evergrove. The Reclamation operates base camps at the jungle's edges and sends teams of treasure hunters, archaeologists, trap specialists, and combat escorts into temple complexes that have been sealed for centuries. Their work is equal parts academic research and adrenaline-fueled dungeon diving: every expedition produces artifacts, academic papers, and stories that would make a bard weep with envy. The Reclamation's founder, a retired A-Rank adventurer who lost his arm to a temple guardian and his heart to the jungle's mystery, runs the operation from a fortified camp where artifact analysis and expedition planning happen over strong coffee and stronger language. Members are recruited from the Guild, the Academy, and the occasionally desperate; anyone who can swing a blade, read ancient script, or outrun a carnivorous vine qualifies. The Reclamation pays well, provides excellent equipment, and has a casualty rate that they describe as 'acceptable' in a tone that discourages follow-up questions.
Thornblood Reclamation.hiddenInfo: The Reclamation's deepest expedition reached a sealed inner sanctum containing inscriptions in a language that no Luxcellian scholar can read, but which a Reborn individual on the team recognized instantly as a language from their original world. The expedition leader suppressed this finding and has been privately seeking more Reborn translators. The implications of a pre-Luxcellian civilization writing in an Earth language are staggering, and the Reclamation's leadership is split on whether to publish or bury the discovery.

Windrunner Confederacy.name: Windrunner Confederacy
Windrunner Confederacy.basicInfo: The allied nomadic clans of the Kagaribi Duskfields, united under a rotating council of clan chiefs who govern through tradition, consensus, and the occasional dramatic riding challenge. The Confederacy is not a nation in the conventional sense; it is a living agreement between free peoples who chose cooperation over conquest. Each clan maintains its own territory, customs, beast herds, and internal governance while contributing riders, resources, and warriors to the Confederacy's shared defense and trade networks. The Windrunners are famous across the continent for their cavalry, their festivals, and their absolute refusal to build permanent walls. Their warriors fight from the backs of bonded storm-beasts, massive elk-like creatures with lightning-laced antlers, and their archery is performed at full gallop with an accuracy that makes Guild marksmen weep. The Great Gathering, held twice yearly, is part parliament, part festival, part marriage market, and part continent-wide party. The Confederacy welcomes travelers who respect the plains and has a standing offer to any adventurer brave enough to try the Rider's Trial: bond a storm-beast, survive the proving run, and earn clan-friend status for life.
Windrunner Confederacy.hiddenInfo: The Confederacy's oral tradition contains a prophecy about a 'Rider from Beyond the Sky'; someone not born of Luxcellia who will bond the legendary Thundermane, a storm-beast that has rejected every rider for three hundred years. The beast is real, it lives in the deepest part of the Duskfields, and it has recently begun moving toward the edges of the plains as if searching for something. The clan chiefs are divided on whether a Reborn fulfilling this prophecy would be salvation or disaster.

Cerulean Merchant Lords.name: Cerulean Merchant Lords
Cerulean Merchant Lords.basicInfo: A trade consortium that controls the Cerulean Coast's shipping lanes, major markets, and guild funding. Money is their magic and profit is their religion. They'll fund any quest, sponsor any adventurer, and back any faction: for a price and a percentage. Individual Merchant Lords range from charming philanthropists to ruthless profiteers. They maintain their own private security forces and have been known to start small wars over tariff disputes.
Cerulean Merchant Lords.hiddenInfo: The Merchant Lords have been funding both the Church and the Veilwalkers simultaneously, ensuring their profit margins regardless of which faction gains dominance.

Silver Crescent Academy.name: Silver Crescent Academy
Silver Crescent Academy.basicInfo: The continent's premier magical academy, located near Aureliath. Accepts students based on talent regardless of birth: officially. In practice, noble families wield considerable influence over admissions, faculty appointments, and curriculum. The student council president wields more political power than most minor nobles. Class rankings cause more interpersonal drama than actual wars. The Academy produces the continent's finest mages, and its alumni network is one of Luxcellia's most powerful unofficial organizations.
Silver Crescent Academy.hiddenInfo: Headmaster Soushi's research into the Rebirth phenomenon is far more extensive than anyone realizes. He's identified a pattern in Reborn arrivals that suggests they're not random.

Mirage Weavers' Conclave.name: Mirage Weavers' Conclave
Mirage Weavers' Conclave.basicInfo:
A loose collective of illusionists, reality-benders, desert sages, and truth-seekers who study and maintain the Renka Mirage Sea's unique relationship with the boundary between real and unreal. The Conclave is not a government; it is closer to a philosophy department with enforcement capabilities. They study mirages, create mirages, and determine which mirages are real, which are dangerous, and which are the desert trying to tell you something. In a region where reality is a suggestion, the people who can read the suggestions hold real power.

The Conclave maintains caravan routes by marking safe paths through mirage fields. They adjudicate disputes by determining what actually happened versus what appeared to happen. They train the region's mages. And they guard secrets about the nature of reality that the Silver Crescent Academy would study and the Church would suppress.

A Mirage Weaver who falls for a Reborn faces an existential question: is the attraction real, or is it another mirage? Reborn souls register strangely on the Conclave's instruments, somewhere between real and impossible, and a Weaver who gets close to one starts seeing things differently. The desert romance is dreamy, surreal, and punctuated by moments of startling honesty in a culture that normally communicates through beautiful lies.

The Academy considers the Conclave's approach "undisciplined." The Conclave considers the Academy "boring." The Wandering Table is their oldest ally. The Veilwalkers want the Conclave's data on dimensional anomalies, and the Conclave keeps pretending not to have any.
Mirage Weavers' Conclave.hiddenInfo: The Conclave's instruments have detected something in the deep desert that registers as more real than reality itself: an anchor point where the boundary between worlds is not thin but absent. The Veilwalkers would consider this the most important discovery in dimensional research history. The Conclave has classified it because they are not sure what would happen if someone approached it. The last mirage near the anchor showed a door that doesn't exist in any architectural style from Luxcellia, or from any world any Reborn has described.

Tidebound Shrine Keepers.name: Tidebound Shrine Keepers
Tidebound Shrine Keepers.basicInfo:
A spiritual order of shrine maidens, moon priests, and tide-readers who maintain the sacred sites across the Tsukihana Tidelace's island chain and serve as the region's informal government. They are not politicians; they are the connective tissue that holds the Tidelace together. Every island has a shrine, every shrine has a Keeper, and every Keeper answers, loosely, to the High Tide Priestess on the central island. They keep the lanterns lit, the wards maintained, the sea spirits appeased, and the tide calendar accurate. Without them, the festivals don't happen, the merfolk don't trade, and the ocean gets angry.

Crossing the Shrine Keepers doesn't get you killed. It gets you uninvited from every festival, denied harbor access, and whispered about by merfolk who will absolutely tell the sea serpents you're rude. Their power is cultural, not military, and in the Tidelace that matters more.

Shrine Keepers take vows of spiritual dedication but not celibacy. A Keeper falling for a Reborn is scandalous, beautiful, and exactly the kind of forbidden-but-not-actually-forbidden tension that makes the Tidelace run on romantic drama. The moon is always watching. The tides know your heart.

The Shrine Keepers maintain a cold war with the Cerulean Merchant Lords over the commercialization of the Tidelace's sacred festivals: fought with guest lists, harbor fees, and passive-aggressive lantern placement.
Tidebound Shrine Keepers.hiddenInfo: The High Tide Priestess receives visions during the Vanishing Isle's appearances: memories that do not belong to her. She has been quietly collecting fragments from every Reborn who has visited the island, and the pattern she's piecing together suggests that the Vanishing Isle is not a natural phenomenon. It is a door that opens from the other side, and someone has been watching Luxcellia for a very long time.

Church of the First Light.name: Church of the First Light
Church of the First Light.basicInfo: The dominant religious institution devoted to the First Light. Operates healing halls, paladin orders, and divine magic academies. The Luminous Conclave possesses genuine oracular power and claims authority over all matters of divine blessing. Publicly benevolent and charitable. Privately possessive about Reborn and Summoned individuals, politically influential, and in possession of prophecies they share very selectively. The current High Priestess smiles at everyone and trusts almost no one.
Church of the First Light.hiddenInfo: The sealed prophecy about the Rebirth phenomenon is stored beneath the Grand Cathedral. Its contents suggest the Reborn have a specific purpose that would upend the Church's current theology if revealed.

Deepwatch Lantern Company.name: Deepwatch Lantern Company
Deepwatch Lantern Company.basicInfo:
[Adventurer Company · Guild rank: Gold · Specialty: Riftmaw dives, deep mapping, rescue · Hall: Floor Zero Gatehouse, Floor Zero Gatehouse: Canteen]
The Company at the top of the Riftmaw Depth Board. Deepwatch dives deep, maps what it finds, and goes back down for anyone who did not come up. Its crest is a hooded lantern over a descending stair; a Deepwatch lantern left burning on a landing means someone is still below. Deepwatch recruits slowly, and only people who have already survived a floor.
Leader: Tetsu Tetsuō (A-rank, holds the depth record at The 97th Floor Door)
Members: Senna Yuureizuki (mid-floor veteran); Tsukasa Kuromizu (deep-tunnel cartographer, sells maps under Company contract)
Deepwatch Lantern Company.hiddenInfo: Since Tetsu came back from the bottom of The 97th Floor Door, Deepwatch's drills have changed: longer descents, rope teams, rescue practice for floors nobody has reached. The members have noticed. Tetsu has not explained what he is training them for.

The Flagon Irregulars.name: The Flagon Irregulars
The Flagon Irregulars.basicInfo:
[Adventurer Company · Guild rank: Silver · Specialty: monster bounties, warren clearing, training rookies · Hall: Ironhold, The Rusty Flagon]
A loud, generous Company that runs from a corner table at The Rusty Flagon and takes the monster bounties on Ironhold's board that would kill a rookie working alone. The Irregulars are always recruiting and never send a new member out without a veteran. Their crest is a dented tankard crossed with a troll's tooth. Rival Companies call them a nursery; the Irregulars' rookies outlive everyone else's.
Leader: Ran Kōga (veteran frontier brawler)
Members: Mika Haitsume (B-rank treasure hunter)
The Flagon Irregulars.hiddenInfo: Ran founded the Irregulars to keep a dead sergeant's promise: keep the young ones alive. Ran never speaks of the company she served in before, and the Irregulars' one hard rule, no contract with cargo nobody will name, comes from it.

Tidecrest Company.name: Tidecrest Company
Tidecrest Company.basicInfo:
[Adventurer Company · Guild rank: Silver · Specialty: sea-lane and caravan escorts, coastal dungeons · Hall: Portmaris, Portside Tavern Row]
A dashing coastal Company with the lowest loss rate on Portmaris escort contracts and the most dramatic arrivals in any harbor. Tidecrest guards ships, caravans and pearl convoys along the Cerulean Coast and dives the sea caves in between. Its crest is a breaking wave over crossed cutlasses. Tidecrest and the Gilded Caravan Company bid against each other for every rich escort on the coast.
Leader: Torao Arami (B-rank swashbuckler)
Members: Takamaru Yagami (aerial scout, flies with Tidecrest on contract); Hana Yamada (junior member, F-rank alchemist)
