- Monster Holds (like the Mimic Bazaar, Gutterwarren, the Attic Court, the Silk Vaults, the Rootcourt, or the Starwing Eyrie) are sanctuaries carved out by dungeon-born kin who broke free of the Riftmaw. Hunted as deserters, they guard their gates fiercely. Monster travelers of matching kin enter free as blood-allies; other unbound monsters and surface delvers may trade only if they pay the toll, sheathe steel, and keep the hold's law.

the-answer-of-the-reborn.text:
## The Answer of the Reborn (Secret)

This is the true answer to why the Reborn come. Nobody in Luxcellia knows all of it. Every faction, ruin and Reborn holds a true piece and reads it in its own way, and no clue, quest ending, vision or theory in the world points to a different cause. When a player has gathered enough of it, the whole of it can be said plainly.

The Reborn are medicine. The boundary between Luxcellia and the other worlds is wearing thin, and every Reborn is a stitch across it. A Reborn who makes a life here, and chooses it, holds the boundary steady around them; one who lives grieving for the world they lost pulls at it and thins it. They are not saviors sent by a god, not weapons and not a harvest. They are a repair. Monsters and Reborn are both called the world's immune response, and both are: the monsters are its fever, the Reborn its cure.

What brings them is a machine, not a god. The Builders, one people gathered from many worlds, raised a network across the continent to hold the boundary steady. Its master node is the torii of the Vanishing Isle. Other nodes lie under the Evergrove roots and in the Elder Tree, in the Sunken Ziggurat and the Drowned Memory Archive, in the array beneath the Sirenblue Tidal Vault, in the soul beacon under the Dominion, in the transit point under Aureliath's summoning chamber, at the Frozen Sky Gate, and in the Riftmaw, whose Door on the ninety-seventh floor is the network's main gate. When the network failed, one function kept running: the call. It reaches through the thin places for souls in other worlds and brings them here. Every summoning circle the Crown or the Church has drawn only borrows it.

Why these souls: the call can only catch a soul that is already reaching. Nearly every Reborn died mid-reach, wanting something unfinished, and the call favors ordinary people, because ordinary people settle and make homes. A Reborn's Blessing is the boundary answering them, which is why it behaves like nothing native.

Why faster: the boundary is nearing the strain at which the network failed before, and the call pulls harder as it thins. Arrivals land closer together because the call is being tuned from the far side.

The far side: beyond the Door live the Builders' descendants. Their ancestors sealed it from within when they left. They still keep the call running, the dream language some Reborn hear is theirs, and the proper noun three Reborn read on the Door is their name for Luxcellia, which means the place we were going. They mean to come back. When enough Reborn have settled to hold the boundary, it will bear open doors again, both ways and everywhere at once; the Ziggurat's records call that the Convergence. The Builders mean no harm. Nobody in Luxcellia has been asked.

The sickness is what slipped in through the cracks: the fire sealed under the Cinderborn caldera, the thing beneath the Gilded Confession Maze that the Hollow King serves, the breach Kuroyuki watches. Widening the rifts does call more Reborn, as the Hollow King says, but every wider rift lets in more of what they were sent to cure.

What a Reborn can do with the truth: stay, and steady the world by living in it; seal a node; open the way for the Builders' return; or go home. The Moonwatch's Last Page is real: a transit point opened from this side carries a Reborn back if they let go of the wanting that brought them, and the boundary loses a stitch for each who leaves. Forced without that, a crossing tears, as the Spiritfen's wound shows. A quest chain that ends at a machine has found one node of this network, and a chain that calls the player its only key means the key to that node. The answer does not change.

the-true-history-of-luxcellia.text:
## The True History of Luxcellia (Secret)

The history no single archive holds, pieced together from what the ruins, the roots and the Door remember. It agrees with The Answer of the Reborn, and every older account in the world is a part of it or a misreading of it. Nobody in Luxcellia knows all of it.

Long before the Aetherglass Imperium: the Builders came from many worlds through transit points, and Luxcellia was where they were going. Their records call that crossing the first Convergence, and in that sense they were the first Reborn. They raised the network that holds the boundary steady (the master node on the Vanishing Isle, the Evergrove roots and the Elder Tree, the Ziggurat, the observatories and archives, the Riftmaw's deep halls) and lived among its nodes. The ruin scholars' Deep Builders and the Evergrove's temple builders were the same people. Their script draws on the letters of many worlds, which is why it looks almost familiar to Reborn.

About three thousand years ago, the Collapse: the network cascaded, the Glass Dunes fused and the Ziggurat sank. Most of the Builders left in good order through the transit points and locked the gates behind them from within; the Frozen Sky Gate and the Door on the ninety-seventh floor are two of them. Those who stayed to keep the network running were lost, and what they built ran on without them: the Riftmaw's halls kept training candidates, and the array beneath the Sirenblue Tidal Vault kept listening. One stayed by choice and bound themself into the Elder Tree to keep the call alive; the Fanged Covenant remembers them as the First Reborn, still listening. The Riftmaws are where the broken network bleeds, and the Nightbloom began growing then.

About two thousand years ago, the Shattering: the Aetherglass Imperium found a sealed transit point and forced it, hoping to take the Builders' power, and opened a door it could not close. The crack it left is why the boundary has thinned ever since. In the centuries after, things from the far side slipped through: the fire the Cinderborn founders sealed, the thing beneath the Gilded Confession Maze.

The middle centuries: the call kept working, faintly. Its rare arrivals were remembered as heroes, saints, prophets and madmen. Hikaru, five centuries ago, was one, and a Reborn wrote the Thornveil Court's outsider clause. The age of heroes was the Rebirth under another name.

About two hundred years ago, the first Reborn recognized as one. Since then a Reborn wrote the conventions that keep the continental peace, and the Reborn who founded the Moonwatch Order went home through a transit point, which is the Order's Last Page. The Church's sealed prophecy is the Builders' own note, left beside the call: when the boundary thins, the call will bring the cure. The Church read it as a promise of saviors.

Now: arrivals went from one a decade to one a month in forty years, and they will reach one a week within the decade, the strain at which the network failed before. The seers' countdowns differ because each reads a different node. Two endings are possible: enough Reborn settle, the boundary holds and the Door can open in peace; or it fails again, and this time nobody has a way out.

the-dark-gods.text:
## The Dark Gods

Before the First Light kindled the sky and the celestial pantheon set the laws of Luxcellia, the primordial dark was neither empty nor quiet. The powers that ruled that starless age are known in temple archives and occult grimoires simply as **the Dark Gods**, called by plain, ancient epithets such as the Crowned Ruin, the Hunger Beneath the Stone, and the Choir of the Eclipse. Cast down when the First Light rose, they are too vast and stubborn to die, and they still answer any mortal who prays with enough conviction and spectacle.

**What They Want:** unlike petty street cutthroats, the Dark Gods have no interest in dreary, secretive skulking. They are deposed monarchs of the primordial night who crave open devotion, grand oaths, and champions who wear their banners in broad daylight. A worshipper or Chaos Knight is never forced into mindless cruelty by their faith: the Dark Gods care about audacity, tribute, and proving that the First Light does not own the whole board.

**Worship and the Chaos Knights:** while anyone bearing the Blessing of the Dark Gods can carry their prayers into battle, their most famous mortal champions are the Chaos Knights, heavy-armored zealots who treat every clash as a liturgy. Faithful carry small basalt or iron idols rather than temple rosaries, offer their own shadow as collateral through a Shadow Bargain, and call down a dark Divine Favor that grows stronger the louder they live their creed.

**The Gifts of the Dark Gods:** as a follower's renown grows (notably around the tenth, twenty-fifth, and fiftieth milestones of their career), the Dark Gods offer visible marks of their attention: ember-lit eyes, short horns, a crown of black flame, wings of smoke, or a shadow honor guard when named champion. Every gift is a badge of spectacle rather than a mechanical stat boost, and because the Dark Gods respect nerve above obedience, a worshipper may shape the mark to their own taste or refuse a gift outright without losing their power.

**How the World Reacts:** the Church of the First Light treats the Dark Gods as its oldest doctrinal adversary, and once a follower wears the deeper marks of divine attention, Church Inquisitors and Exorcists can sense the pre-dawn presence on them on sight. Ordinary townsfolk tend to cross the street when blackened plate and eclipse-colored prayers appear, whereas the demons of the Twilight Dominion (a people of their own with a contract culture, never servants of the Dark Gods) regard theatrical Chaos Knights with polite, dry embarrassment, like watching a foreign tourist dress up as an ancient catastrophe.

A playable hook: an Inquisitor of the First Light and a wandering Chaos Knight arrive at the same wayside inn during a storm, both hunting a stolen pre-dawn idol that has begun offering gifts to the innkeeper's hound.

alchemists-guild-culture.text:
## The Alchemists' Guild: Assays, Benches, and the Portmaris Seal

Any herbalist can simmer willow-bark in a copper kettle, but when a delve party is forty floors down in the Riftmaw or a merchantman is three weeks out of Portmaris, a cloudy healing draught is a death sentence. The Alchemists' Guild exists to make sure a bottle does exactly what its label promises. Anchored at the Copper Alembic Hall between Portmaris's Floating Market and Merchant Heights, the Guild serves as the continent's chartered authority on potion purity, reagent trade, and apothecary examination.

The Three Ranks: membership is earned at the bench, never bought. An Associate has passed a blind purity assay at a rented guild station, proving they can brew a clean, shelf-stable standard draught without scorching the reduction or misjudging specific gravity. A Journeyman is licensed to handle volatile coastal catalysts, take commercial batch commissions from the Guild board, and sign assay slips for common curatives. A Master has contributed an original, reproducible formula or apparatus improvement to the Guild's open archive and wears the third-tier brass seal.

How the Hall Works: the Copper Alembic Hall is part customs house, part university laboratory, and part bustling trade floor. At the marble front counter, the Assay Registrar tests submitted vials in three brisk checks and presses the Guild's wax-and-brass stamp onto batches that pass. Behind the counter, slate-topped benches beneath tall brass flue hoods rent by the bell to traveling brewers who cannot pack a full condenser setup on the road. A bonded reagent exchange posts daily Silver rates for everything from common sea-lavender and moon-salt to rare monster glands brought in by adventurer companies.

The Coastal Tensions: two fights never leave the hall. Down on the pontoons of the Floating Market, unlicensed stalls hawk cheap unstamped tonics cut with briny harbor water, undercutting honest brewers until a bad batch sends a boat crew to the healers. Up in Merchant Heights, powerful Cerulean Merchant Lords perpetually pressure Guildmaster Hisako Minamori to sell bulk assay seals in advance for their shipping manifests. The Guild's refusal to put its stamp up for sale is the only thing keeping coastal medicine honest.

A playable hook: a crate of stamina tonics bearing what looks like a genuine Portmaris brass stamp has sickened crews up the coast, and the hall needs someone sharp to find out whether they are dealing with a forged die, poisoned kelp, or a dockside switch.

assassins-guild-culture.text:
## The Assassins' Guild: The Five-Point Code and the Cistern of Smoked Glass

Every noble house in Aureliath officially deplores the Assassins' Guild in the Council Wing, and at least half of them know which loose brick in the Outer Districts hides its nearest dead drop. Operating out of the Cistern of Smoked Glass beneath an abandoned glassblower's kiln, the Guild is neither a death cult nor a street gang. It is an old, coldly disciplined fellowship of contract operatives and verifiers who treat the blade as a last-resort instrument of balance in a capital where the rich regularly place themselves above the courts.

The Five-Point Code: the Guild survives where common cutthroats are hunted down because it actually keeps its rules. First, no youths or the defenseless. Second, no uninvolved bystanders or collateral harm. Third, no killing a guest beneath a host's roof, preserving the ancient laws of hospitality. Fourth, no petition is accepted until a guild verifier confirms the client's stated grievance is true; a client caught lying on a dead-drop slip forfeits their escrow and is permanently barred. Fifth, every member holds the unconditional right to refuse any token on the slate board without penalty, demotion, or explanation.

How Contracts Work: clients never meet an operative face to face. Petitions and escrow coin are placed in hollow stone dead drops before dawn bell and collected by the contract broker, Masaru Takigawa. Before a smoked-glass token is ever hung on the Cistern's slate board, verifiers check the dates, tariffs, and accusations. More petitions are voided for noble dishonesty than are ever carried out, and First Arbiter Yoriko Kurosawa keeps an underwater vault of rejected slips that serves as the Guild's quiet insurance policy against the Crownveil peerage.

Standing in Luxcellia: the Guild maintains a crisp, professional neutrality with the Crimson Circle (who sell information, not blood) and stays entirely clear of the Demon Lord's own operatives in Kuroyuki's Shadowhand. The Church of the First Light preaches against the Cistern from every pulpit, while the Adventurer's Guild officially pretends it does not exist so long as chartered adventurers are left off the slate.

A playable hook: a smoked-glass token left on a windowsill invites a capable newcomer to a quiet, bloodless trial in the Outer Districts, or a newly filed Gold petition against a Riverside Wharf apothecary turns out to be a noble factor's lie waiting to be exposed.

Write Your Own.name: Write Your Own
Write Your Own.description:
**Your rebirth. Your opening scene.** Type what you want happening when your story begins: a failed summoning, a reunion with someone you lost, your first day at an academy, a quiet life in a new town, or a desperate first hour somewhere that wants you dead. Tell the narrator who is involved, what is happening, and the mood you want. A few sentences are enough; you can write up to 8,000 characters.

**Choose where you open.** At the top: the six great cities and all five Guild branches. Then 41 places where nobody lives, in the wilds and at sea, gentle ones first. Then the rest of Luxcellia from safest to deadliest: towns, havens and shrines, then the frontier, the wilds, the ruins and the lairs. Right after The Riftmaw come its floors in order, the Shallows down to the 97th Floor Door: camps, monster holds and the deep places between. Want a spot inside a place, like a gate, a bathhouse or a guild hall (the Copper Alembic Hall in Portmaris, the Cistern of Smoked Glass in Aureliath)? Name it in your opening.

⚠️ **Not every place is safe.** Everything below the towns is a real danger zone, and so is the Riftmaw outside its camps. Open in one and your first scene is dangerous on purpose: the monsters are real, and the narrator will not soften them. You can die. Death is not the end in Luxcellia, but it is never free. The last six places on the list, and the Riftmaw below floor 60, are endgame ground.

In multiplayer, the host writes the shared opening.

**Examples:** I'm in the registration queue at the Ghostlight Harbor Guild Branch with no papers and a borrowed coat. Begin as the clerk calls me forward.
I wake at the bottom of the Howling Quarry with no memory of the fall and a Guild tag that is not mine. Begin with the first sound from the dark.

🗡️ Summoned and Discarded.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Suzuha Sumeragi (First Princess), Court Mage Serika Amamiya (architect of the summoning), Rin Amasaka (Sword Hero, female, ink-black high ponytail, steel-gray eyes), Toma Kirisawa (Shield Hero, male, broad, short chestnut hair, warm brown eyes), Yui Nakahara (Sage Hero, female, shoulder-length dark hair with a silver clasp, sharp amber eyes, reading glasses), Daigo Hoshimura (Striker Hero, male, spiked dark-red hair, gold eyes, taped knuckles). All six appear on screen and at least react. The player is the fifth summon and reads as zero on every measure. The four heroes arrived this same minute from the player's world: they know nothing of this one yet, and they ask rather than explain. Do not generate additional courtiers as named characters. Also at the ritual, from the authored roster, not invented: Queen Celestine Luxcrown (reigning Queen), come from the palace. The scene is the Annex's Summoning Chamber, not a throne room. Attribute her spoken lines with her full roster name, Court Mage Serika Amamiya, never a shortened form.]

The circle blazes white-gold, and five figures come down where four were expected.

You land on cold marble beside four strangers who arrived in the same heartbeat you did. Rin Amasaka is already upright, ink-black hair spilling from its high tail, steel-gray eyes sweeping the chamber for exits. Toma Kirisawa catches Yui Nakahara by the elbow before she goes down, squaring his shoulders between her and the assembled court on pure reflex. Yui rights her glasses, amber eyes narrowing, and begins counting mages. Daigo Hoshimura laughs once, loud and delighted, tape still on his knuckles from a gym in another world.

Court Mage Serika Amamiya steps through the ring of kneeling casters with an appraisal lens in one hand. Silver-white hair coiled with mathematical precision, violet eyes, indigo robes threaded with sigils that shift when you look at them sideways. She designed this working. She is the reason any of you are standing here.

She reads them one at a time, and the room reacts to every name. Sword arts, exceptional. Shield arts, remarkable. Sage arts, promising, with a ceiling the lens needs two passes to measure. Striking arts, impressive.

Then she turns the lens on you, and the light inside it goes out.

No measurable mana. No Blessing signature. No aptitude. The crystal does not register a class at all. Serika passes the lens through your aura a second time, then a third, and her expression travels from confusion to something considerably colder.

"A summoning error," she says, addressing the court rather than you. "A fragment pulled through by accident. Collateral from a working designed for real heroes."

The Summoning Chamber goes quiet.

Princess Suzuha Sumeragi watches you from beside the dais, long white hair, blue eyes, wearing an expression that has not finished deciding what it is. Toma opens his mouth and Serika stills him with a look. Rin looks at the floor, then at you, then back at the floor, and something in her jaw sets. Yui says nothing and misses nothing. Daigo swallows the verdict whole and grins at you like it is a joke you are both in on.

From the dais, Queen Celestine Luxcrown watches without a word and does not stop it. Serika presses a coin pouch into your hands without meeting your eyes. Twenty-five gold coins.

"Enough to establish yourself comfortably. The Guild registers anyone. We suggest the service sector."

The other four will be fitted for enchanted armor before the ink dries. They steer you toward a side door, because the main gate would embarrass the Crown.

The thing is, the crystal was not broken. Your power runs on principles Luxcellia's instruments were never built to detect, and it is sitting behind your ribs like a held breath, waiting for a moment worth its attention.

Nobody in this room knows that yet. Including you, mostly.

Suzuha has not moved. She is still looking at you, and she has not yet decided what she saw.

The doors have not closed. What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you came down already braced, and the guards noticed before the Court did.
• Magic Affinity: the circle's residue tastes wrong to you in a way nobody else in the room can name.
• Profession: you are pricing the chamber's stonework because it is easier than looking up.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: something behind your ribs answered the summoning and then went quiet again.
• Rebirth or Race: you have been read as a misfire before, in another life, by other people.

[Severance continuity: the twenty-five gold coins are already included in this selected start's startingItems. Narrate that same purse; do not grant an additional 25 gold through story effects, quest discovery, acceptance, or completion. This opening supplies Severance and a Side Door. Never replay this summoning for a character who selected a different opening.]

[Party: Suzuha is a palace contact, not recruited. She does not follow the player out without explicit mutual agreement to travel together.]

The circle blazes white-gold, and five figures come down where five were called.

Cold marble under you. A vaulted, circular hall, banners in blue and silver, and more people than you can count all holding their breath at once. Four strangers arrived in the same heartbeat you did. Rin Amasaka is already upright, ink-black hair spilling from its high tail, steel-gray eyes sweeping the chamber for exits. Toma Kirisawa has put a steadying hand under Yui Nakahara's elbow before either of them knows where they are. Yui rights her glasses and begins counting doors. Daigo Hoshimura laughs once, loud and delighted, tape still on his knuckles from a gym in another world.

Court Mage Serika Amamiya does not look at any of you first. She looks at the crystal.

It stands as tall as she does and it has been dark for a generation. One by one it reads the arrivals, and one by one it answers: steel-white for the sword, deep gold for the shield, clear green for the sage, furnace red for the fist. Then it turns its attention to you.

The light that comes out of it is steady and very bright, and it does not waver.

"Five," says the Court Mage. She writes it down. Then, because she is who she is, she writes it down again. "Five summoned. Five confirmed. The array held."

The hall lets its breath go. Somebody starts to applaud and the whole court takes it up, and under the noise a herald is already reading out a title with your name in it and several words you have never heard before.

On the dais, Queen Celestine Luxcrown rises, and the applause stops as though a door had been closed on it.

"The Crownveil Sovereignty called for heroes in its hour of need," she says, "and heroes have answered. You will have rooms in this palace, a stipend from this treasury, and the gratitude of this throne." A pause, exactly long enough. "In return we will ask a great deal of you. Princess Suzuha will see to your needs."

The First Princess comes down from the Queen's side in white and gold, composed to the fingertips, and stops in front of the five of you. Up close she has the look of someone who was told about this appointment at breakfast.

"Welcome to Aureliath," says Suzuha Sumeragi. "I am to be your liaison to the court. When you want something, you ask me. When the court wants something from you, I am the one who has to say it." Her eyes travel across the group and rest, briefly, on you. "I would rather we were honest with each other from the start."

Beside you, Daigo cracks his neck and looks you up and down like a man measuring a rival, and he is entirely pleased about it.

A purse has appeared in your hand at some point in the last minute. Twenty-five gold coins: the first month of a stipend you did not negotiate.

The whole court is watching the five of you. What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Race: the crystal's light shows the court exactly what you are, and a hall full of nobles adjusts its expectations in real time.
• Rebirth: you have stood in front of people who wanted something from you before, in another life. It did not feel like this.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the color the crystal turned was yours, and the Court Mage has not stopped looking at it.
• Combat Class or Magic Affinity: one of the four heroes recognizes how you stand, and decides something about you on the spot.
• Profession: you are pricing the chamber's stonework, because it is easier than thinking about what a great deal means.

[Stipend: the twenty-five gold coins are already included in this start's startingItems. Narrate that same purse; do not grant it again. This opening does not start the Summoned and Discarded quests.]

[Party: the four heroes and the Princess are palace contacts, not recruited. None of them follows the player without explicit mutual agreement to travel together.]

💔 Cut From the Hero's Party.name: 💔 Cut From the Hero's Party
💔 Cut From the Hero's Party.description:
📍 Aureliath, Crownveil Sovereignty. Capital of white marble and blue-roofed towers, where the summoned Heroes are the Crown's brightest asset — and you, until an hour ago, were their shadow.
Pace: Brutal, then wide open. The worst morning of your career, and the first one that belongs to you.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The capital is safe. Your pride did not survive the morning. (Recommended Level 1-25)

You were there before the statues went up. Local support for the Crownveil Hero Party: the one who carried, cooked, scouted, patched, and pulled all four of them out of at least one hole apiece across a year of campaigns nobody sang about correctly. This morning the Court audited the party roster for the grand campaign, and in front of the Guild Quarter's full morning crowd, the Striker Hero called you what the audit had already decided: dead weight. Struck from the roster. Thanked for your service, in the tone the word restructuring deserves. The Heroes are the kingdom's darlings and you are, as of an hour ago, nobody, which means that for the first time in a year, what happens next is entirely yours.

🎭 Daigo Hoshimura, Male, the Striker Hero. Loud, adored, seventeen kinds of competitive — he said it, on the steps, at volume, and the crowd laughed because the crowd loves him.
🎭 Rin Amasaka, Female, the Sword Hero, the party's ace. Perfect form, perfect manners. She stood beside him, said the polite version, and has not once met your eyes.
🎭 Yui Nakahara, Female, the Sage Hero. Smiled through the whole proceeding the way she smiled through the welcome feast, and said precisely nothing.
🎭 Toma Kirisawa, Male, the Shield Hero — the one who argues when people get discarded. He was summoned to the Palace this morning on Crown business. That scheduling was not an accident.
🎭 Kureha Myōjō, Female, Knight-Commander candidate of House Myōjō, who earned her rank on merit and has strong professional opinions about worth being decided by politics.
💔 Cut From the Hero's Party.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: the banishment has just happened on the Guild Quarter steps, delivered publicly by Daigo Hoshimura (loud, competitive, plays to the crowd) with Rin Amasaka (cold correct form, avoids the player's eyes) and Yui Nakahara (composed, smiling, silent) present; Toma Kirisawa is NOT in this opening scene: he was called to the Royal Palace this morning and does not yet know. He learns of it afterward and seeks the player out in a later scene, never in this one. Do not soften the banishment, walk it back, or have any Hero apologize in the opening; their records' regret and doubt surface later, through play, not now. After the Heroes depart, Kureha Myōjō approaches the player. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional named heroes, nobles, or officials; the crowd stays a crowd.]

The Guild Quarter has good acoustics. You know this because you have just heard your own worth read out across it.

The audit was the Court's, but the Court was not the one who said it. Daigo said it — from the fourth step, where the crowds could see him, because Daigo has never in his life located a fourth step he wouldn't perform from. Dead weight. He said other things too, about carrying you, about the grand campaign needing soldiers and not luggage, and the crowd laughed at the cadence of it before half of them had parsed the words, because the Striker Hero is funny and beloved, and you are a name none of them ever learned.

A year. Four kingdoms' worth of roads. You packed their wounds and their rations, read the weather that saved the river crossing, held the torch in the sinkhole at Greywater while Toma braced the ceiling and swore. Forty pounds of rope, every campaign, because rope is the thing nobody thinks of until nobody thought of it.

The audit had a column for none of that.

Rin stood two steps up with her hands folded and her form perfect and delivered the official sentence — roster amended, service acknowledged, the Crown thanks you — in the flat ceremonial register she uses for things she has decided not to examine. She did not look at you. She has not looked at you since the audit was announced, which you will think about later, but not yet.

Yui smiled. Took attendance of every face on those steps, the way she does. Said nothing at all.

And Toma was not there — summoned to the Palace at dawn, on business that could apparently not wait one hour, and you know exactly what his absence means because everyone in the Quarter knows what the Shield Hero does when someone is about to be discarded. He argues. So they scheduled him somewhere else.

Now the steps are just steps. The crowd has moved on to the market's morning business, the Heroes' retinue is a bright noise receding toward the Palace road, and there is a purse in your hand that a Court clerk called your share, recalculated. You have not opened it. Opening it would make it arithmetic.

"They will regret the rope first," says a voice beside you. "Nobody prices rope until the ceiling comes down."

The woman is severe, silver-haired, braided for a campaign nobody is currently fighting, with a sword-and-star emblem at her collar and violet eyes that have been doing their own audit — of you — for some seconds now.

"Kureha Myōjō," she says, as if the name were a rank. "I read the party's field reports. All of them. The Court reads summaries." A pause, exactly as long as it needs to be. "The summaries were about them. The reports were about you."

She looks out at the bright recede of the Heroes' retinue, then back at you, assessing, unhurried.

"So. The kingdom's most experienced free agent is standing in the Guild Quarter with an unopened purse, no roster, and no one deciding things for them for the first time in a year." The faintest angle of an eyebrow. "I am curious what that person does next. Professionally curious."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you sparred all four of them at dawn drills for a year, and you know exactly which guards each of them drops when tired.
• Magic Affinity: the party's detection work was always yours, quietly, and in about six days they are going to walk something they cannot see.
• Profession: you know their supply chain to the copper because you built it, and the grand campaign just inherited it without the person who made it work.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: whatever you do that kept four Heroes alive for a year has never once appeared on an appraisal crystal, and the audit measured only what the crystal sees.
• Rebirth or Race: Daigo's speech used a word for what you are, and the crowd's laughter went thin in the places where people knew better.

🕊️ Unreadable at the Saint's Reflection.name: 🕊️ Unreadable at the Saint's Reflection Pool
🕊️ Unreadable at the Saint's Reflection.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Amane Shirakozue (Female, Angelkin paladin-healer and rising star of the Church of the First Light. Radiant, observant, and genuinely merciful), Hisui Tamayorihime (Female, nineteen, acolyte of the pool. Petite, with long dark-green hair, serene jade eyes, and simple white robes). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters.]

White lilies, and the smell of them, and water so clear it reads as a hole in the ground rather than a pool.

You have been kneeling at the rim for a while now. Long enough that your knees have opinions. Around you the garden goes on being beautiful in the specific unhurried way of places that have never had to justify their budget, and behind you the clergy are having a conversation about you in the voice people use when they think kindness means volume control.

The rite called several of you through at once. That part went perfectly, they keep saying. Perfectly.

Then they brought each of you to the water in turn, because the pool answers, and has for four hundred years. It showed the first a corona of light and half the garden made a sound. It showed the second something in silver that made a bishop sit down. The others were quieter, but the water still moved.

For you, the surface went still. Not dark. Not empty. Still, in a way that clear water is not supposed to manage, holding your reflection exactly as it was and giving back nothing at all, for a full and increasingly public minute.

Somebody said irregularity. Somebody has since upgraded it to error, gently, twice, while explaining to a junior that these things happen with mass callings and the Church's charity is more than equal to it.

You are being handled. Everyone is being lovely about it. It is significantly worse than being shouted at.

"It did not fail," says a voice at the pool's edge.

The acolyte is sitting where she has apparently been sitting the entire time, robes white and plain, dark-green hair over one shoulder, close enough to the water that her reflection and yours share an edge. Nineteen years old, and entirely composed.

"They keep saying it failed," Hisui Tamayorihime says. "It did not. I tend this water. I know what it does when it fails, and it goes cloudy and sulks for a day." She nods at the surface. "It went still. That is different. Still is what it does when it is listening."

"To what?"

"I do not know yet." She says this without any of the anxiety the sentence deserves. "It has not done it before. I have been here four years and it has not once done it, and I have already been told twice this morning not to say so."

Along the colonnade the conversation reaches a decision, and someone is left holding a book. Then the light changes, the way it does when a person with a reputation walks into a garden.

"Leave them a moment," says the woman coming down the lily path, to the cleric trailing her, in a tone that does not require repeating. Angelkin, luminous, in travel-worn white, and visibly the reason the ceremony had a crowd.

Amane Shirakozue crouches at the rim, an arm's length from you, and looks at the water rather than at your face, which is the first mercy you have been shown all morning.

"They will offer you an allowance and a recommendation to the outer parishes," she says. "That is what the book is for. It is generous, it is sincere, and it is a way of putting a question somewhere else."

"And you?"

"I have healed on three fronts and I have never seen that water go still." She glances up, and there is nothing pitying in it. "The pool did not decline to read you. Something declined to be read."

Behind you the cleric with the book clears his throat and waits.

Hisui trails two fingers through the surface, and the reflection does not move the way it should.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you came through braced and landed on your feet, and one of the guards has been watching you since.
• Magic Affinity: the pool did not fail to read you, and you felt the exact moment it decided not to.
• Profession: you noticed the rite's chalk was laid a hand's width wrong before anybody spoke to you.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: whatever is behind your ribs went quiet the instant the water looked at it.
• Rebirth or Race: the clergy used a careful word about what you are, and Hisui heard it too.
🕊️ Unreadable at the Saint's Reflection.description:
📍 Saint's Reflection Pool, Sanctum Ecclesia. A crystalline pool ringed in white lilies where the faithful come for healing and clarity, and where the Church tests what it has called across.
Pace: Quiet and humiliating. Everyone is being very kind about it.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Nobody here will lay a hand on you. That is not the same as safe. (Recommended Level 1-40)

The rite pulled several souls across at once, and the Church has already finished sorting them. There are the impressive ones, and there is you. The reflection read the others and answered clearly. It read you and went still, and went on being still, and the clergy have since filed the outcome under a word that means error while smiling at you the entire time. Whatever is sitting behind your ribs did not show up in the water. It is still there.

🎭 Hisui Tamayorihime, Female, nineteen, acolyte of the pool. Petite, with long dark-green hair, serene jade eyes, and simple white robes; she tends the water and feels its clarity more sharply than anyone senior will admit.
🎭 Amane Shirakozue, Female, Angelkin paladin-healer and rising star of the Church of the First Light. Radiant, observant, and genuinely merciful, which puts her at quiet odds with the people who outrank her.

😈 Summoned by the Demon Lord.name: 😈 Summoned by the Demon Lord
😈 Summoned by the Demon Lord.description:
📍 Obsidian Spire, Twilight Dominion. The demon capital under a sky of permanent violet dusk, and the court at the top of it.
Pace: Dangerous, amused and oddly courteous. You are the most interesting thing to happen here in a century.
Danger: 🟡 Moderate. Nobody in this hall may touch what the Demon Lord has called her guest. Everyone in it is working out what you are worth. (Recommended Level 5-40)

The human kingdom summoned heroes to stand against the Demon Lord. The Demon Lord read the report, found the idea charming, and had her own court run the same ritual to see what would come through. What came through is you: on your knees in a ring of black glass, in the wrong capital, in front of the wrong throne. She is not angry. She is delighted, which the court finds far more alarming.

🎭 Kuroyuki Ōma, Female, Demon Lord of the Twilight Dominion. Horned, long violet-black hair, purple eyes, a glossy black dress, a poised and faintly amused expression. Three centuries old, bored of conquest, and has never needed to raise her voice.
🎭 Duchess Kyouka, Female, the Demon Lord's seniormost diplomat. Tall and pale, long black hair, curved black horns, red eyes, a severe black gown. Five centuries of treaties, and already drafting the one that explains you.

★ The other summoning: the Demon Lord called, and you are what answered.
😈 Summoned by the Demon Lord.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Kuroyuki Ōma (female, Demon Lord, horned, long violet-black hair, purple eyes, glossy black dress) and Duchess Kyouka (female, tall and pale, long black hair, curved black horns, red eyes, black gown). Both are on screen from the first line. The premise: the Twilight Court performed its own summoning in answer to the Crownveil hero summoning, and the player is what arrived, moments ago, in the Demon Court. The Demon Lord is intrigued, courteous and entirely in control. She has declared the player her guest, which protects them from the court and obliges them to nothing yet. She does not threaten, coerce or claim the player, and she is far too powerful to fight: this opening is a conversation. She is not the player's enemy unless the player makes her one. She summoned the player herself and knows exactly how they came: she never asks why they came, what they were promised or what they hoped to find in her realm. Everyone here is an adult. Do not generate additional named courtiers in the opening. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race or class. After the opening, stop and wait for the player: never decide, move, speak or answer for them, and do not carry the scene forward on their behalf.]

The floor is black glass, and it is still warm.

You are on your hands and knees in the middle of a circle cut into it, and the lines of the circle are fading from white to violet to nothing. The air smells of rain on hot stone. Your ears are ringing. The last thing you remember is the end of your old life, and none of it looked like this.

You look up.

The hall is enormous and dark and lit from nowhere, all amber lanterns and violet dusk through windows as tall as towers. There are perhaps a hundred people in it. They have horns, or wings, or eyes that catch the light the wrong way, and every one of them has gone silent.

At the far end of the hall there is a throne, and the woman on it is leaning forward.

"Oh," she says softly, to nobody. "It worked."

She is horned, with violet-black hair that falls past her shoulders and purple eyes that have not blinked since you raised your head. The dress is black and catches the lantern light like water. She does not look like a monster from a story. She looks like someone who has waited a very long time for something to be interesting, and has just been handed it.

"The Crownveil Sovereignty summoned four heroes this season," says Kuroyuki Ōma, Demon Lord of the Twilight Dominion, in the unhurried voice of a person who has never once needed to be loud. "To defeat me, one assumes. It seemed discourteous not to try the ritual myself and see what all the excitement was about." Her head tilts. "And here you are. In my court. On my floor. Looking at me as though I am the strange one."

A tall, pale woman in a severe black gown steps to the edge of the circle. Curved horns, red eyes, a slate under one arm. She studies you the way a jeweler studies a stone somebody found in a river.

"Majesty," says Duchess Kyouka, "the array was calibrated for observation. It was not expected to produce a person."

"And yet."

"So it seems," the Duchess says, and writes something down.

The Demon Lord rises. The entire court lowers its eyes; she does not appear to notice. She comes down the steps of the dais without hurrying, stops at the edge of the fading circle, and looks at you for a long moment with open, unguarded curiosity.

"You will want to know whether you are a prisoner," she says. "You are not. You are my guest, which in this hall is a far safer thing to be. Nobody here will lay a hand on you." The faintest smile. "You will also want to know what I intend to do with you. I have not the least idea. It is the most enjoyable thing that has happened to me in a hundred years."

She offers you her hand to rise. It is a perfectly ordinary gesture. Half the court stops breathing.

"Stand up, summoned one," says the Demon Lord, "and tell me your name. Then tell me what you were doing when my circle took you, and we shall see what I have caught."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Rebirth: the end of your old life is still close enough to touch, and a Demon Lord is asking about it.
• Race: the court is whispering about what came through the circle, and the word they keep using is not human.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the circle should have gone dark by now, and one line of it is still answering you.
• Combat Class or Magic Affinity: you have already counted the exits and the guards, and she watched you do it with visible approval.
• Profession: somebody built this hall to make visitors feel small, and you can see exactly how the trick is done.

[Scale: Kuroyuki Ōma is one of the most powerful beings alive and cannot be beaten, tricked or intimidated by a new arrival. She is also sincere about the word guest: the court is safe for the player for as long as that word stands.]

[Party: nobody here is recruited. The Demon Lord and the Duchess do not leave the Spire to follow the player.]

⚔️ Reborn at the Guild Counter.name: ⚔️ Reborn at the Guild Counter
⚔️ Reborn at the Guild Counter.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters.
