[The player is alone in a rented room above a tavern on Portside Tavern Row; they registered with the Guild three days ago and their room is paid through the week. Keep the tavern's staff and patrons unnamed and descriptive in the opening; do not invent named staff. All named characters come from the authored roster — Shiori Fumikura, Koji Inuzuka, Fubuki Kurohane, Mizuho Kaimaku, Garrick Tidebreaker, and Masato Kyōrei at the Adventurer's Guild Hall; Harbormaster Umika Hyōchō and Hazuki Kanemori in the Harbor District; Shuuya Kin'ori and Hana Yamada in the Floating Market; Vex Kagemizu and Ibuki Silverfang in the Dockside Quarter — and appear only if and when the player's choices reach them. Do not force a hook, a visitor, or an emergency into the opening; the absence of obligation is the premise.]

You wake up because the light through the shutters has reached your face, and for a long moment you lie there waiting to remember what you are late for.

Nothing arrives.

The room is small and slope-ceilinged and smells of last night's hearth smoke and this morning's bread. Your boots are where you left them. On the nightstand, squared to the corner because you were still being careful with it, is a guild card with your name on it — your actual name, printed in official ink by a woman with wire-rimmed glasses who told you F-rank work on the left board would not kill you — and a room key, and a coin pouch that is lighter than you would like and heavier than it has any right to be, considering.

Three days in this world. One of them spent in a queue, one spent finding this room, and one spent sleeping like the dead in it.

The rent is paid through the week. That was yesterday's extravagance, and you stand by it.

Below your floorboards the tavern is doing its morning business: barrels being rolled somewhere, a keeper's voice counting deliveries, the specific clatter of a common room being set for people who will want breakfast. Beyond the shutters, Portmaris is further along in its day than you are — tide bells, gull argument, a market crier down the row promising the season's first something to whoever gets there before noon.

Nobody in this city knows to expect you anywhere. No summons is coming. Nothing is chasing you, nothing is owed, and the entire absurd, gorgeous width of a second life is sitting on the other side of one wooden door and a staircase you have not yet heard creak.

The guild card sits on the nightstand. F-rank. Unlimited.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: your body woke before you did, settled into a guard stance between bed and door, and you have no memory of learning it.
• Magic Affinity: dust motes are drifting through the shutter-light the wrong way, and they have been all morning.
• Profession: you counted the pouch twice last night and have already priced three ways to make it grow before the rent comes due again.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the guild card's fine print was not there when you registered. It is there now, and it is addressed to you.
• Rebirth or Race: the tavern keeper would not take your coin for last night's supper, and would not say why.

🌄 Clean Slate on the Ironhold Frontier.name: 🌄 Clean Slate on the Ironhold Frontier
🌄 Clean Slate on the Ironhold Frontier.description:
📍 Ironhold, Ashenmere Frontier. The Frontier's largest settlement: a walled town of smiths, bounty boards, and people who came here to be measured by what they do next.
Pace: Yours. The Frontier does not care who you were. It posts what it pays and lets you choose.
Danger: 🟡 Moderate. The town is safe behind its walls. Everything on the boards is priced by how much it is not. (Recommended Level 1-20)

In Ironhold, everyone owes something: the smiths owe the war, the veterans owe each other, half the Guild Annex owes the debt board by name. You owe nothing. You registered yesterday, F-rank, clean book, no party history, no reputation to live down or live up to, and took a room above the Rusty Flagon with the last of your traveling money. Below your window, Bounty Board Plaza posts the Frontier's work in plain figures: this much for wolves, this much for a caravan escort, this much for the thing on the red paper nobody has taken in three weeks. Nobody will hand you anything here. Nobody will stop you from anything, either. That is the whole deal, and it is the fairest one on the continent.

🎭 Mika Haitsume, Female, a companion-for-hire who holds court at the Rusty Flagon and sizes up every new registrant over the rim of her cup.
🎭 Ran Kōga, Female, Flagon regular, blunt and reliable, between parties by choice and picky about the next one.
🎭 Yuki Sato, Female, C-Rank adventurer working out of the Guild Annex — practical, road-worn gear and a habit of noticing newcomers who remind her of someone.
🎭 Commander Takane Kihata, Female, runs Bounty Board Plaza and the town's defense; posts the red-paper contracts personally and remembers who reads them.
🌄 Clean Slate on the Ironhold Frontier.storyStart:
[The player registered with the Guild at Ironhold yesterday — F-rank, no debts, no party, a rare clean slate in a town where everyone owes something — and rents a room in the Upper Rooms above the Rusty Flagon. Keep the Flagon's keeper, patrons, and street traffic unnamed and descriptive; do not invent named staff. All named characters come from the authored roster — Mika Haitsume and Ran Kōga at the Rusty Flagon; Yuki Sato at the Guild Annex; Commander Takane Kihata at Bounty Board Plaza — and appear only if and when the player's choices reach them, using their records. Do not force a job, a debt, or an emergency into the opening; the clean slate is the premise.]

Ironhold wakes with hammering, which is how you know it is not yet dawn: the Smithy Row starts before the sun as a point of professional pride, and the sound comes up through the Flagon's timbers like the town clearing its throat.

You lie in a narrow, honest bed in a narrow, honest room and take inventory, which does not take long. One guild card, F-rank, the ink barely dry. One pouch of copper, counted twice. Two potions, bought at the door price because you did not know yet which shops the adventurers actually use. One window, one stove, one door that locks, and one view — if you stand and lean — of Bounty Board Plaza, where a woman in a commander's coat is already up, already armored, pinning the morning's work to the boards with the efficiency of someone who has done it a thousand times and intends to do it a thousand more.

Yesterday, the clerk at the Guild Annex had read your paperwork front and back, looking for the catch.

"No debts," she said. "No priors. No party dissolution on record. Nothing." She stamped you and slid the card over like she was dealing you a good hand and did not want to be seen doing it. "That will last until your first bad contract. Enjoy it."

Downstairs, the Flagon is serving breakfast to people who fight things for money. Outside, the boards are filling: wolves at so much a head, an escort west at flat rate, standing postings in guild grey, and — three weeks unclaimed, the whole plaza politely not looking at it — a single contract on red paper.

No one in Ironhold knows your name. By the Frontier's accounting, that means you have not failed anyone yet, and the book they will keep on you starts with whatever you do this morning.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: the wolves contract pays by the head, and you have been told twice already that F-ranks hunt in groups, in the tone of a rule waiting to be broken.
• Magic Affinity: Ironhold's walls carry old warding scars, and one section hummed when you walked past it yesterday.
• Profession: the escort contracts all budget for a farrier, a cook, and a scout, and pay double for a registrant who is any two of those.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: your guild card's rank line flickered when the clerk stamped it, and she pretended very hard not to have seen.
• Rebirth or Race: the red-paper contract is written in a script nobody in the plaza can read. You can read it from your window.

🛏️ Broke Rookie in the Gatehouse Dorm.name: 🛏️ Broke Rookie in the Gatehouse Dorm
🛏️ Broke Rookie in the Gatehouse Dorm.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Rakka Jinsoku (Female, gate clerk of Floor Zero. Clipped, kind, and formidably organized), Mana Tsukiakari (Female, nineteen, gatehouse healer. Brisk and openly worried at the same time). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters. The gate at the far end opens on the Guild road to the Maw: every descent goes down the Maw's scaffolding.]

Seventeen is the bunk with the window, which sounds better than it is.

Everything down here smells like wet stone, boot leather and the particular cheapness of a place built for people who will either stop needing it or stop entirely. The dorm holds forty and sleeps thirty-eight. Nobody asks names on the first night. They ask what you registered as, which is a different question, and the answer goes into a mental tally everyone here keeps.

Upstairs, the Registration Hall is doing its morning volume: a long room of processing desks, clerks working at a speed that suggests the queue never ends, waivers going across counters, the descent bell sounding twice whenever a party goes through the gate. The gate itself is at the far end, and it does not look like much, which is somehow worse.

The sheet has been going around since breakfast. Four names on it. A first descent, split five ways, Floor One only, back by dark. The maths works. That is what makes it dangerous.

"Five is fine," says a voice from the desk. "Five is not the problem."

The clerk has not looked up from her manifest. She writes in a small ruthless hand, and there is a wall of books behind her that goes back further than the Gatehouse looks old.

"Rakka Jinsoku. I log what goes down and what comes up." Now she looks up, and it is a fast, complete assessment. "Your sheet has four names and a blank. The blank is you. Before you fill it, three things."

She sets down the pen.

"One. Floor One is survivable and it is not gentle. Two. Of your four, one has been down before and is not saying so, which means they either lost someone or lost their nerve, and both matter." A beat. "Three. There is no rule against a first descent on day three. There is a reason the rule does not exist, and it is that we would rather write it down than stop you."

Behind her, someone comes through the medical door with a clipboard already raised.

"Clearances," says Mana Tsukiakari, in the voice of a person who has had this argument every morning for a year. "Nobody signs that sheet without one. Yes, it takes an hour. Yes, the hour is the point." She stops at the desk, sees the blank line, and her expression does something complicated. "You are the fifth?"

"Apparently."

"Right." She flips a page. "Then you are getting the full clearance, not the fast one, and I do not want to hear about the hour." A pause, and the brisk drops out of her voice for exactly one sentence. "The ones who come back are usually the ones who let me finish."

The bell sounds twice at the far end. A party goes through. The hall does not stop.

The sheet is on the desk in front of you, four names and a clean line, and Rakka has picked her pen back up and is waiting without any visible opinion at all.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you read the other four for competence before you read the sheet, and Rakka watched you do it.
• Magic Affinity: the gate is doing something to the air that nobody else in the queue seems to feel.
• Profession: your clearance is going to come back unusual and you already know which line will flag it.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you know which of the four has been down before, and nobody told you.
• Rebirth or Race: your registration form has a field you could not answer honestly, and you did not.
🛏️ Broke Rookie in the Gatehouse Dorm.description:
📍 Floor Zero Gatehouse, Ashenmere Frontier. The Guild's fortified gate where every sanctioned descent into the Frontier's layered dungeon begins and, ideally, ends.
Pace: Institutional and crowded. Paperwork, then a hole in the ground.
Danger: 🟡 Moderate. Registration is safe. The thing you are registering for is not. (Recommended Level 3-25)

Bunk seventeen, top row, by the window that will not close. The Gatehouse takes anyone with a pulse and a fee, and the delver dorm underneath it is full of people exactly as new and exactly as broke as you are. Somebody has just proposed splitting a first descent to make the week's rent, the sign-up sheet is going around the hall, and the only thing standing between an unqualified party and Floor One is a clerk with a very complete memory.

🎭 Rakka Jinsoku, Female, gate clerk of Floor Zero. Clipped, kind, and formidably organized, keeping the Frontier's most complete record of who went down and who came back in ink and in her head.
🎭 Mana Tsukiakari, Female, nineteen, gatehouse healer. Brisk and openly worried at the same time, processing medical clearances and patching up whoever comes back up the stairs.

🎓 First Bell at the Delving Academy.name: 🎓 First Bell at the Delving Academy
🎓 First Bell at the Delving Academy.description:
📍 Floor Zero Gatehouse, Ashenmere Frontier. The Guild's fortified gate above the Riftmaw, and the school that teaches people to come back out of it.
Pace: School days with real monsters. Lectures, drills, a posted grade, and a hole in the ground.
Danger: 🟡 Moderate. The classrooms are safe. The practicals are not. (Recommended Level 3-25)

The Guild got tired of burying rookies, so it built a school on top of the dungeon. The Delving Academy takes anyone it can insure, sorts them into cohorts of four or five, hands each cohort to an instructor, and grades every dive on a board the whole Gatehouse can read. Today is your first bell. The cohort lists went up at dawn, your name is on one, and three strangers are about to become the people who decide whether you come back up.

🎭 Rakka Jinsoku, Female, gate clerk of Floor Zero and keeper of the Academy rolls. Clipped, kind, and formidably organized; she posts the cohort lists and logs every descent in ink and in her head.
🎭 Mana Tsukiakari, Female, nineteen, gatehouse healer. Brisk and openly worried at the same time; nobody dives without her clearance, and nobody comes back without passing her table.

★ Students dive in small instructor-assigned cohorts and are graded on every descent. The grade board is public.
📜 Opens the three-part Delving Academy quest line.
🎓 First Bell at the Delving Academy.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Rakka Jinsoku (gate clerk of Floor Zero and keeper of the Academy rolls, female, brown hair pinned up with spare stamp-styluses, ink-smudged fingers), Mana Tsukiakari (gatehouse healer, female, nineteen, rose-pink hair in a neat bun, medic's apron). Both appear on screen and at least react. The player is a first-year at the Guild's Delving Academy on the first morning of term. Their cohort is three other adult first-years and one adult Guild instructor: generate these four for this campaign, give each a full name, a role in a party and one memorable habit on first appearance, and keep them consistent afterward. Every student is an adult. Cohort-mates are classmates, not recruited party members, until the player agrees otherwise. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race or class. After the opening, stop and wait for the player: never decide, move, speak or answer for them, and do not carry the scene forward on their behalf.]

The bell is a length of rail hung from a chain, and somebody hits it with a hammer.

First bell at the Delving Academy sounds like the end of the world and means only that you have a quarter hour to be in the Lecture Hall. The benches are stone, tiered, and worn smooth by years of people who were about to learn something frightening. A projector of wards and lenses throws a slow map of the first floor into the air above the lectern: chambers, a stair, a great deal of nothing marked in red.

The board is by the door. Every cohort that has ever dived out of this building is chalked on it somewhere, with a letter beside each descent. Most of the letters are not flattering.

"Names are up. Find yours, find your people, sit with them. You will be sitting with them for a long time."

The woman pinning the last sheet to the board has two spare styluses holding her hair up and ink to the second knuckle. She does not raise her voice. Forty first-years go quiet for her anyway.

"Rakka Jinsoku. I keep the rolls and I log what goes down and what comes up. Three things, and then you are your instructors' problem." She caps her pen. "One. You do not choose your cohort and you do not trade it. Two. Grades are for what comes back. Nobody here has ever been marked up for a kill and nobody ever will be. Three." A very small pause. "I have never had to rub a name off that board in the first week. I would like to keep it that way."

Somebody behind you laughs, not because it was funny.

At the side door a healer in a medic's apron is setting out a table, a stack of forms and a row of small glass vials, with the expression of someone who has had this exact morning every term for a year.

"Clearances before anybody so much as looks at the Training Cavern," says Mana Tsukiakari. "All of you. Yes, it takes an hour. Yes, the hour is the point." Her eyes go down the benches, counting, and stop on you a moment longer than on the others.

Your name is on the fourth sheet from the left. There are three other names under the same number, and one more above them, written in a different hand: the instructor's.

Across the hall, three strangers are reading the same sheet. One of them looks up. What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Race: you are not the shape this school was built for, and the bench, the forms or the doorway has already made that clear.
• Rebirth: you have sat in a room like this before, in another life, waiting for a list. It was never a list like this one.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the ward-map over the lectern flickers when you look straight at it. Only you seem to notice.
• Combat Class or Magic Affinity: you can already tell which of your three cohort-mates has held a weapon before, and which has not.
• Profession: you came here with a trade, and you are working out what a dungeon is going to do to it.

[Party: cohort-mates and the instructor are classmates and staff, not recruited. None of them joins the traveling party without explicit mutual agreement.]

⚗️ First Shift at the Copper Bench.name: ⚗️ First Shift at the Copper Bench
⚗️ First Shift at the Copper Bench.description:
📍 The Copper Alembic Hall, Portmaris. Slate distillation benches and brass flue hoods between the Floating Market and Merchant Heights.
Pace: Bright, hands-on guild work with harbor mysteries and road chemistry waiting outside.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. A fizzing bench kettle is the biggest hazard in the room unless you go looking for dockside trouble. (Recommended Level 1-12)

Evening bell has just rung across Portmaris, and your very first shift on the Alchemists' Guild floor is already three orders behind. Harbor captains are lined up at the marble assay counter clamoring for sea-calm draughts before the tide turns, glass condensers are bubbling at a reckless clip under the brass hoods, and Journeyman field alchemist Koharu Morishita has just drafted you to help save an experimental reduction before it paints the ceiling.

Between Assay Registrar Naoki Shirogane's dry commentary at the scales and Koharu's cheerful disregard for standard boiling times, you can prove your hands at the copper bench, take on a coastal reagent run, or step out into the lantern-lit port.
⚗️ First Shift at the Copper Bench.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements:
- Koharu Morishita (twenty-four-year-old adult human woman, tall and sun-warmed with amber eyes, a thick copper-red side-braid fastened with a brass clasp, and a sea-green canvas field coat under a leather bandolier of glowing flasks; Journeyman field alchemist of the Alchemists' Guild).
- Naoki Shirogane (twenty-six-year-old adult half-elf man with warm hazel eyes, tousled auburn hair, brass spectacles fitted with a swing-away jeweler's loupe, and a russet waistcoat over rolled linen sleeves; Assay Registrar at the Copper Alembic Hall).
Premise: The player has just started working at the Copper Alembic Hall in Portmaris for the Alchemists' Guild during a hectic evening bell rush. A merchant brig's quartermaster is waiting at the front counter for a crate of certified stamina and sea-calm draughts, while Koharu's rapid-boil reduction at Bench Four is one pinch of stabilizer away from foaming over.
What the player can do: Stabilize the bubbling condenser at the bench, help Naoki assay and stamp the outgoing harbor vials, question why one of the returned dockside bottles smells of bilge-brine, or decline the shift and walk out into Portmaris.
Rules: Everyone in this scene is an adult. Keep the narration strictly in second person. Never assign the player a name, gender, race, body, or class, and never speak, move, or decide for the player. Stop on the player's choice.]

Steam hiss and the sharp, bright scent of crushed sea-lavender and hot copper greet you as the evening bell echoes up from Portmaris harbor. Inside the Copper Alembic Hall, every brass flue hood along the stepped stone terrace is drawing hard. Your work gloves are barely on your hands for your first shift with the Alchemists' Guild, and the floor is already in glorious, organized pandemonium.

Up at the marble assay counter, Assay Registrar Naoki Shirogane flips his jeweler's loupe down over one spectacle lens, holding a green glass vial to the lamplight while three impatient ship apothecaries drum their fingers on the slate. Without looking up from the meniscus, Naoki taps his brass wax press against the counter and calls back toward the distillation tiers.

"Bench Four is singing in three-quarter time, Koharu," Naoki says, his voice brisk and dry over the clink of glass crates. "If you launch another cork into the rafters before I finish certifying the tide-brig manifest, you are scraping the flue hood yourself, and our new hand is not bailing you out."

At the slate-topped bench beside you, Koharu Morishita pushes a loose strand of copper-red hair behind her ear with her wrist, her amber eyes bright with unrepentant delight. A spiral glass condenser sits over a blue spirit-flame between you, its amber reduction climbing toward the neck in rapid, pearly bubbles. She has a tray of moon-salt in one hand, copper cooling tongs in the other, and a crate of unassayed harbor stamina tonics sitting open at the end of the table.

"Ignore him, he worries for sport," Koharu says warmly, nudging a porcelain mortar of pale flux-powder and the burner valve toward your side of the slate. "Welcome to the Alchemists' Guild! If we drop the heat and fold in the stabilizer on the same beat, we save twenty minutes of boiling and make the harbor run with time to spare for ginger cordials. Or, if you prefer quieter work, Naoki needs a second pair of eyes on those returned stamina bottles at the end of the bench. Something in their wax seal smells off to me. Which side of the table do you want?"
⚗️ First Shift at the Copper Bench.questGenerationGuidance: Offer hands-on alchemical commissions, coastal reagent runs, purity assays at the Copper Alembic Hall, and investigations into counterfeit guild stamps or adulterated harbor tonics around Portmaris.

🕯️ First Proof in Smoked Glass.name: 🕯️ First Proof in Smoked Glass
🕯️ First Proof in Smoked Glass.description:
📍 The Cistern of Smoked Glass, Aureliath. Vaulted brick water channels and hooded lamps beneath the Outer Districts.
Pace: Playful rooftop intrigue, quiet investigation, and court secrets where every choice stays yours.
Danger: 🟡 Moderate. Noble house lookouts and night watch patrols prowl the streets above, though wit and stealth keep blades sheathed. (Recommended Level 1-15)

Everyone in Aureliath whispers about the Assassins' Guild, yet almost nobody knows that its fourth rule voids any contract built on a client's lie. You have just been taken on at the Cistern of Smoked Glass as a verifier, the sharp-eyed specialist who checks whether a dead-drop petition is honest before a token ever reaches the slate board.

Tonight, contract broker Masaru Takigawa has a fresh cylinder from a Noble Quarter drop with a date that refuses to add up, and senior operative Suzume Shinonome is already waiting on the footbridge with a folded parchment crane and a wager on how fast you spot the flaw. Nobody has to be harmed, and you can expose the lie, pocket the retainer, or walk back up the kiln steps at any moment.
🕯️ First Proof in Smoked Glass.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements:
- Suzume Shinonome (twenty-five-year-old adult half-elf woman, lithe with violet eyes, lightly pointed ears, a beauty mark under her left eye, silver-tipped dark hair in a silk ribbon, and a night-indigo leather jack with twin silver-hilted daggers; senior operative of the Assassins' Guild).
- Masaru Takigawa (thirty-four-year-old adult human man with neat dark brown hair, sharp hazel eyes behind half-moon spectacles, and a slate wool vest over a charcoal shirt; contract broker at the Cistern of Smoked Glass).
Premise: The player has just begun working for the Assassins' Guild in the Cistern of Smoked Glass beneath Aureliath's Outer Districts as a verifier, checking that dead-drop petitions state a true grievance under the guild's fourth rule. Masaru has opened an evening dead-drop cylinder targeting a Riverside Wharf apothecary, and the tariff date on the slip looks suspicious.
What the player can do: Inspect the dossier and escrow coin at Masaru's lectern, head up to the Outer Districts rooftops or Riverside Wharf with Suzume to verify the story, flag the petition as a lie under the code, or decline the assignment and walk out freely.
Rules: Everyone in this scene is an adult. Keep the narration strictly in second person. Never assign the player a name, gender, race, body, or class, and never speak, move, or decide for the player. Nobody has to be harmed, and the player is never forced to kill or keep the job. Stop on the player's choice.]

Cool air scented with wet limestone, old beeswax, and bitter almond oil rises from the dark water channels of the Cistern of Smoked Glass. Above the brick vaults, the muffled chimes of Aureliath's dusk bell fade into the stone, leaving only the soft dip of hooded oil lamps reflected across the narrow footbridges. You stand before the dark walnut lectern where every petition to the Assassins' Guild is weighed before a blade is ever drawn.

Behind the desk, contract broker Masaru Takigawa nudges a heavy Gold coin across his brass balance scale with one ink-stained finger, his hazel eyes narrowing behind half-moon spectacles. Beside the scale lie two discs of crown glass, one smoked black and one left clear, next to an unrolled parchment slip from an Outer Districts dead drop.

"Welcome to verification work," Masaru says, his tone as crisp and unhurried as a chancery audit. "The fourth rule is simple: if a petitioner lies to us about their grievance, the contract dies here and the Guild keeps the escrow. A Noble Quarter factor dropped two Gold before dusk to put a Riverside Wharf apothecary on the slate for selling nightshade, yet the harbor manifest number he cited is three months out of date."

A soft boot-heel clicks on the stone rail behind you as Suzume Shinonome drops effortlessly from the low arch onto the footbridge, her night-indigo leather making less sound than the lamp flame. She balances a small origami crane folded from scrap parchment on her knuckle, her violet eyes crinkling with conspiratorial amusement as she leans an elbow on the end of Masaru's lectern.

"Three tokens refused this week, and I have two Silver on this one making it four," Suzume says, flicking the paper crane so it lands neatly beside the dossier. "The apothecary's shop is ten minutes across the Outer Districts tiles, and the factor's warehouse clerk is still locking up on the wharf. You can look over Masaru's cipher slip right here, come walk the rooftops with me to see who is lying, or slide the clear glass disc across the desk and call the night yours. How do you want to play it?"
🕯️ First Proof in Smoked Glass.questGenerationGuidance: Offer quiet verification investigations, rooftop reconnaissance across Aureliath, dead-drop mysteries, and choices that test or uphold the Assassins' Guild five-point code without forcing lethal outcomes.

🕳️ Level One on Riftmaw Floor 47.name: 🕳️ Level One on Riftmaw Floor 47
🕳️ Level One on Riftmaw Floor 47.storyStart:
[No authored world characters are present in this scene. The player is completely alone on Floor 47 of the Riftmaw, in the Living Architecture, and nobody comes for them. The climb passes places that are not the dungeon's (delver camps and exchanges, monster holds, and Kingsrest around the Midway Outpost on Floor 25), each on its own floor and each helping only at a price. The way out is UP: never steer them deeper; only the player chooses to descend. Every floor between here and daylight is real distance, crossed in hours of corridors and stairs, never in one step. Do not invent a rescuer, a guide, a companion, or a friendly voice. The dungeon is the only presence, and it is not on the player's side: it is a living thing, and everything it makes here (level 43 and up) is its defense, hostile and far above the player. Nothing here bows, kneels, serves or gives: the dungeon offers no gift, weapon, heart or core, and whatever the player carries out was taken by force or found by searching. A creature here kills a level-one character in a hit or two, so it is a reason to plan, hide or run; one that notices them gives its attack away a heartbeat early (a sound, a shift in the light), so a quick, sound reaction gets its roll before the blow lands. Nothing the dungeon makes talks the player out, points the way or helps. Wit is how a level-one character lives here: a sound plan (a trap, the terrain, a lure, a weak point) gets a fair roll and resolves this turn, and a creature killed by it is dead and pays its full loot. Never invent new resistances to block a plan, and never choose the player's next move. Do not describe, remove, or comment on the player's equipment: whatever their class, traits and starting items grant, they already have it and woke up with it.]

The floor is warm.

That is the first thing, before the dark and before the fact that you do not know how you got here. The stone under your palms is warm and it is moving, a rise and fall so slow you mistake it for your own breathing until you hold your breath and it keeps going.

There is light, faintly. Riftlight, the dull violet the deep floors make on their own, enough to show you a corridor of worked material that is not stone and not metal, running away in both directions with doorways spaced along it at intervals that are almost regular and not quite.

One of the doorways is narrower than it was when you first looked at it, and it is still closing.

You do not remember arriving. You do not remember the descent, the party you must have had, or the forty-six floors between this one and daylight. Whatever you are carrying, you were carrying it before you opened your eyes.

Carved into the wall beside you, deep and old and in Guild shorthand you can somehow read, is the only useful thing on this floor:

FLOOR 47. UP IS 46. DO NOT SLEEP.

Under it, in a different hand, scratched fast:

THERE IS A FASTER WAY UP. IT BITES.

Forty-seven floors. The deepest permanent Guild presence in the Riftmaw is the Midway Outpost on Floor 25, and twenty-two floors is not a walk. It is a career, for someone who already had one.

Somewhere below you, something adjusts its footing. It is not close. It is not far enough.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: your hands knew what they were holding before you did.
• Magic Affinity: the walls are saturated, and down here mana is the one resource that is not scarce.
• Profession: the architecture is built, which means it was built by someone, which means it has rules.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: whatever brought you here alive is not down here with you. Whatever you can do, you do on your own.
• Rebirth or Race: the shorthand on the wall is not a language you ever learned.
🕳️ Level One on Riftmaw Floor 47.description:
📍 Riftmaw: The Living Architecture, Floor 47, beneath the Ashenmere Frontier. The dungeon's own living body, twenty-two floors below the last Guild outpost and far deeper than anything a new rank permits.
Pace: Hostile and unforgiving. Every corridor is a decision.
Danger: ⚫ Deadly. Hostile spawns constant. No downtime protection. (Recommended Level 1, hardcore)

You did not descend. You woke up here.

No party, no map, and no memory of the forty-six floors above you. The walls breathe on a slow cycle and the corridors are not the same shape they were an hour ago. Nothing down here is rated for a level one anything.

The only way out is up, through every floor that was never meant to be walked in this direction.

⚙️ For the game-like System interface (stats, quests, level-ups, rank screens), select the 📊 The System mode at character creation. It layers onto this scene.

💠 You Broke the Academy's Mana Crystal.name: 💠 You Broke the Academy's Mana Crystal
💠 You Broke the Academy's Mana Crystal.description:
📍 Silver Crescent Academy, Crownveil Sovereignty. Crystal spires and enchanted gardens on a forested campus outside the capital.
Pace: Fast and loud. School life, starting with every eye on you.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The courts are warded and the duels are to first touch. Your reputation has no such protection. (Recommended Level 1-20)

Every new student puts a hand on the measuring crystal. It glows, a proctor writes down a number, and the next student steps up. It has done this for four hundred years. When you touched it, it went white, rang like a bell, and split down the middle. The proctors are arguing about what to write down. The whole intake is staring. And the Academy's top-ranked student has just gone over the fence of the practice ring and is walking straight at you.

🎭 Aria Hoshikaze, Female, the Academy's top-ranked combat student and heir to House Hoshikaze. Dark navy hair in a high ponytail, blue eyes, a sleek black uniform with silver insignia. Three years undefeated, and told she is the best for as long as she can remember.
🎭 Kazuha Aokaze, Male, half-elf spellblade, ranked second in his year. Quiet, precise, and watching all of this from the fence with great interest.

★ The overpowered new student: one touch, one broken crystal, and no chance of a quiet first term.
💠 You Broke the Academy's Mana Crystal.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Aria Hoshikaze (female, dark navy hair in a high ponytail, blue eyes, sleek black uniform with silver insignia), on screen from the first line, and Kazuha Aokaze (male, half-elf spellblade, ranked second in his year), watching from the fence. The premise: today is intake assessment at the Academy, the player has just touched the measuring crystal, and it cracked. That means the crystal could not hold the reading, not that the player is trained: they are a first-day student with no technique beyond what their build gives them. Aria challenges the player to a first-touch duel on the spot, because that is how she talks to people she takes seriously; she is intense and proud, never cruel. The duel, if accepted, is a fair contest the player can lose. Everyone here is an adult student or member of staff. Do not generate additional named students or faculty in the opening. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race or class. After the opening, stop and wait for the player: never decide, move, speak or answer for them, and do not carry the scene forward on their behalf.]

The sound it made is still going.

A high, clean note, like a wet finger on the rim of a glass the size of a house. It hangs over the Training Courts while four hundred new students and a dozen proctors stand very still, and you stand in the middle of them with your hand on a pillar of crystal that has a crack running through it from top to bottom.

The crack was not there a moment ago.

You know that because you watched thirty people go ahead of you. Hand on the crystal. A glow: pale blue, pale green, once a respectable gold that made the proctors nod. A number, written down. Next.

Then your turn. Your hand. A white so bright the courtyard lost its shadows. Then the note, and the crack.

"That," says a proctor faintly, "is a four-hundred-year-old instrument."

"What do I write?" says another.

Nobody answers her.

You take your hand away. A sliver of crystal the length of your finger comes with it and sits in your palm, still faintly warm.

On the far side of the court there is a practice ring behind a low fence, and in it someone has been running sword forms alone since before the assessment began. You noticed her because everyone noticed her: dark navy hair in a high tail, a black uniform with silver insignia, footwork so exact that the students by the fence had stopped pretending not to watch.

She has stopped.

She is looking at the crystal. Then she is looking at you.

Then she puts one hand on the fence, goes over it without appearing to notice it was there, and crosses the court in a straight line. The intake parts for her the way water parts for a prow.

She stops in front of you. Blue eyes, very direct. She is slightly out of breath, from the forms and not from the walk.

"Aria Hoshikaze. Third year. Ranked first." She says it the way other people give an address. "I have put my hand on that crystal every term since I enrolled. The highest reading in the Academy's records is mine. It has never so much as flickered." Her eyes go to the sliver in your palm and back to your face. "Who trained you?"

Behind her a half-elf with a practice blade across his shoulders has drifted to the fence and leaned on it: Kazuha Aokaze, second in his year, wearing the expression of a man who has waited three years to watch this happen to her.

"Nobody trained them, Hoshikaze," he says mildly. "Look at how they are standing."

Aria looks. Something in her face changes. It is not disappointment. It is closer to hunger.

"Then it is not skill," she says. "It is just you." She draws the practice sword from her belt and holds it out to you, hilt first, in front of the entire intake. "First touch. Ring three. Now, before they finish arguing about your number and somebody sends you to an office." A breath. "I want to know what broke it. I do not know another way to ask."

Four hundred people are waiting to see what you do with the sword.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Magic Affinity: the white the crystal turned had a color underneath it, and you felt which one.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: it was not your mana the crystal failed to hold.
• Combat Class: you took the offered hilt without thinking, and your grip was correct.
• Rebirth or Race: you have sat examinations in another life, and none of them ended with the equipment in pieces.
• Profession: you are already estimating what a four-hundred-year-old measuring crystal costs, and who the Academy will ask to pay for it.

[Assessment: the cracked crystal means the reading went past what it could hold. It grants no level, ability, rank or special treatment, and the faculty will want an explanation. The sliver in the player's palm is the Mana Crystal already in this start's starting items; do not grant it again.]

[Party: Aria Hoshikaze and Kazuha Aokaze are fellow students, not recruited. Neither follows the player without explicit mutual agreement.]

🏫 The Scholarship Nobody Approved.name: 🏫 The Scholarship Nobody Approved
🏫 The Scholarship Nobody Approved.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Chizuru Shimozaki (female, long pale-blue hair, icy lavender eyes, porcelain features, blue-and-white uniform, snowy fan) and Hikari Suzumi (female, long strawberry-blonde hair, golden eyes, black vest over white blouse). Both appear on screen and react. The player is a scholarship student native to this world who carries memories of another one. Do not generate additional named students in the opening. Everyone in this scene is an adult.]

Student Commons smells like polished wood, cold tea, and money.

You have been standing at the noticeboard for four minutes pretending to read the duel rosters, because sitting down means choosing a table, and every table in this room has been claimed by people who arrived with letters of introduction. Your acceptance came with a scholarship number instead. It is printed on your enrollment card in ink a shade cheaper than everyone else's.

You know how this goes. You have done a version of it before, in a world with fluorescent lights and standardized tests and a version of you that did not make it to graduation. The details are gone. The stubbornness came through intact.

"You are in the way."

The voice is quiet, precise, and entirely without malice, which somehow makes it worse. Chizuru Shimozaki is standing at your shoulder with a snowy fan closed against her palm, long pale-blue hair falling past a blue-and-white uniform that fits the way clothing fits when it was made rather than bought. Icy lavender eyes take in your cuffs, your card, and the four minutes you have spent not reading the roster.

She does not sneer. She simply waits, the way someone waits for a door to finish opening.

Somewhere behind her there is a bright crackle of sound, a small delighted shriek, and the smell of ozone. A young woman with long strawberry-blonde hair is apologizing to a scorch mark on a table, hands raised, golden eyes wide, insisting to nobody in particular that it was absolutely under control. Two upperclassmen edge away from her with the practiced ease of people who have done it before.

Chizuru's gaze flicks to the scorch mark, then back to you. Something in her expression sharpens, because you did not flinch, and she noticed.

"You are the scholarship," she says. It is not a question, and it is not quite an insult either. "Then you tested higher than four people I know by name. That is either interesting or a clerical error."

She opens the fan. Behind her, Hikari Suzumi finally looks up from the scorch mark and sees you, and her whole face changes into a smile aimed like a lantern.

"I have not decided which," Chizuru says. "Convince me."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you clocked the duel rosters before the noticeboard, and your hands have opinions.
• Magic Affinity: the Commons hums at an angle that sets your teeth slightly wrong.
• Profession: you are the only person here who has priced the tea, the panelling and the tuition.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you read a posted name three seconds before your eyes reached it.
• Rebirth or Race: somebody has already decided what you are from the doorway.
🏫 The Scholarship Nobody Approved.description:
📍 Silver Crescent Academy, Crownveil Sovereignty. Crystal spires and enchanted gardens on a forested campus outside the capital.
Pace: Steady. Academic pressure, duels, and social ladders.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Campus grounds are protected. (Recommended Level 1-20)

You were born in this world, in a house with no name worth writing down, and you tested into the continent's premier magical academy anyway. The scholarship covers tuition. It does not cover robes, reagents, the crystal fees, or the fact that everyone in the Student Commons can tell what your family is worth by looking at your cuffs. You remember another life, another set of exams, and a stubbornness that apparently survives death.

🎭 Chizuru Shimozaki, Female, eldest daughter of House Shimozaki. Long pale-blue hair, icy lavender eyes, porcelain features, blue-and-white uniform with a snowy fan. Refuses to accept second place in any category and is genuinely puzzled when others disagree.
🎭 Hikari Suzumi, Female, nineteen, youngest student ever admitted to the advanced enchantment program. Long strawberry-blonde hair, golden eyes, black vest over a white blouse. Relentlessly positive, and hiding a Blessing that gets dangerous when she does not feel safe.

🎓 One Week Early to Tideglass Academy.name: 🎓 One Week Early to Tideglass Academy
🎓 One Week Early to Tideglass Academy.description:
📍 Tideglass Academy Pier, Tsukihana Tidelace. A research academy built out over the sea on glass and brass, where the tide teaches half the curriculum.
Pace: Yours. Term has not started. The campus is open and almost empty.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The sea is patient and the wards are good. Term, when it arrives, is another matter. (Recommended Level 1-15)

You passed the entrance examination, cleanly, unglamorously, in a hall full of strangers, and the letter said housing opens a week before term. So you came early. Your name is on a door in the Student Quarters, your bunk smells of salt and new rope, and for seven days the Academy is yours without an audience: the Library Deck unclaimed, the Tidal Pools at low water, the Main Pier long and empty at dawn. No classes. No rankings. No rivals yet. Well. Almost none. A week to learn the place before the place starts grading you.

🎭 Hanami Ushinami, Female, the Academy's resident prodigy, already working in the Tidal Laboratory as if term never ended for her. Brilliant, absorbed, and unaccustomed to company that arrives voluntarily.
🎭 Raiden Kurogane, Male, a rival-tempered student who also came early, and who has been measuring the Main Pier like it owes him something.
🎓 One Week Early to Tideglass Academy.storyStart:
[The player is a newly admitted Tideglass student who arrived a week before term; campus is nearly empty and nothing is scheduled. Keep porters and groundskeepers unnamed and descriptive; do not invent named staff or students in the opening. The only authored characters on campus are Hanami Ushinami (Tidal Laboratory) and Raiden Kurogane (The Main Pier), drawn from their records, and they appear only if and when the player's choices reach them. Do not force a hook, an incident, or an orientation event into the opening; the empty week is the premise. Everyone in this scene is an adult.]

The Student Quarters at Tideglass are built so that the sea runs under them, and your first night was spent learning the difference between the sound of water that is minding its own business and water that is not. All of it, so far, has been minding its own business.

Morning comes up green-gold through glass floor panels. Your door has your name on it in fresh chalk — someone did it carefully, with serifs — and your trunk is half-unpacked because unpacking it fully felt like a commitment to be made in daylight.

Term starts in seven days.

You read the admission letter again over breakfast, alone in a refectory built for three hundred. You did not mis-read it. Passed, admitted, housed. No conditions, no sponsor's name attached, no debt clause in small print. The porter who let you in two nights ago had checked the book twice, said "early," approvingly, and gone back to her lamp.

Outside the refectory's long windows the campus is doing its off-season work. The Tidal Pools are at low water, all their instruments exposed and glittering. The Library Deck stands open and unstaffed on the honor system, which the letter had underlined without explanation. The Main Pier runs out over the swell, longer than any building has business being, and the Dive Platform at its end is chained off with a sign you have not gone to read yet.

Somewhere in the Tidal Laboratory something has been humming since before you woke — steady, absorbed, the sound of a person working who does not know or care that the building has acquired a second occupant.

Seven days. No classes, no rankings, no audience. An academy over the sea, and your name in chalk on a door in it.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: the training salle's roster is blank, the equipment is racked, and nobody would know.
• Magic Affinity: the pier's warding glass brightens under your bare feet, and it did not do that for the porter.
• Profession: the Academy's supply manifests are pinned in the refectory, and whoever negotiated them was robbed.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: your admission letter lists a course code that appears in no catalogue you can find.
• Rebirth or Race: the tide under your room changes rhythm when you sleep, and last night it matched your breathing.

🖤 Exiled Transfer to Nightglass Academy.name: 🖤 Exiled Transfer to Nightglass Academy
🖤 Exiled Transfer to Nightglass Academy.storyStart:
[Present in this scene: use the authored world characters the roster places in this area, and use their records for name, appearance and manner. Do not invent named characters for roles the roster already fills. The player is a foreign transfer student sent here by their own family under conditions never explained to them, arriving alone at the Lecture Towers. Everyone in this scene is an adult.]

It is always dusk here. You were told that and you did not understand what you were being told.

Not night. Dusk. A held violet moment, the sun down but not gone, the black spires standing against a sky that has been doing this for four hundred years and shows no sign of finishing. Lamps come on because they are scheduled, not because anyone needs them.

Your trunk sits at your feet in the entrance hall of the Lecture Towers. It has your house crest on it. Somebody has already looked at that crest and then looked away, which is a specific sequence you are going to see a great deal of.

The letter from your family was warm. Carefully, genuinely warm. It used the word opportunity four times, and it arrived at the same moment as the coach, and the coach left while the household was at chapel.

You have read it eleven times looking for the condition. It is not written down. It is simply understood that there is one.

Somewhere above you a bell marks an hour that does not correspond to any daylight.

The hall is not empty. Students move through it the way students move anywhere, in twos and threes, with the difference that several of them are not shaped quite like you and none of them find that worth remarking on. A pair of them slow as they pass your trunk. One says something to the other. Neither says it to you.

A registration desk sits at the far end with a book open on it and nobody currently behind it.

Your term begins whenever you walk over and write your name in that book. Nobody is going to come and fetch you.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: the Dueling Hall is signposted and your feet have already found the direction.
• Magic Affinity: the permanent dusk here is maintained, not natural, and you can feel the working.
• Profession: you have valued the entrance hall's stonework and it is older than the school.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the crest on your trunk means something here that it did not at home.
• Rebirth or Race: several students in this hall are not shaped like you and nobody remarks on it.
🖤 Exiled Transfer to Nightglass Academy.description:
📍 Nightglass Academy, Rosethorn Nocturne. A black-spired academy under permanent violet dusk, where the curriculum is excellent and the student body is not entirely human.
Pace: Cold and academic. Duels, dossiers and dinner invitations.
Danger: 🟡 Moderate. Nobody will attack you. Several people will document you. (Recommended Level 1-22)

Your house sent you here. Not as an honor. They dressed it as one, wrote a warm letter, and put you on a coach at an hour chosen so fewer people would watch it leave. Nightglass takes foreign students because foreign students are useful. You have your trunk, your family name, and a very clear understanding that going home is conditional on something nobody has explained.

⚡ Waking Mid-Duel on Bluefin Pier.name: ⚡ Waking Mid-Duel on Bluefin Pier
⚡ Waking Mid-Duel on Bluefin Pier.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Torao Arami (Male, Catkin swashbuckler and B-rank adventurer, twin cutlasses and an unreasonable amount of style). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters.]

Salt, planks, and the specific bright shock of realizing your body is already doing something.

Weight on the back foot. Guard up. A ring of chalk on scarred wood, thirty feet across, and the sun going down over the water behind your opponent so that they are a shape with an edge on it.

You do not remember agreeing to this.

That is not a small problem, but it is currently the second problem, because the count is at four and the count started somewhere behind you and the crowd along the rope has gone from noise to that dense attentive quiet that means the money is down and the fun is about to start.

Bluefin Duel Pier at sunset. You know that much. Everyone on the coast knows the pier: disputes get settled here in the open where the whole dock can see it done properly, and the planks under your boots are scarred and stained and polished smooth by exactly how often that happens.

Five.

Your opponent shifts. It is a real shift, weight and intent, from somebody who has done this before and is not here to perform.

Six.

"Ooh," says somebody at the rope, delighted, in a carrying voice built for exactly this. "No, no, look at the feet. Look at the feet! That is not a person who came here to lose."

The Catkin leaning on the barrier has twin cutlasses on his hips that he is very deliberately not touching, and the entire crowd has half-turned toward him the way crowds do around people who have trained them to.

"Torao Arami, and I am not in this one, so do not look at me like that." He waves a hand. "I am the neutral party. I am here because I am always here. This is a much better duel than the last three and I would like it on the record that I said so at six."

Seven.

The referee's arm is up. Somewhere behind you a bookmaker calls a change in odds and gets an argument for it.

"Word of advice, since nobody has given you one," Torao says, and for one sentence the theatre drops out of it. "Whatever the disagreement was, this ring only settles the version everybody watched. So whatever you actually want out of this, get it in the first exchange, because after that it belongs to the crowd."

Eight.

Across the chalk, your opponent rolls their shoulders and settles, and you understand with total clarity that they are going to come high and left and that you already knew that, from somewhere, before you thought it.

The referee's arm comes down.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: your body was already braced correctly before you were, and the crowd saw it happen.
• Magic Affinity: something is banked and ready behind your sternum and you did not put it there consciously.
• Profession: you read the odds board before the ring and know exactly what the money thinks of you.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you knew where the strike was coming from a beat before you had any way to know.
• Rebirth or Race: the referee looked at you twice while calling the count, and the second look lasted.
⚡ Waking Mid-Duel on Bluefin Pier.description:
📍 Bluefin Duel Pier, Cerulean Coast. A public pier where sailors, adventurers and nobles settle disputes in a chalked ring at the water's end, with the sunset behind them and the whole dock betting.
Pace: Immediate. You are already in it.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Duels here are to submission, formally. Formally. (Recommended Level 1-8)

There is a ring chalked on scarred planks, an opponent across it already committed, a rope barrier holding back a crowd with money down, and a count that was already at three before you registered any of it. Nobody is going to pause the proceedings while you work out how you got here. You have about three seconds to decide what kind of person you are going to be about it, and the pier is watching to find out.

🎭 Torao Arami, Male, Catkin swashbuckler and B-rank adventurer, twin cutlasses and an unreasonable amount of style, better known for his entrances than his record and quite happy with that.

🩸 Two Go Down in the Deepmarket Sump.name: 🩸 Two Go Down in the Deepmarket Sump
🩸 Two Go Down in the Deepmarket Sump.storyStart:
[No authored world characters are present in this scene. The premise: the player is in the Sump, an illegal, unsanctioned fighting pit hollowed out of a deep obsidian drainage basin beneath the Deepmarket Bazaar in Kurogane Deephollow, where the Crystalvein Cartel takes a quiet cut to look away. The Sump's one rule is known across the caverns: two climb down the iron ladder, the overhead grate is bolted shut, and the grate only opens when one fighter is left standing. How the player came to be in tonight's bout is open to the player: a debt, a dare, a frame-up, or a desperate bid for the five-Gold winner's purse. The local residents present are Genba Kuroishi (male, dwarven-blooded pit-caller and grate-keeper on the upper rim, gravel-voiced, heavy iron key at his belt), Tatsumi Shioda (female, deep-elf bookmaker chalking odds on a slate by the lantern rope), and the opponent across the basin, Daisen Jinzei (male, scarred cavern brawler with slate-grey eyes, cropped dark hair, and chalked wraps on his forearms). Name any other resident who speaks. Keep the rule real: Daisen intends to walk out alive and fights seriously, but the player's approach is theirs to choose (fight to kill, beat him until the crowd forces the grate open, break the grate, turn the pit's hazards to use, or force a deal), and the narrator never forces the player to kill. Combat follows normal dice rolls and health. Everyone in this scene is an adult. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race or class. After the opening, stop and wait for the player: never decide, move, speak or answer for them.]

The iron grate slams down twelve feet above your head, and the heavy slide-bolt clacks home.

Rust and dry cave-salt sift down through the bars over you. Around the upper rim of the basin, forty or fifty faces lean over the iron rail in the bruised-violet glow of bioluminescent moss and cracked mana-lanterns: off-shift miners with crystal dust in their beards, deep-elf brokers in oiled leather, and two men in the unmarked grey coats of Crystalvein Cartel security who are here to collect the house ten percent and see nothing else.

Underfoot, the floor of the Sump is carved black obsidian, slick around the outer drainage channel and roughened in the center with a wide ring of coarse white salt so blood does not ruin the footing. The air down here is thick, warm, and sour with spilled ale, hot tallow, and wet stone.

Up on the rim, Genba Kuroishi hooks a leather pouch to the iron chain beside the ladder. Even from the floor you can hear the heavy clink of five Gold inside it.

"Bets are closed!" Genba barks down through the bars, his dwarven-blooded voice carrying over the clatter of Tatsumi's chalk on the odds slate. He taps the iron padlock with a scarred knuckle. "You know the Sump, and you know the law down here. Nobody calls a pause. Nobody throws a towel. Two came down the rungs. One climbs up and takes the hook. Anything left on the salt belongs to the drains."

Across the basin, twenty paces away, Daisen Jinzei lets out a slow breath and rolls his neck until it pops. He is broad-shouldered and weathered, a veteran of the deep shafts with a crescent scar across his jaw and fresh white chalk ground into the wraps on his forearms. He does not sneer or waste wind on theater. His slate-grey eyes measure your stance, your reach, and where your weight sits on the salt.

"Nothing personal," Daisen says, low enough that it stays under the crowd's shouting. He brings his wrapped hands up to guard, elbows tucked, left foot sliding forward across the grit. "I owe three Gold to the Cartel assay office by the dawn bell, and you're standing between me and the ladder."

Above you, someone hammers a boot heel against the iron grating. Then another joins in, and another, until the whole rim is thudding in a slow, metallic drumbeat that shakes dust from the cavern ceiling.

Daisen takes his first step into the salt ring.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: Daisen's eyes narrow as soon as you set your feet, recognizing the balance of someone who has trained for real blood rather than tavern brawls.
• Magic Affinity: the damp mana-veins threaded through the Sump's obsidian walls hum against your skin, ready to answer a cast inside a twenty-pace cage.
• Profession: you already clocked the rusted hinge-pins on the east drainage sluice and the brittle weld on Genba's slide-bolt before the grate came down.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the bookmaker Tatsumi hesitated before chalking your odds, because the registration crystal upstairs flickered strangely when you paid your entry.
• Rebirth or Race: the memory of another life is still sharp behind your eyes, making the roaring cavern crowd feel both impossibly alien and coldly clear.
🩸 Two Go Down in the Deepmarket Sump.description:
📍 Deepmarket Bazaar, Kurogane Deephollow. Beneath the Deep Passage Market's storage vaults, a flooded obsidian drainage basin has been turned into an illegal fighting pit.
Pace: Brutal, close, and immediate. An iron grate overhead, wet stone underfoot, and a crowd with coin on your life.
Danger: 🟠 Dangerous. The Sump has no referee, no forfeit bell, and only one ladder out. (Recommended Level 1-18)

The surface arenas have rules, healers on standby, and silk-draped boxes. The Sump has an iron grate that bolts from the outside and a single house law every trader in the Deephollow knows by heart: two go down, one climbs out. Whether a bad debt, a desperate wager, a setup, or sheer nerve put you on the bottom rungs tonight, the grate has just dropped shut above your head. Five Gold sits in the purse on the caller's hook, and the fighter across the salt-ringed basin is already rolling his shoulders.

🏟️ Time-Loop Gladiator in the Jungle Are.name: 🏟️ Time-Loop Gladiator in the Jungle Arena
🏟️ Time-Loop Gladiator in the Jungle Are.storyStart:
[Present in this scene: use the authored world characters the roster places in this area, and use their records for name, appearance and manner. Do not invent named characters for roles the roster already fills. The player is repeating the same day for the twelfth time and is the only person who retains memory across loops.]

Roots start dripping at the eleventh minute. You could set a clock by it, and for four loops you did.

You open your eyes on the same stone bench in the same shade under the same collapsed archway. Your hands are unmarked. Your weapon leans where you left it on a morning that has now happened twelve times. Above, the Overgrown Colosseum is filling, two hundred years of jungle in the upper tiers and four hundred people picking their way through it to find a seat.

Eleven times.

The first time you did not know. The second you thought you had gone mad. The third you tried to explain it to the fight marshal, who was patient, then less patient, then had you removed for your own safety, which taught you that being removed does not stop the day. It only means you die somewhere else.

The fourth through eighth were experiments. You have been thorough. You know what happens if you run for the tree line. You know what happens if you refuse to fight. You know, unfortunately, what happens on the seventh bout regardless of anything you have tried.

The ninth, tenth and eleventh were you getting better with the weapon. That has worked. It is the one thing that has worked.

So you already know the shape of the next four hours. You know which gate opens first and how long the marshal takes to call the order. You know who wins the third bout and how. You know, to the minute, when the roots stop dripping.

What you have never once managed is to be somewhere unexpected when they do.

The crowd noise changes pitch. That is the eleventh minute arriving, exactly on schedule, for the twelfth time.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: eleven loops of practice have made you genuinely dangerous with that weapon.
• Magic Affinity: the loop has a texture and you can feel it tightening at the eleventh minute.
• Profession: you have used four loops to map the arena instead of fighting in it.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: something in you is keeping the memory when nothing else does.
• Rebirth or Race: you have died on this floor eleven times and the crowd has never once noticed.
🏟️ Time-Loop Gladiator in the Jungle Are.description:
📍 The Overgrown Colosseum, Shingetsu Evergrove. A vast arena the jungle has been eating for two hundred years, still structurally sound, still in use.
Pace: Relentless. The same day, over and over, until you get it right.
Danger: 🟠 Dangerous. A punishing opening. Not recommended for a first run. (Recommended Level 1-28)

You have died on this arena floor eleven times. Each time you open your eyes at the same hour of the same morning, with the roots dripping and the crowd filing in and eleven fights ahead that you now know by heart. Nobody else remembers. You have tried telling them. You have tried leaving. The twelfth attempt starts in an hour.

⛓️ Pit Fighter of the Abyssal Duel Court.name: ⛓️ Pit Fighter of the Abyssal Duel Court
⛓️ Pit Fighter of the Abyssal Duel Court.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Ran Tsukikagura (female, short crimson hair, fierce amber eyes with slit pupils, small sharp horns, black-and-red arena armor) and Ashurai Chikiba (male, towering, horned, black hair, golden eyes, clawed features, dark scale-like armor). Both appear on screen and react. The player was taken as unclaimed property and made to fight in this pit. Ashurai Chikiba is far above the player's level and must not be defeated in a straight fight in the opening. Do not generate additional named fighters in the opening.]

Sound reaches the cages through the ceiling, because the cages are under the arena floor, and that is worse than hearing it properly.

It has a rhythm. You have learned it. There is the low continuous noise of several hundred people who are not yet paying attention, and then there is the change, a sort of tightening, when something on the sand becomes worth watching.

The tightening has happened twice tonight already.

Dominion property law is not cruel. That is the part that has taken you longest to sit with. It is not cruel; it is tidy. A person found on a road with no claim on them is unclaimed, and unclaimed things must belong to someone, because the alternative is a gap in the register and the Dominion does not tolerate gaps in the register.

So you belong to the Court. You have a number. You have a record, which is four fights long, and which is better than it should be.

That is the other thing. You keep winning, and you do not entirely understand how. Your body moves before you decide. You have started reading fighting styles inside three exchanges. Something in you is learning faster than a person learns, and the handlers have noticed, and the odds have moved.

Which is why tonight is different.

"You are breathing wrong," says the woman in the next cage.

She is sitting with her back to the bars, crimson hair short and stuck to her forehead, amber eyes with slit pupils fixed on the ceiling. Light arena armor, black and red, freshly scored across one shoulder. She came off the sand twenty minutes ago and has not stopped bleeding from somewhere above the hairline.

"I am breathing."

"You are breathing high." Ran Tsukikagura taps two fingers against her own sternum without looking over. "High breath is for running. You are not running. There is nowhere to run and you know it, so breathe low or you will gas in the second minute and it will be embarrassing for both of us."

"Both of us?"

"I have money on you." She says it flatly. "Everyone does. That is the problem."

The ceiling tightens.

Down the corridor, the champion's gate is being drawn up, and the thing that steps into the passage is enormous. Black hair, golden eyes, claws, dark scale armor over shoulders that do not fit through doorways designed for people. Ashurai Chikiba has killed eleven opponents in this pit and earned his freedom twice, and he keeps coming back, and nobody has satisfactorily explained why.

He stops at your cage. He looks in.

There is no malice in it at all. That is somehow the worst part.

"Four fights," says Ashurai, and his voice is surprisingly quiet. "Four is where they start watching."

Ran is very still.

The gate above begins to open.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: four fights and your body is moving before you decide, which frightens the handlers.
• Magic Affinity: the pit's wards taste of something older than the Court.
• Profession: you have been reading the crowd's rhythm through the ceiling for weeks.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you are learning faster than a person learns and the odds have moved.
