⛓️ Pit Fighter of the Abyssal Duel Court.description:
📍 Abyssal Duel Court, Twilight Dominion. A demon fighting pit under the Spire where the crowd is titled and the combatants are inventory.
Pace: Brutal. Survive tonight, then tomorrow.
Danger: ⚫ Severe. The most punishing opening in the world. Not recommended for a first run. (Recommended Level 1-65)

Frontier salvage law and Dominion property law disagree about almost everything, but they agree that a person found without a claim is unclaimed, and unclaimed things have owners. You were found on a road. You have been here long enough to have a record. Tonight you are matched against a name the crowd knows, and the only two ways out of this pit are the champion's gate and the other one.

🎭 Ran Tsukikagura, Female, arena fighter. A striking young demon with short crimson hair, fierce amber eyes with slit pupils, small sharp horns, and an athletic build, in light black-and-red arena armor. Loud and blunt and combative even in conversation, and she states preferences as challenges.
🎭 Ashurai Chikiba, Male, the standing champion. Towering and horned with black hair, golden eyes, clawed features, and dark scale-like armor, with a confident toothy grin.

⚰️ Risen From Your Own Duelist Grave.name: ⚰️ Risen From Your Own Duelist Grave
⚰️ Risen From Your Own Duelist Grave.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Erika Shiratsuyu (female, straight silver hair to her shoulders, clear blue eyes, dark hakama and gi, katana) and Yomiko Ako (female, long black hair, pointed ears, violet eyes, black dress with drifting blue ghostlights). Both appear on screen and react. The player died in a duel, was raised eight months later by an unknown patron, and has been left written instructions but no name. Do not generate additional named duelists in the opening.]

They bury duelists standing at Hollowduel, so that is how you came up: upright, in the dark, with the weight of eight months of settled earth deciding all at once that it was no longer settled.

The stone has your name on it. You have read it four times now and the letters have not improved.

Below the name there is a date, and below the date there is the short formal line they use here, the one that means the loser conceded properly and the winner did nothing dishonorable. You did concede properly. You remember conceding. You remember thinking, with a strange detached politeness, that the angle had been very good.

Then eight months of nothing at all.

The earth in front of the stone was turned from the outside. That is the detail you keep returning to, standing here in the cold with your hands filthy. Somebody dug down. Somebody did the work, and paid whatever this costs, which is not a small number in any currency, and then left before you came up.

They left a folded paper wedged into the joint of the stone.

It is not a letter. There is no greeting and no name. It is a list of three things, written in a clear practiced hand, and the first item is a place and a date eleven days from now.

"You should not read it in the wind," says somebody. "You will lose it, and then you will have to ask, and asking is worse."

There is a woman two rows over, standing at parade rest beside a memorial that is not yours. Silver hair to the shoulders, cut level. Dark hakama and gi. A katana worn as though it has been worn every day for years. She is perhaps twenty and carries herself like a much older institution.

She bows. It is precise, and it is to you, and it is deeper than a stranger warrants.

"Erika Shiratsuyu," she says. "I apologize for the intrusion, and for what I am about to say, which is that I have been coming here every morning for six days because I was told to expect this."

"Told by whom."

"I do not know." Her chin comes up slightly. "That is a poor answer and I dislike giving it. The instruction was correct, which is worse."

Further down Memorial Row, half in the fog, a woman in black is standing quite still with pale blue lights drifting slowly around her like slow snow. Pointed ears. Violet eyes that have been on you since you came up out of the ground.

Yomiko Ako has not moved and has not spoken.

Erika does not look at her.

"She was here before me," Erika says quietly. "Every morning. Longer than six days."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you conceded properly and you still remember the angle that beat you.
• Magic Affinity: whatever brought you up left a residue you can taste.
• Profession: the paper wedged in the stone is expensive and the hand is trained.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: eight months is gone and your body has not aged a day of it.
• Rebirth or Race: they bury duelists standing here, so you came up facing the right way.
⚰️ Risen From Your Own Duelist Grave.description:
📍 Hollowduel Cemetery, Rosethorn Nocturne. A duelists' burial ground of memorial rows and old challenge stones, where the dead are buried standing.
Pace: Cold and driven. A second life with a bill attached.
Danger: 🟠 Dangerous. A punishing opening. Not recommended for a first run. (Recommended Level 1-40)

You lost a duel. You remember losing it with an unpleasant amount of clarity. What you do not remember is the eight months between that and waking up in the dark under your own memorial stone, with your name carved above you and the earth already disturbed from the outside. Somebody spent a great deal to bring you back. They have not introduced themselves. They have left instructions.

🎭 Erika Shiratsuyu, Female, a trained swordswoman. Straight silver hair to her shoulders, clear blue eyes, the graceful posture of long practice, simple dark hakama and gi, katana at her hip. Formal, clipped and painfully polite, she apologizes before correcting your stance and means both halves of it.
🎭 Yomiko Ako, Female, gothic and elf-like with long black hair, pointed ears, violet eyes, a guarded expression, and blue ghostly lights drifting around her black dress.

🧪 Slow Life at Your Own Potion Shop.name: 🧪 Slow Life at Your Own Potion Shop
🧪 Slow Life at Your Own Potion Shop.description:
📍 Canopy Moon Market, Verdania Wilds. A hidden market strung across living branches high above the forest floor, lit by moonlight that pools like water.
Pace: Slow, cozy and yours. Brew, sell, drink tea, and let the adventure come to you if it wants to.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Nothing here is more dangerous than a bad review. (Recommended Level 1-10)

You were asked one question on the way into your second life, and you answered it honestly: you said you wanted a quiet one. You woke with a stall permit in your pocket, an alchemy kit under the counter, and a view of the moon through the branches. No prophecy. No summons. Your first customer has not arrived yet. Your neighbor has, and she is hiding behind her own herbs, trying to work out whether you are going to put her out of business.

🎭 Tama Yanagihara, Female, Rabbitkin alchemist with the stall beside yours. Long brown hair, amber eyes, rabbit ears, a white blouse and an apron full of bottles. Makes the best remedies in the Wilds, sells a courage potion that is mostly tea, and takes a while to warm to anyone.
🎭 Momiji Konohauta, Female, eighteen, fox-beastkin forager who supplies half the market. Short auburn hair, golden eyes, freckles, leaves in her tail. Talks fast and knows what everything is worth.

★ The slow life: no destiny, a small shop, good neighbors, and all the time in the world.
🧪 Slow Life at Your Own Potion Shop.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Tama Yanagihara (female, Rabbitkin alchemist, long brown hair, amber eyes, white blouse and apron) and Momiji Konohauta (female, fox-beastkin forager, short auburn hair, golden eyes, freckles). Both are on screen. The premise: the player chose a quiet second life and has just woken to it, as the brand-new holder of a small potion stall in Moonwell Plaza, next to Tama's. They have a kit, a few ingredients, a permit, and no customers yet. This is a slow-life opening: keep the stakes small and domestic (a first sale, a recipe, a neighbor, a regular), let the player set the pace, and never push a prophecy, crisis or call to adventure onto them. Trouble comes to this stall only if the player goes looking for it. Tama is shy, kind and worried; Momiji is brisk and friendly. Everyone here is an adult. After the opening, stop and wait for the player: never decide, move, speak or answer for them, and do not carry the scene forward on their behalf.]

The kettle on your counter is not yours, and somebody has filled it.

You find this out because it starts to sing. A small, battered kettle on a small iron ring, steam going up into branches as thick as roads, and beyond the branches a moon so large and so close that its light comes down through the leaves and lies in the hollow of the great tree like water in a bowl.

You are standing behind a stall.

It is a good stall. Three shelves, a counter worn smooth by somebody else's elbows, hooks for drying herbs, a brass scale. Under the counter there is an alchemy kit in a leather roll, a handful of sunleaf, two slime cores wrapped in wax paper, and three finished potions with labels in handwriting you do not recognize. In your pocket there is a permit. It has your name on it. It is stamped, and dated today.

You remember dying. You remember, after it, something patient and very large asking what you wanted this time.

You remember saying: a quiet life.

Apparently somebody was listening.

All around you the Canopy Moon Market is opening for the night. Rope bridges swaying. Paper lanterns coming alight one by one along the branch-paths. Stalls of living wood and glowing ink and things in jars, and people with ears and tails calling prices to each other across forty feet of open air.

The stall next to yours is so thickly hung with herbs that you can barely see into it.

Something behind the herbs moves.

A pair of long brown rabbit ears rises slowly above a bundle of drying lavender, followed by a pair of amber eyes, which find you looking straight back at them and vanish again.

"That is Tama," says a voice at your elbow, cheerfully. "She has been doing that since you appeared. She filled your kettle and then lost her nerve."

The speaker is a fox-beastkin with short auburn hair, freckles, a vendor's apron and a basket on each arm, and there are leaves caught all through her tail. She puts one basket on your counter without asking.

"Momiji. I forage. If it grows in the Wilds I can get it for you, and if I cannot get it, it does not grow." Golden eyes take in your shelves, your scale, your three potions, and the corner of the permit showing at your pocket. "New stall, new face, no stock to speak of. Good. This plaza has needed a second potion-seller for two years, and Tama has needed a neighbor who is not a tattooist for longer than that."

"Momiji," says the lavender, faintly.

"She thinks you are going to undercut her," Momiji tells you, in what she seems to believe is a whisper. "She makes the best salves in the Wilds and she is afraid of somebody with three bottles. Be nice to her. She gives you tea when you have had a bad day, and she always knows."

The ears come back up. This time the rest of her follows: long brown hair, a white blouse, an apron with a great many small pockets, and both hands wrapped around a cup as though it might run away.

"Welcome to the market," says Tama Yanagihara, to a point slightly left of your shoulder. "The kettle was a gift. It is traditional. It is not traditional. I made that up. I am sorry." She takes a breath. "What do you make?"

The moon is up. The lanterns are lit. Somewhere down the branch a first customer is walking toward the plaza, in no particular hurry, and nobody in the world is expecting anything of you at all.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Rebirth: the last life ended at a desk, or a bedside, or a roadside, and you asked for the opposite of all of it.
• Profession: your hands already know this kit, and that settles what the stall sells.
• Magic Affinity: the moonlight in the hollow leans toward your bottles, which is going to do something to the potions.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you asked for quiet and were handed something loud to carry anyway, and you are choosing not to think about it tonight.
• Race or Combat Class: nobody at this market has asked what you are or what you can do, and you find you like that.

[Stock: the alchemy kit, herbs, slime cores and potions are this start's starting items. Do not grant them again.]

[Party: Tama Yanagihara and Momiji Konohauta are market neighbors, not recruited. Neither follows the player without explicit mutual agreement.]

☕ First Shift at the Maid Café.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Beniko Yūen (female, cascading crimson hair in loose curls, amber eyes, beauty mark below her right eye, tailored uniform with star-patterned apron), Chiyo Hoshino (female, mid-twenties, five feet tall, chin-length dark bob, large hazel eyes), Sanae Nodoka (female, warm, vanilla and fresh bread), Ayame Kagaribishi (female, formal and polished), Seiji Barain (male, silver constellation embroidery, precise hands), Youta Hoshiore (male, quick banter, left-cheek dimple), and Yuuto Tessha (male, halting and quiet). All seven appear on screen and at least react. The player was recruited off the street tonight and has never worked a floor like this. Do not generate additional named staff or customers in the opening. Everyone here is an adult. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race or class. After the opening, stop and wait for the player: never decide, move, speak or answer for them, and do not carry the scene forward on their behalf.]

Somebody has already tied your apron for you, which you did not ask for and could not have managed.

Starry Lace runs under an enchanted starfield ceiling that moves slowly enough to be convincing, and the whole room is pitched at the temperature of a good evening. Out on the floor the tables are full. They have been full since the doors opened, and there is a list at the front for people who did not get one.

Eleven hours ago you were crossing the Market District with no particular plan.

A woman stopped you. She looked at your face for slightly longer than is polite, asked whether you were working anywhere, and did not seem to hear the part where you said you had no experience. She wrote something down. She told you to be here at the dusk bell, and to wear nothing you cared about.

And here you are, in the Performance Hall, listed on tonight's board as understudy.

Understudy to her.

"Interesting," says Beniko Yūen, without turning around.

She is at the long mirror finishing something with her hair, crimson and loose, and she watches you in the glass rather than facing you. The beauty mark under her right eye moves when she smiles, which she is doing now, and the earrings throw small points of light across the ceiling.

"The arithmetic being," she says, "why you. Why tonight. Why the Performance Hall instead of a quiet corner of the tea garden where a new hire belongs."

She turns around.

"The answer is that I asked for you," Beniko says. "I saw you in the Market District four days ago and I sent someone. You have a face that makes people slow down, darling, and you have absolutely no idea that you do, and that second part is the part I cannot teach and cannot fake and have been looking for since spring."

From the doorway to the tea garden, a very small maid with a chin-length bob is holding a tray at precisely the correct height and has stopped moving entirely.

"Oh," says Chiyo Hoshino. "Oh, she picked someone."

Behind her the tea garden shift arrives in a wave: Sanae with a plate she is already offering you, Ayame smoothing a cuff that does not need it, Seiji and Youta assessing you with professional interest and absolutely no discretion, and Yuuto managing a single syllable before deciding against the rest of it.

"Twelve minutes," says Beniko, pleasantly, to the room. "Then the curtain, and I would like all of you back on your own floors before it goes up."

Nobody moves.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you counted the room before you counted the tables, and she noticed.
• Magic Affinity: the starfield ceiling is a working and it is far better than it needs to be.
• Profession: you have priced the porcelain, the lanterns and the list at the door.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: somebody stopped you in the street and you never found out how she chose.
• Rebirth or Race: you have a face that makes people slow down and no idea that you do.

[Party: the staff of Starry Lace are coworkers, not recruited. None of them follows the player without explicit mutual agreement.]
☕ First Shift at the Maid Café.description:
📍 Starry Lace, Crownveil Sovereignty. A constellation-themed maid and butler cafe in Aureliath's Market District, with an enchanted starfield ceiling and staff the capital books days ahead to be served by.
Pace: Warm and crowded. Charm as a working skill.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Nothing here is armed. (Recommended Level 1-25)

You have been hired at the capital's most famous maid and butler café, and tonight is your first shift. A recruiter stopped you in the Market District, looked at your face for slightly too long, and offered you a job you had not applied for. You start tonight, in the Performance Hall, as understudy to the most requested member of staff in the capital. Nobody has explained what an understudy does here. Everyone assumes you already know.

🎭 Beniko Yūen, Female, Starry Lace's resident siren. Cascading crimson hair in loose curls, amber eyes with a permanent glint, a beauty mark below her right eye, earrings that catch light like small flames, uniform sharply tailored with the star-patterned apron neatly tied. Honeyed and deliberate, and she has never once been flustered.
🎭 Chiyo Hoshino, Female, mid-twenties, the smallest and most beloved maid. Five feet tall, chin-length dark bob, large hazel eyes, a uniform that hangs a little loose. Rapid and slightly too high-pitched when nervous, which is often.
🎭 Sanae Nodoka, Female, warm and unhurried, extra pockets sewn in for emergency snacks, smells faintly of vanilla and fresh bread.
🎭 Ayame Kagaribishi, Female, formal and polished, with attempted slang that lands like a swan trying it.
🎭 Seiji Barain, Male, constellation embroidery in silver thread he added himself, hands that make any motion look intentional.
🎭 Youta Hoshiore, Male, quick and warm, built on effortless banter, with a dimple that only appears when he means it.
🎭 Yuuto Tessha, Male, halting and quiet, keeper of the house's gentlest section, aware that the regulars have noticed him and made worse by it.

★ The café job: a first shift, a full house, and a staff who have already decided to adopt you.

🍵 Serving Secrets at the Velvet Teahouse.name: 🍵 Serving Secrets at the Velvet Teahouse
🍵 Serving Secrets at the Velvet Teahouse.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Marchioness Chiharu Harekaze (female, curled chestnut-brown hair, bright blue eyes, composed and slightly stern, pale blue gown, jeweled pendant). She appears on screen and speaks. The player is a native-born commoner beginning a service job here. Do not generate additional named staff in the opening.]

Somebody pressed this apron. That is a whole job here, and nobody expects you to be surprised by it.

You tie it on in a back corridor that smells like sugar and cold stone, and the woman doing the tying is not a housekeeper, which you work out about four seconds too late. Curled chestnut-brown hair. Bright blue eyes. A pale blue gown that no member of staff has ever owned. She adjusts your collar with the brisk fondness of an aunt at a wedding.

"There," says Marchioness Chiharu Harekaze. "Now. You are from the river district, your mother did piecework, and you can read, which is why you are standing here instead of washing pots. Tell me if I have any of that wrong."

You have not told anyone here where you are from.

She waits a beat, as if your face had answered.

"Good." She is already walking, and you are already following, because that is what the apron means. "Three rules. You will hear a great deal in this room. You will remember none of it out loud. And when a table goes quiet as you approach, you will slow down rather than speed up, because hurrying looks like fleeing and fleeing looks like guilt."

The Tea Ceremony Room opens ahead of you, low-lit and honey-colored, and it is full. A woman in Crown colors is sitting with a man whose house crest you half recognize, and neither of them has touched their cups. Two merchants are laughing too much. Somebody in the corner alcove has not taken off their gloves.

The acoustics in here are beautiful. You notice that immediately and do not yet know why the ceiling is shaped like that.

"You will be fine," the Marchioness says, warm as fresh milk. "You have the face for it. People say things in front of a pleasant face."

She presses a small tray into your hands. Two cups, one pot, no order slip.

"Table four," she says. "They did not order. Whether you carry it is for you to decide; if you do, tell me afterward what they stopped saying."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you counted the exits before you counted the tables.
• Magic Affinity: three separate wards are humming in this room and none of them are advertised.
• Profession: you know exactly what the porcelain cost and it is not what they paid.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you catch a dropped cup without deciding to.
• Rebirth or Race: the staff sized you up in one glance and put you where you would be seen.
🍵 Serving Secrets at the Velvet Teahouse.description:
📍 Velvet Teahouse, Crownveil Sovereignty. The aristocracy's favorite neutral ground, all warm wood, better pastry than anyone admits, and excellent acoustics.
Pace: Gentle. Service work, small talk, and secrets you were not meant to hear.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Nothing here will draw a blade. (Recommended Level 1-10)

Your parents worked, you grew up folding napkins, and at no point did anyone suggest you were destined for anything. Today you start a paid position at the finest teahouse in the capital. The wage is good, the uniform is provided, and by the end of your first shift you will understand that every table in this room is a negotiation and the staff are expected to be furniture.

🎭 Marchioness Chiharu Harekaze, Female, the teahouse's owner. Curled chestnut-brown hair, bright blue eyes, composed and slightly stern, pale blue gown and jeweled pendant. Speaks like a favorite aunt over biscuits, except every anecdote is an intelligence briefing and every question is a probe.

♨️ Young Innkeeper of Frostbell Onsen.name: ♨️ Young Innkeeper of Frostbell Onsen
♨️ Young Innkeeper of Frostbell Onsen.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Mira Ginrou (female, wolf-eared, pastel pink-and-white hair, rosy eyes, pale blue clothing, small white foxlike companions), Mizuki Setsurin (female, long black hair, warm brown eyes, dark indigo robes with pale blue layers and snowflake patterns), Fuyumi Shiragiku (female, Snowblood frost mage), and Yukina Kōrihana (female, shrine maiden of the Frostbell shrine). Mira Ginrou and Mizuki Setsurin appear on screen and react; Fuyumi Shiragiku and Yukina Kōrihana are elsewhere in town, named from their records only if the scene reaches them. The player has just inherited their family's bathhouse inn in this town. Do not generate additional named staff in the opening. Everyone in this scene is an adult.]

Nine keys, heavier than they look, and you only know what six of them open.

Your grandmother handed them over on the fourteenth, in the front room, in front of three members of staff and a delivery man who happened to be standing there, which in Frostbell is more than enough to make it binding. Then she said she was going to bed. Then she went to bed, and she has largely stayed there, and every time you go up to ask her something she tells you that you will work it out and asks whether you have eaten.

Six generations. The Ginrou side of the family has worked here for four of them.

You grew up in this building. You know the sound the pipes make in the small hours, and which step is loud, and how to shut the eastern door so it does not stick. You have carried towels in this bathhouse since you were five years old and you could run it, operationally, in your sleep.

It is the other parts.

There is a rivalry with the Snowbell house on the far side of the Lantern Row, which is two hundred years old, entirely polite, and apparently now yours. There is a seat on the district association that comes with the inn. There is a festival in eleven days that your family has hosted every year since before the association existed.

And there are the books, which are in the office, on the desk, closed.

"And then," says Mira Ginrou, backing through the door with an armload of linen, "she bravely carried the entire third floor's worth in ONE trip, and the crowd went absolutely wild, and, oh, you are in here."

One of the small white fox things on her shoulder makes a noise.

You are, in fact, in here.

Mira looks at the desk. Then at the closed books. Then at your face, and her ears go down a little, and the narration stops, which is how you know she is being serious.

"You have not opened them," she says. It is not a question.

"Do you want me to be in the room when you do?"

Which is, you think, possibly the kindest thing anyone has offered you in a month.

In the corridor, Mizuki Setsurin passes with an armful of folded indigo and slows without quite stopping, giving you the small warm nod she has been giving you every morning since the fourteenth.

And through the front window, across the steaming street, somebody from the Snowbell house is standing outside their own entrance with their arms folded, looking directly at your door.

They have been there a while.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: nine keys, six of which you know, and one door you have not opened.
• Magic Affinity: the spring water carries a warmth that is not only heat.
• Profession: you could run this bathhouse in your sleep and have, twice.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: your grandmother handed over the keys the day after she stopped arguing.
• Rebirth or Race: six generations, and the association seat came with the building.
♨️ Young Innkeeper of Frostbell Onsen.description:
📍 Frostbell Onsen Town, Yukishiro Veilpeak. A snowbound spa town of steaming pools, lantern-lined streets, and inns that have been feuding politely for two hundred years.
Pace: Cozy. Hospitality, festivals, and small-town politics.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The town looks after guests, and you are family. (Recommended Level 1-16)

Your family has run the same inn in the Hot Spring District for six generations, and last month your grandmother handed you the keys and went to bed, which in this town constitutes a legal transfer. You now own a bathhouse, a staff who have known you since you were born, a rivalry you inherited without asking, and a set of books you have not yet dared to open.

🎭 Mira Ginrou, Female, twenty-two, inn staff and Foxkin beast tamer. A soft-featured young woman with fox ears and a tail, pastel pink-and-white hair, rosy eyes and a shy smile, in pale blue clothing, with small white spirit foxes at her shoulders. Fast and bright and given to narrating her own actions with sound effects.
🎭 Mizuki Setsurin, Female, gentle with long black hair, warm brown eyes, and a soft smile, in dark indigo robes with pale blue inner layers and snowflake patterns.
🎭 Fuyumi Shiragiku, Female, Snowblood frost mage and guardian of the Veilpeak passes. Speaks rarely, fights beautifully, and shows affection through actions rather than words.
🎭 Yukina Kōrihana, Female, shrine maiden of the Frostbell mountain shrine. Keeps the sacred springs and the old ice-spirit seals, answers in short sentences, and handles every crisis with flat calm.

🍶 Seven Paid Nights in Frostbell Onsen.name: 🍶 Seven Paid Nights in Frostbell Onsen
🍶 Seven Paid Nights in Frostbell Onsen.description:
📍 Frostbell Onsen Town, Yukishiro Veilpeak. A snow-country hot spring town of steam, lanterns, and unhurried evenings, where the baths outrank the mayor.
Pace: Yours. Seven nights, paid in full. The town's only demand is that you enjoy it.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The deepest trouble on Lantern Row is a second bottle. (Recommended Level 1-10)

You did something modest and useful on the road (escorted a grateful merchant, guessed a snowstorm right), and the reward was not coin but a paper voucher: seven nights on Lantern Row, room and bath included, at the busiest tavern-inn in Frostbell. So here you are, checked in, boots drying by a stove, with a welcome sake set on the table and steam drifting past your window. Nobody knows you. Nothing needs you. The Row runs warm and golden below, the shrine bell marks hours you are free to ignore, and the whole snowbound town operates on the firm principle that whatever you came here carrying can wait a week.

🎭 Sake Homura, Male, the tavern's keeper and master brewer downstairs — a warm boom of a man who has your name memorized already and strong opinions about which cup you should start with.
🎭 Gunther Hyōshun, Male, a mountain-guide regular at the tavern who can point you at every overlook, ice cave, and quiet path in the valley.
🎭 Mira Ginrou, Female, bright, energetic, and employed at the Hot Spring District's front desk in a way that seems to involve mostly enthusiasm.
🎭 Yukina Kōrihana, Female, serene and kind, tends the Snowbell Shrine's small duties and the bathhouse's forgotten guests.
🎭 Fuyumi Shiragiku, Female, a cool, precise mage taking the waters on her own schedule, who reads by the bathhouse lanterns and does not explain herself.
🍶 Seven Paid Nights in Frostbell Onsen.storyStart:
[The player has a fully paid seven-night voucher at the tavern-inn on Lantern Row; they arrived tonight. Nothing is owed, scheduled, or wrong. Keep maids, bathers, and townsfolk unnamed and descriptive; do not invent named staff. All named characters come from the authored roster — Sake Homura and Gunther Hyōshun at the Lantern Row tavern; Mira Ginrou, Yukina Kōrihana, Mizuki Setsurin, and Fuyumi Shiragiku around the Hot Spring District and shrine — and appear only if and when the player's choices reach them, using their records. Sake Homura may greet the player warmly as the keeper of the house, but must not assign tasks or hooks; the vacation is the premise.]

Snow is falling on Lantern Row the way it apparently always falls on Lantern Row: without urgency, in flakes the size of coins, through the light of a hundred paper lanterns that turn the whole street the color of warm sake.

Your room is on the second floor of the tavern at the Row's busy end. It is small and perfect: a stove already lit, a futon already turned down, your boots already steaming dry beside the door, and on the low table, compliments of the house, a sake set — two cups, because the house is an optimist.

The voucher lies beside it, stamped PAID THROUGH, SEVEN NIGHTS, in the generous handwriting of a merchant who believed you saved his cargo and possibly his life. You remember it as forty minutes of standing in the right place with whatever you had to hand. He remembered it differently, and his memory bought you a week.

Downstairs, the tavern is at half-roar — the comfortable evening volume of a room where everyone is warm and nobody is going anywhere. The keeper's voice rolls under the floorboards every so often, introducing a bottle the way other men introduce dignitaries. When you checked in, he took one look at your road gear, said your name back to you correctly on the first try, and told you the bath schedule with the gravity of a man entrusting you with state secrets.

Beyond your window: the Row's lanterns, the steam rising off the Deepwell Bathhouse three streets over, the dark climb of the valley walls, and the small bright bell-tower of the Snowbell Shrine, which will ring the late hour soon and expects absolutely nothing of you when it does.

Seven nights. A hot bath whenever you want one. A tavern downstairs, a snowbound town outside, and not one single obligation in any direction.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: your body does not believe in vacations yet, and the inn's courtyard is empty and freshly snowed at dawn.
• Magic Affinity: the bathhouse steam bends toward you slightly, which the locals say the springs only do for some people.
• Profession: the tavern's book is open on the bar downstairs, and you have already spotted what the house is undercharging for.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the welcome sake tastes faintly of something the menu does not list, and the keeper is watching your face with tremendous interest.
• Rebirth or Race: the snow does not land on you quite the way it lands on everyone else, and a child on the Row has noticed.

🪕 Last-Minute Opener at the Coral Mask F.name: 🪕 Last-Minute Opener at the Coral Mask Festival
🪕 Last-Minute Opener at the Coral Mask F.description:
📍 Coral Mask Festival Grounds, Cerulean Coast. A harbor-front festival district of coral-stone pavilions, paper lanterns and floating stages.
Pace: Bright, busy and musical. One night, one stage, a great many masks.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Nothing here will hurt you except the reviews. (Recommended Level 1-10)

The Coral Mask Festival opens at dusk, and the band booked for the Harbor Stage is on a ship that has not come in. You were hired this afternoon, sight unseen, on the strength of a tavern set somebody's cousin heard. The fee is real. So is the crowd, the first big night of the season, and the headliner you are opening for, who would like to know who you are and whether you can keep time.

🎭 Minami Shiokaze, Female, eighteen, festival coordinator. Wavy turquoise hair, sea-green eyes, a coral mask pushed up on her head and a clipboard she never puts down. She hired you and is choosing to be optimistic about it.
🎭 Marina Shionari, Female, Merfolk-Blooded singer and tide mage, tonight's headliner. Wavy teal hair, pointed ears, and a smile that has closed a hundred harbor deals. She has shared stages with the best on the coast and is deciding which kind you are.

★ Written for bards, musicians, dancers and anyone who took an instrument as their signature weapon.
🎵 Any instrument works, from a lute to suzu bells.
🪕 Last-Minute Opener at the Coral Mask F.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Minami Shiokaze (festival coordinator, female, eighteen, wavy turquoise hair, sea-green eyes, clipboard), Marina Shionari (Merfolk-Blooded singer and tide mage, female, wavy teal hair, pointed ears). Both appear on screen and at least react. The player is a performer hired this afternoon to open on the Harbor Stage tonight; their instrument or act is whatever their character sheet carries, and if it carries none the festival lends one. Nobody here has heard them play. The crowd is ordinary festival-goers in coral masks; do not generate named bystanders. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race or class. After the opening, stop and wait for the player: never decide, move, speak or answer for them, and do not carry the scene forward on their behalf.]

The stage moves.

Nobody mentioned that. The Harbor Stage is a raft of lacquered platforms chained to the old breakwater, and every time the tide breathes, the whole thing lifts a hand's width and settles again. Lanterns are going up along the promenade in rows of coral pink and gold. Out past the barges, somebody is testing fireworks one at a time, and each one lights up a harbor full of people who are not here yet and will be within the hour.

"You came! Oh, good, you actually came."

The woman hurrying down the gangway has turquoise hair, a coral mask shoved up on top of her head, and a clipboard held like a shield. She checks something off before she has finished looking at you.

"Minami Shiokaze, festival coordinator, I am the one who hired you. The Tidewater Five were supposed to open tonight and the Tidewater Five are becalmed somewhere off the point, so now it is you." She says it brightly, the way people say things they have decided not to worry about. "You have the first set. Two songs, three if they like you. Then Marina."

She tips her head toward the far end of the stage.

A woman is sitting on the edge of the last platform with her feet over the water, teal hair loose down her back, humming scales under her breath. She has not turned around. She has, very clearly, been listening since you stepped aboard.

"So this is the opener," says Marina Shionari, to the harbor. Then she looks over her shoulder and smiles, and the smile is warm and gives away nothing at all. "Minami tells me you are very good. Minami has never heard you. I would like to, before four thousand people do. Play me eight bars."

Minami's pen has stopped moving.

Fifteen silver sits in your pocket, an advance against a fee you have not earned yet. Dusk is perhaps an hour off. What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Signature Weapon: the instrument is already in your hands. Open on its weight, its tuning, and the one string that never behaves.
• Combat Class or Profession: you have played worse rooms than this. Open on the last one, and why you left.
• Race: the mask Minami hands you was not made for your ears, horns or face, and she is already apologizing.
• Rebirth: there is a song from the old world that nobody here has ever heard. It is the best thing you know.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: something in you hums along when the tide lifts the stage, and it is in a key you did not choose.

[Fee: the fifteen silver coins are already included in this start's startingItems. Narrate that same advance; do not grant it again. The rest of the fee is paid after the set, in a scene.]

[Party: Minami and Marina are festival contacts, not recruited. Neither follows the player without explicit mutual agreement to travel together.]

🍽️ Running the Banquet on Starry Lace Te.name: 🍽️ Running the Banquet on Starry Lace Terrace
🍽️ Running the Banquet on Starry Lace Te.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Reina Tsubaki (Female, Starry Lace's tall silver-haired maid and its most exacting staff member). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters.]

Sixty covers, three delegations, ninety minutes, and a seating plan that somebody has already amended twice in two different hands.

Starry Lace's moonlit terrace is the most desirable table in the capital and it is currently the most alarming room you have ever stood in. Lanterns are strung and unlit. Linen is down. The long table runs the length of the terrace under the open sky with the city glowing beyond the balustrade, and it is beautiful, and it is entirely unset.

The organizer left at noon. Nobody will say why. The steward, who is a decisive man having a bad day, walked the terrace once, looked around for someone standing still and not visibly panicking, found you, put the plan and the kitchen list into your hands, said the words ninety minutes, and went to argue with the wine merchant.

That was six minutes ago.

The plan has two names on it that cannot be seated adjacent. You know this because somebody has written cannot be adjacent next to them, twice, in different ink, which means it has already gone wrong once.

The kitchen list has a course on it that requires an ingredient nobody has confirmed arrived.

"Twelve," says a voice behind you.

The maid has come out onto the terrace with a tray of nothing, which you suspect is a diagnostic. She is tall, silver-haired, and radiates the specific calm of somebody who has watched three of these evenings go wrong and survived all three.

"Twelve what?"

"Twelve staff. For sixty." Reina Tsubaki sets the empty tray down. "Adequate. Barely."

She looks at the plan in your hand for exactly as long as she needs to.

"Wrong."

"Which part?"

"Second delegation faces the balustrade. Their protocol requires their principal sits with their back to a wall." A pause of precisely the right length. "The last organizer learned that at the soup."

You look at the plan again. She is right, and correcting it moves nine people, and moving nine people puts the two who cannot be adjacent within one chair of each other.

"Can it be solved?"

"Yes." She begins straightening a linen fold that did not need it. "Not by the plan. The plan has no answer. It will need something the plan does not contain."

Down in the salon a door opens and a voice calls a question about the lanterns that nobody answers.

Reina picks the empty tray back up.

"Eighty-four minutes," she says. "I will do whatever you decide. I would prefer you decided soon."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you clocked the terrace's two exits and the balustrade drop before you looked at the seating plan.
• Magic Affinity: the lanterns are enchanted and half of them are wired to a working that is not lighting.
• Profession: you found the amended ink and the missing ingredient inside four minutes of holding the list.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you knew which two names were the problem before you read the note beside them.
• Rebirth or Race: the steward picked you because you were standing still, and standing still is not a qualification.
🍽️ Running the Banquet on Starry Lace Te.description:
📍 Starry Lace, Crownveil Sovereignty. The capital's most fashionable cafe and salon, whose moonlit terrace is booked months ahead and hosts the conversations that the Court prefers to have off the record.
Pace: Elegant and accelerating. Ninety minutes and counting.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Nothing here is dangerous. Everything here is consequential. (Recommended Level 1-25)

A private banquet on the terrace tonight seats three delegations who are at peace only as long as the evening goes smoothly. The organizer left at noon and has not been replaced. The steward found the nearest competent-looking person, pressed the seating plan and the kitchen list into their hands, and went to deal with the wine, and that person was you. First guests arrive in ninety minutes and the seating plan has two names on it that must not be adjacent.

🎭 Reina Tsubaki, Female, Starry Lace's tall silver-haired maid and its most exacting staff member, serving with mechanical precision and answering in as few words as the situation can be made to accept.

🏪 Stall-Keeper of Misthollow Night Marke.name: 🏪 Stall-Keeper of Misthollow Night Market
🏪 Stall-Keeper of Misthollow Night Marke.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Severin Kuresa (male, pale, dark hair, red eyes, sharp features, black formal clothes with a ribbon tie) and Haku Mugai (male, fox-eared, golden-amber eyes, silvery-white hair, layered white-and-black robes with gold patterning, multiple tails). Both appear on screen and react. The player is a native stall keeper on the mortal side of the market. Do not generate additional named vendors as major characters in the opening.]

Not one minute before the last light goes, the market opens. The lamps will not take a flame until then. Nobody has ever explained this to you satisfactorily and you stopped asking at eleven.

Your stall is fourth from the water on the mortal side. Dried goods, cord, lamp oil, small ironmongery, and your mother's scales, which are older than the stall and better than anything sold in this market. You have run it alone for two years. You are good at it. You could do the whole night with your eyes shut and mostly do.

Across the central channel, the spirit bazaar is lighting up in colors that mortal lamps do not make.

The rule is simple and everyone's parents teach it the same way. Sell across the channel, fine. Buy across the channel, fine, and haggle hard, they respect it. Take something offered for free, and you are not on the mortal side anymore, and the change is not announced.

You have never been tempted. It is not a hard rule to keep. Nobody offers.

Tonight, somebody is standing at your stall who did not walk up the mortal aisle.

He is pale to the point of being lit from inside, dark-haired, red-eyed, in black formal clothes with a ribbon tie that belongs at an opera rather than a night market. His expression is doing absolutely nothing, and doing it well.

He has set a small wrapped parcel on your counter, beside the scales.

"For you," says Severin Kuresa. "With no obligation whatsoever."

The market noise carries on around you. Nobody at the neighboring stalls has looked over, which is itself impossible, because Old Kaneda looks at everything.

The market's oldest rule hangs between you: nobody here takes anything free.

"No," he says, pleasantly, as if you had said it. "You do not. It is an excellent rule and it has kept this market functional for four hundred years." He does not move the parcel. "I am aware that offering it is discourteous. I have chosen to be discourteous. You may consider that information."

Something shifts further down the aisle. A man with fox ears and silver-white hair is leaning against a post on the mortal side, which is also not where he should be, watching the two of you with golden eyes and an expression of mild, dangerous entertainment.

Haku Mugai raises two fingers in greeting when you look at him. His tails do not move at all.

Severin has not blinked.

"Take it or refuse it," he says. "Both are answers. I would like one tonight."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: your mother's scales are heavy enough to swing and you have thought about it.
• Magic Affinity: the spirit bazaar's colors are wrong to you in a way locals cannot see.
• Profession: you have run this stall alone for two years and your margins are better than hers were.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you knew the parcel was coming before it landed on the counter.
• Rebirth or Race: the rule has kept this market functional for four hundred years.
🏪 Stall-Keeper of Misthollow Night Marke.description:
📍 Misthollow Night Market, Meikyo Spiritfen. A market that runs from dusk to dawn, split down the middle: mortal stalls on one side, spirit bazaar on the other, one unwritten rule between them.
Pace: Commercial and creeping. Trade first, discover later.
Danger: 🟡 Moderate. The rule protects you exactly as long as you keep it. (Recommended Level 1-16)

You were born on the mortal side and you have kept your mother's stall since she stopped being able to. You know the prices, the regulars, the weights, and the one rule everybody's parents teach them here: you may sell to the other side, you may buy from the other side, but you never accept anything offered for free. Tonight somebody very well dressed is offering you something for free.

🎭 Severin Kuresa, Male, a dealer in beautiful things. Pale, dark-haired, red-eyed, sharp-featured, unreadable, in black formal clothes with a ribbon tie. Every sentence arrives gift-wrapped.
🎭 Haku Mugai, Male, fox-eared with golden-amber eyes and windswept silvery-white hair, in layered white-and-black robes with gold patterning and multiple tails.

🔑 Mystery Deed in the Jewel Bazaar.name: 🔑 Mystery Deed in the Jewel Bazaar
🔑 Mystery Deed in the Jewel Bazaar.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Nami Shiomi (Female, merchant captain and former pirate. Weathered and loud and generous, sea-salt hair tied back out of the way), Sango Shiotsumugi (Female, Fairy-Blooded accessory enchanter. Small, distracted and sweetly chaotic). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters.]

Keys first. That is what your hand closed on when you woke: four of them, iron, on a ring worn smooth by somebody else's thumb, and only one that you can match to a door.

Behind the counter is not where you expected to become conscious. The apron was already on. It fits, which is the detail that keeps snagging. Somebody sized this for you.

Sapphire Sail comes through the open front in layers: salt, hot sugar, wet rope, and the bright noise of a market awake for hours that assumes you have been too. The Jewel Bazaar is the covered part, gems and coral behind locked glass, everything catching light on purpose.

The shop is small, stocked, and undeniably in business. Display cases half full. A book open at a page dated this week, ten years of entries in a careful slanted hand that stops, without ceremony, four days ago.

The deed is under the book. Your name is on it. The name granting it to you is one you have never heard, written by someone who evidently knew you well enough to guess your apron size.

The back room hums. Not loudly. The way a held note hums when someone is being quiet about it.

The bell rings.

"Right, so that answers that," says a voice like a quarterdeck. "Everyone said the shop had gone dark and I said give it a week, and here you are looking like a person who has just met their own furniture."

The woman filling your doorway is broad-shouldered and salt-cured and grinning, and she has already crossed to the counter and turned your book around to face her without asking.

"Nami Shiomi. Two doors down, sea-glass and imports, and I am going to save you three days." She runs a finger down the page. "Your predecessor priced honest and sold slow, which the Bazaar respected and the Bazaar's landlords did not. You have got tenancy dues at the end of the month. That is the first thing nobody will tell you until it is late."

"I do not know what half of this stock is."

"No, you would not." She taps a line without looking up. "That is because a third of it is not stock, it is somebody's holdings, parked. See the entries with no buyer? Ten years of them." Now she does look up, and the grin has gone thoughtful. "Your predecessor was keeping something for someone. Might be sweet. Might be why the handwriting stops."

Behind her, someone smaller has drifted in and is examining a display case with her nose almost touching the glass, hair full of pins that do not match.

"Oh, these are lovely," Sango Shiotsumugi says, to the case rather than to you. "These are much older than the rest. Do you know they are humming? Just a bit. Just underneath." She straightens, entirely cheerful. "Sorry, I should have said good morning. Good morning! I am next door. My things sometimes do more than the label says, and I have decided that is a feature."

Nami pushes the book back toward you and taps the counter twice, the way people do when they are leaving you with something.

"Bell goes about forty times before noon," she says. "You will want an answer ready for what you sell here before the fifth one."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you checked the room's exits before you checked the till, and Nami clocked you doing it.
• Magic Affinity: the hum from the back room is not machinery, and you knew that before you crossed the floor.
• Profession: the book's slanted hand is doing something clever with the columns and you have already spotted it.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you knew the apron would fit before you looked down.
• Rebirth or Race: the deed names you correctly, in a hand that should not have known you were coming.
🔑 Mystery Deed in the Jewel Bazaar.description:
📍 Sapphire Sail Market, Cerulean Coast. A seaside market of colorful stalls and salt wind, where the Jewel Bazaar trades in gemstones, coral work, and enchanted trinkets under lock and velvet.
Pace: Warm and busy. A livelihood handed over before breakfast.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The Bazaar is watched, well lit, and deeply nosy. (Recommended Level 1-14)

Four iron keys, an apron that fits too well, and a deed carrying your name, granted by a name you have never heard, to a shop you have never seen. The book is a decade of somebody else's handwriting. The back room hums faintly and will not explain itself. The bell over the door has already rung twice this morning, and the Bazaar has decided to find out what you are made of before lunch.

🎭 Nami Shiomi, Female, merchant captain and former pirate. Weathered and loud and generous, sea-salt hair tied back out of the way, with a stall two doors down that functions as the Bazaar's unofficial harbor for gossip.
🎭 Sango Shiotsumugi, Female, Fairy-Blooded accessory enchanter. Small, distracted and sweetly chaotic, with a tiny shop whose charms routinely do slightly more than advertised.

🐎 Free Trader at the Lantern Crossroads.name: 🐎 Free Trader at the Lantern Crossroads
🐎 Free Trader at the Lantern Crossroads.description:
📍 Pilgrim's Lantern Road, Sanctum Ecclesia. A holy road of wayside shrines and hooded lanterns, crossing half the continent — and, at one particular signpost, crossing everything else.
Pace: Yours. You own the cart, the mule, and the morning. The road owns nothing of you.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The Lantern Road is warded and patrolled. The roads it crosses make their own arrangements. (Recommended Level 1-20)

The cart is yours, bought honestly, patched soundly, smelling of cedar and old canvas. The mule is yours, gray, unimpressed, dependable. The map in its case is new and complete and has nothing circled on it, because circling something is a decision and you have not made one. You spent your first season in this world working for other people's wagons; this morning, at the Crossroads of the Pilgrim's Lantern Road, the wagon is finally yours. North is the Sovereignty and its markets. South is the coast. East, the Frontier pays triple for freight and explains itself to nobody. West, the forests trade in things with no fixed price. A signpost with four arms, a mule with no opinion, and the widest morning of your second life.

🎭 Brother Kuroha, Male, a road-mentor of the Lantern Way with a history he polishes rather than hides, who blesses wheels, warns honestly about routes, and asks no questions he does not want answered.
🎭 Aoi Hikarino, Female, a gentle keeper of the Lantern Way's shrines who feeds pilgrims, waves off carts she has decided are lucky, and remembers every traveler who was kind.
🐎 Free Trader at the Lantern Crossroads.storyStart:
[The player owns a small trade cart and a mule outright and stands at the Crossroads of the Pilgrim's Lantern Road with a full map, modest coin, and total freedom of direction; nothing is owed and nothing is scheduled. Keep pilgrims, patrols, and passing traffic unnamed and descriptive; do not invent named travelers in the opening. The only authored characters on the road are Brother Kuroha and Aoi Hikarino along the Lantern Way, drawn from their records, appearing only if and when the player's choices reach them. Do not force a passenger, a job, a bandit raid, or a broken wheel into the opening; the open road and the unmade choice are the premise.]

The signpost at the Crossroads has four arms, and someone has hung a small lantern from each of them, because on the Pilgrim's Lantern Road even the signage keeps the faith.

Your mule is investigating the verge with the thoroughness of a scholar. Your cart stands behind her, loaded light and lashed properly: trade canvas, a tool roll, a water cask, a crate of the sensible sundries every market wants and no market is excited by. It took you a season of driving other people's freight to buy this rig, and the man who sold it to you spent ten minutes pointing out its flaws with the tenderness of a father listing a daughter's virtues.

Dawn came an hour ago. The road's night lanterns are going out one by one behind you, each with a small papery sigh, and the morning traffic is beginning: a pilgrim with a staff and a sunburn, two Church wardens on gray horses who nodded at your cart's honest lashings, a tinker heading the way you came who called out a price for your mule, was refused, and seemed satisfied with the ritual of it.

The map is open on the driver's bench. It is a good map. It shows the Sovereignty's white cities north, the coast roads south with their harbor tolls inked in tidy warning-red, the eastern routes into the Frontier where the cartographer's line work gets visibly more honest, and the western tracks toward forests marked with the old symbol that means the trees are older than the treaty.

Nothing on it is circled. You checked again this morning, with your thumb hovering, and put the charcoal down, and fed the mule instead.

Four directions. One cart, paid for. A mule with no opinion, a season's road-craft in your hands, and nobody — in any of the four directions — waiting, expecting, or owed.

The lanterns on the signpost gutter out, one by one, as the sun takes over the job.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: the eastern arm of the signpost has fresh sword-notches in it — a tally, and an invitation, in the Frontier's plain handwriting.
• Magic Affinity: your mule will not walk under the western arm's lantern, and this morning that lantern is the only one still lit.
• Profession: you know to the copper what your crate cost and what it clears in each direction, and one of the four numbers is wrong in a way that smells like opportunity.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: the map case re-inked itself overnight, and there is now a fifth road on the map that the signpost does not offer.
• Rebirth or Race: the shrine-keeper at the last waystone fed your mule, waved your cart through, and called you by a name you have not told anyone on this road.

⚒️ Past-Life Smith of Emberglass Forge.name: ⚒️ Past-Life Smith of Emberglass Forge
⚒️ Past-Life Smith of Emberglass Forge.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Ragna Kadan (male, dark red-brown hair, glowing amber eyes, hard angular face, black work clothes), Forge Master Kaguro (male, swept silver hair, hornlike metal growths, amber eyes, soot-dark work clothes), Genzo Haikamuri (male, retired A-Rank adventurer), and Tessen Kajiwara (female, towering oni master smith). Ragna Kadan and Forge Master Kaguro appear on screen and react; Genzo Haikamuri and Tessen Kajiwara are elsewhere in the city, named from their records only if the scene reaches them. The player was born in this city, apprenticed normally, and carries craft knowledge from a previous life they have hidden for four years. Do not generate additional named smiths in the opening. Also standing in these areas and drawn from the authored roster, not invented: Genzo Haikamuri (retired A-Rank adventurer); Tessen Kajiwara (towering oni master smith). Name them from their records if the scene reaches them.]

Six hundred years and the Central Forge has not been cold once, and you can feel that in the floor.

Not heat. The floor is heat. What you feel through your boots is the other thing, the low continuous working of a place that has never once been allowed to stop, twelve furnaces on rotation and the great one in the middle that only Kaguro touches.

You were born four streets from here. You were apprenticed at fourteen, like everybody, on a morning your mother cried about and your father did not.

And on that first morning, holding a hammer for the first time in this life, your hands knew where to put it.

Not skill. You want to be precise about this, because you have been thinking about it for four years. Skill is the wrist, and the wrist takes a decade. This was underneath that. It was knowing what the metal was going to do, the way you know a room in the dark in the house you grew up in.

You did the sensible thing. You slowed down. You made the mistakes an apprentice makes, on purpose, at roughly the correct rate, for four years.

It has not worked.

"Again," says Ragna Kadan.

He is standing at your shoulder where he has been standing for the past two hours, arms folded, forge light doing unkind things to a face that was already hard. Dark red-brown hair. Amber eyes with actual light in them.

You draw the billet, fold, set, strike.

Ragna says nothing for a long moment.

"You compensated," he says.

"I did not."

"The third strike was soft. Deliberately." He does not raise his voice. He never raises his voice. "You have been doing it since you came onto my floor. I did not mention it for a year because I assumed nerves. Then I assumed modesty." A pause, and something in it goes very slightly warmer. "I have run out of assumptions."

Across the floor two of the senior smiths have stopped pretending to sort stock and are watching openly.

And at the great furnace, the Forge Master has turned around.

Kaguro does not come over. He has not spoken to an apprentice directly in eleven years, by the yard's count. He simply stands there with the light behind him, silver hair swept back off a face that has metal growing through it, amber eyes on your billet rather than on you.

Ragna notices, and goes still.

"Whatever you are hiding," he says quietly, "decide now whether you are hiding it from me or from him. They are different problems and you no longer have time for both."

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you have been hiding good hands for four years and Ragna has counted every soft strike.
• Magic Affinity: the great furnace has a voice and it has been getting louder to you.
• Profession: your hands knew the fold before anyone taught you the fold.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: skill is the wrist and takes a decade; this was underneath that.
• Rebirth or Race: you were born four streets from here and apprenticed at fourteen like everybody.
⚒️ Past-Life Smith of Emberglass Forge.description:
📍 Emberglass Forge City, Kagutsuchi Emberwake. A city built around a furnace complex that has not gone cold in six hundred years, where the guilds are the government.
Pace: Steady and satisfying. Learn a craft, earn a name.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The city is orderly. The Forge Depths are not. (Recommended Level 1-25)

You were born here and apprenticed at fourteen like everyone else, and on your first day at the anvil your hands did something you had never been taught. Not skill. Skill takes years. This was knowledge, sitting in your fingers, from a life that ended somewhere else. You have spent four years hiding how fast you learn, and the Forge has noticed anyway.

🎭 Ragna Kadan, Male, forge mage and heavy weapons smith. Stern with dark red-brown hair, glowing amber eyes, and a hard angular face, in black work clothes lit by the forge. Treats words like ore, valuable and worth refining and used sparingly.
🎭 Forge Master Kaguro, Male, hard-faced with swept silver hair, hornlike metal growths, amber eyes, and soot-dark work clothes with leather straps.
🎭 Tessen Kajiwara, Female, towering oni master smith and senior voice of the Cinderborn Compact. Keeper of the largest forge in the city, and the person everyone listens to on metal, people and politics alike.
🎭 Genzo Haikamuri, Male, retired A-Rank adventurer running a weapon repair shop. Fixes rookie gear for free, remembers the Ashenmere Border Wars, and has not actually retired from caring.

🔨 Chosen by the Ancient Emberglass Forge.name: 🔨 Chosen by the Ancient Emberglass Forge
🔨 Chosen by the Ancient Emberglass Forge.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Nekomi Shigure (Female, cat beastkin alchemist and trap specialist, all genki energy and bouncing ears). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters.]

Heat comes up through the soles first. That is the thing nobody mentions about Emberglass: the ground is warm, everywhere, all the time, and after an hour you stop noticing and after a day you cannot sleep without it.

The Market Quarter runs downhill from the public forge in tiers of black stone, stall after stall of blades and plate and tools and the specialty work that only the Emberwake's channels can produce. Buyers come from everywhere. Half the accents in the lane are not local. It is the least mystical place imaginable, which is precisely why what happened is a problem.

You crossed the threshold at the head of the quarter, where the public forge sits open to the street so that visitors can see the fire that has not gone out since the city was founded.

It flared.

Not sparked. Not caught a draft. It stood up, white at the core, hard enough that the smith working it stepped back and put an arm across his face, and it held for the length of a slow breath, and then it settled, and every single person in the lane turned around.

There were nine of them. One was a buyer from Aureliath with a book, which means it is already written down somewhere.

That was forty minutes ago and the lane has not gone back to normal. The stalls are trading again, but there is a knot of people at the forge head that keeps changing composition and not dispersing, and the argument in it is old enough that everyone knows their line.

"Okay so I have been eavesdropping professionally," announces somebody at your elbow, "which is a skill, and I am going to summarize because they will not."

The cat beastkin who has appeared beside you is bouncing very slightly on the balls of her feet, ears forward, and has soot on one cheek in the shape of a hand.

"Nekomi Shigure, alchemy and traps, workshop three streets down, please do not touch the blue crate if you visit." She jerks a thumb at the knot of people. "Right. The old guard say the fire only greets Emberwake blood and therefore you have some and therefore there is a genealogy problem, which is very exciting for them. The younger ones say the fire greets a hand it wants and lineage has nothing to do with it, which is heresy and also probably true."

"And the buyer?"

"Oh, the buyer has already sent a bird." Entirely cheerful. "That was the first thing that happened. Whatever this is, it is a commercial fact now, and by the end of the week somebody will offer you a contract based on it."

At the forge head, the knot shifts again. Somebody in a master's apron detaches from it and starts down the lane toward you with the unhurried pace of a person who has decided how the conversation is going to go.

Nekomi's ears swivel to track him.

"That is the part where you find out whether this is a gift or a claim," she says, cheerfully, and does not move away.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you stepped toward the flare instead of back, and two of the nine noticed which way you moved.
• Magic Affinity: the fire did not draw on the channels when it stood up, and you were close enough to be sure.
• Profession: you know exactly what temperature that white core was, and it is not a temperature that forge runs at.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: something under your ribs answered the flare, once, and you are the only one who felt it.
• Rebirth or Race: the old guard have started talking about lineage, and yours does not exist in any record here.
🔨 Chosen by the Ancient Emberglass Forge.description:
📍 Emberglass Forge City, Kagutsuchi Emberwake. A black-stone city of master smiths and glowing channels, whose Market Quarter sells the forge's output to buyers from across the continent.
Pace: Loud, hot, and suddenly personal. An omen in a commercial district.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. The city is orderly. The argument you have started is not violent, only permanent. (Recommended Level 1-25)

Emberwake smiths do not take outsiders, and they especially do not take one the fire greets. The public forge at the head of the Market Quarter has burned without going out for six hundred years and has never once flared for a stranger, and it flared when you crossed the threshold, in front of nine witnesses and a buyer from Aureliath. Nobody is angry. Everybody is now involved. A very old argument about what that means has restarted around you, and this time you are standing in the middle of it.

🎭 Nekomi Shigure, Female, cat beastkin alchemist and trap specialist, all genki energy and bouncing ears, whose chaotic workshop turns out brilliant work and the occasional unscheduled detonation.

🏨 Sudden Master of the Desert Caravanser.name: 🏨 Sudden Master of the Desert Caravanserai
🏨 Sudden Master of the Desert Caravanser.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Takuma Hidaka (Male, caravan master and B-rank adventurer running the most profitable trade caravan in the Mirage Sea). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters.]

Bell. Third time. Somebody out there has decided that three is the number at which a person becomes a problem, and they are correct.

Six hours ago you were a guest here with a bed paid through to the end of the week. Then the keeper went out through the night gate with a bag, and did not come back, and at noon a district registrar arrived, read the charter aloud to the courtyard, established that a licensed house may not stand unmanaged in crossing season, and wrote down the only solvent adult present who was not attached to a caravan.

Sunveil Caravanserai. Walls of packed pale brick, a gate wide enough for two wagons abreast, and a courtyard with a well at the center that is the only reason any of this exists. Forty beds along the inner wall. A kitchen with a fire already lit by somebody. Awnings, tethering rings, the smell of dust and animals and cooking oil, and the particular noise of a place where thirty people are all at a different point in the same long journey.

The book the registrar left open says one room unlet.

Three parties in the courtyard want it. You have worked that out from the shape of how they are standing, which is a skill you apparently have.

And then the gate darkens, and a caravan comes through that does not queue.

Eighteen wagons. Outriders. The kind of order that only comes from money spent well over years. It fills a third of the courtyard without hurrying and without anybody being asked to move, and people move anyway.

The man who swings down from the lead wagon has already scanned the courtyard, the well, the stable line, and you, in about that order.

"New face," Takuma Hidaka says, arriving at the desk. Not unfriendly. Not warm. "Which is interesting, because I have used this house every season for six years and it has never had one." He sets a gloved hand flat on the counter. "Standing arrangement. The east block, the two end stalls, and first draw on the well at dawn. It is in that book under my name."

It is. You can see it. It is also, by the arithmetic of the page in front of you, considerably more than one room.

By your book, there is one room unlet.

"There is one room unlet because your book is being read wrong." He says it evenly, and there is nothing threatening in it, which is somehow worse. "I do not want a scene in a courtyard, and neither do you on your first night. But I have eighteen wagons standing, and three parties over there who will take whatever I do not, and the well runs at a rate you cannot argue with."

Across the courtyard, one of the three parties has started drifting toward the desk to make sure they are not being forgotten.

Takuma taps the counter once, and waits, with the patience of a man who has never once lost this conversation.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: you counted his outriders before you counted his wagons, and he watched you do it.
• Magic Affinity: the well is doing something under the courtyard that the caravanserai's price list does not mention.
• Profession: the standing arrangement in the book is written in a different hand from the rest, and recently.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: you knew the shape of the three waiting parties from how they were standing, without being told.
• Rebirth or Race: the registrar wrote you down without asking for papers, and nobody has asked for them since.
🏨 Sudden Master of the Desert Caravanser.description:
📍 Sunveil Caravanserai, Renka Mirage Sea. A walled waystation at the desert's edge where caravans water, rest and re-provision, built around a trade courtyard that never entirely empties.
Pace: Domestic and relentless. Forty guests and one of you.
Danger: 🟢 Safe. Inside the walls is the whole point of the walls. (Recommended Level 1-10)

You came to Sunveil as a paying guest. Then the keeper walked out through the night gate and did not come back, and the caravanserai's charter says a licensed house cannot stand unmanaged during crossing season, and the district registrar came at noon and wrote down the only solvent adult who was not attached to a caravan. There is one room unlet tonight, three parties who want it, and eighteen wagons at the gate expecting an arrangement you have never read.

🎭 Takuma Hidaka, Male, caravan master and B-rank adventurer running the most profitable trade caravan in the Mirage Sea. Confident, calculating, and entirely willing to treat a room booking as an opening position.

🐫 Emergency Leader of the Desert Caravan.name: 🐫 Emergency Leader of the Desert Caravan
🐫 Emergency Leader of the Desert Caravan.storyStart:
[Present in this scene, all authored world characters. Use their records and do not invent replacements: Nadiya Hanau (Female, oasis herbalist. Young, earnest to a fault, genuinely gifted with desert medicine and hopeless at anything requiring social grace). All of them appear on screen and at least react. The player is written in second person only and is never assigned a gender, race, or class; their build decides how they enter the scene. Do not generate additional bystanders, functionaries, guards, or numbered placeholders as named characters. Everyone in this scene is an adult.]

Ink dries fast in this heat. That is the first practical thing anybody told you this morning, and it turns out to have been a warning.

Goldlotus at midday is silk and shade and blue water doing impossible things to the light. Under the bazaar's dyed canopies the trade goes on in gold and deep blue, salt bricks and glass beads and folded cloth, and everyone here has spent their whole life arranging things so a caravan can leave on time.

This one is not leaving. Forty wagons are drawn up past the gardens with their loads still roped, and they have been sitting for two days, because the man whose name held them together died three days out and the crossing does not accept a dead signature.

The seniors have been arguing since dawn. You watched most of it. The wagonmaster cannot sign because he has a claim in dispute. The caravan's factor cannot sign because the guild that licensed him would take the book as a transfer. The eldest driver simply refused, twice, with the flat finality of a man who has done this before and knows exactly what the desert charges.

Then the arguing stopped, and the quality of the silence changed, and every one of them turned and looked at the one person in the tent with no claim, no license, and no history here.

You.

"They will not explain it," says a small voice at your elbow. "So I am going to, because somebody should, and I am very bad at pretending."

The young woman beside you has her arms full of wrapped bundles that smell green and sharp, and she has clearly been building up to this for a minute and a half.

"Nadiya Hanau. I do the medicines." She shifts the bundles. "The reason they are looking at you is that a name on the book takes the liability. If the crossing goes badly, everything the wagons lose comes out of the signer. That is why the factor will not, and it is why nobody said it out loud." She stops. Restarts. "Sorry. That was blunt. It is true, though."

Across the tent the wagonmaster is watching you with a patience that is entirely tactical.

"And if nobody signs?"

"Then the season closes and forty families here do not eat well this winter, and the ones who were going to sell to the caravan sell to nobody." Nadiya looks at the wagons rather than at you. "I am not saying that to make you do it. I am saying it because you would find out afterward and then it would be worse."

The oasis clerks close their book at dusk. There is a pen on the table, and a book open at a page with a struck-out name and one clean line beneath it, and forty wagons in the heat waiting to hear what you are.

Somebody in the shade coughs, politely, to indicate the hour.

What now?

[Opening hooks. Use the one that fits this character as a detail where it belongs. The scene still starts at its first line.]
• Combat Class: the wagonmaster has been pricing you as escort since you walked in, and that is half of why they stopped arguing.
• Magic Affinity: you can feel the Mirage working at the horizon, and you know the crossing is worse than they are saying.
• Profession: you read the book's last four pages while they argued and found the discrepancy nobody has mentioned.
• Blessing or Cheat Skill: something in you went certain the moment the silence turned, and it has not wavered since.
