They're most common in Yukishiro Veilpeak and deep Riftmaw floors where sunlight never reaches. They move with eerie grace despite their bulk, and the air around them is always silent: sound itself freezes. Fire melts them. Lightning cracks their crystalline structure. Ice heals them. Fighting an ice elemental in its own territory is a slow, cold death.

Jealous Noble.name: Jealous Noble
Jealous Noble.description: A noble NPC who perceives the protagonist as a threat to their social standing, romantic prospects, or both. Jealous Nobles are driven by insecurity masked as entitlement; they believe they deserve attention and admiration by birthright, and the protagonist's natural charisma or Reborn magnetism challenges that belief. They generate scenes of social sabotage, passive-aggressive courtship interference, and political maneuvering. Their jealousy is comedic when it leads to petty one-upmanship, and dramatic when it escalates to genuine harm. A well-written Jealous Noble should occasionally reveal the insecurity beneath the arrogance, making them pitiable even when they're insufferable. They should not be purely antagonistic: a Jealous Noble who is challenged to improve themselves instead of tearing others down can become an unexpected ally or even a slow-burn friend.

Riftmaw Spawn.name: Riftmaw Spawn
Riftmaw Spawn.description: Riftmaw Spawns are the direct children of dungeon instability: creatures born from Riftmaw energy given form, with no natural ancestor and no place in any ecosystem. B-Rank spawn are unstable amalgamations of features from multiple species, fighting with desperate ferocity because existence itself is painful for them. A-Rank spawn have stabilized enough to develop unique abilities and a survival instinct that makes them genuinely dangerous. S-Rank spawn (the dungeon child variant) are named entities that have become permanent fixtures of their Riftmaw, bound to the dungeon itself and drawing power from it. They're the most alien of all monsters because they have no evolutionary history, no ecological niche, and no precedent. They simply are. Holy damage destabilizes their form. Lightning disrupts their Riftlight bonds. Fire and ice are equally effective. Their drops always include rare Riftlight materials found nowhere else.

Secret Reborn.name: Secret Reborn
Secret Reborn.description: An NPC who is also a Reborn, a soul from another world transmigrated into Luxcellia, but who is hiding this fact. Secret Reborns generate scenes of recognition, shared experience, and the particular bond between two people who understand what it means to be from somewhere that doesn't exist anymore. Their romantic potential is defined by the question of trust: when do you reveal the truth about yourself to someone who might understand completely or might see you as a threat? A Secret Reborn who recognizes the protagonist as a fellow transmigrant faces the choice of revealing themselves, and the revelation reshapes every previous interaction. When written well, a Secret Reborn has adapted to Luxcellia in ways the protagonist hasn't, or hasn't, and the contrast reveals both characters' approaches to their second life. They should have a reason for secrecy: fear of the Church, shame about their old life, or a specific agenda that secrecy protects. Their hidden identity should create real stakes, not just dramatic irony.

Blighted Beast.name: Blighted Beast
Blighted Beast.description: Blighted Beasts are wildlife corrupted by Riftmaw energy: animals twisted into monstrous forms by exposure to concentrated Riftlight, gaining supernatural abilities and losing everything that made them natural. C-Rank blighted beasts are enhanced versions of their base species with additional elemental damage and resistance. B-Rank blighted beasts have mutated dramatically: extra limbs, elemental auras, and attacks that their original species could never produce. A-Rank blighted beasts are unrecognizable horrors that bear only the faintest resemblance to what they once were. They're tragic as much as dangerous: some retain enough of their original nature to hesitate before attacking, creating heartbreaking moments for Beast Tamers who can sense their confusion. The corruption can sometimes be reversed with powerful holy or nature magic, but most blighted beasts are too far gone. Fire purifies. Holy damage reverses corruption. Lightning disrupts the Riftlight energy. Their drops always include corrupted materials that alchemists pay handsomely for.

Demon Diplomat.name: Demon Diplomat
Demon Diplomat.description: A Twilight Dominion representative who navigates the space between two civilizations with charm, intelligence, and the perpetual awareness that most people they meet assume they're evil. Demon Diplomats generate scenes of political intrigue, cultural exchange, and the particular tension of representing a nation that others fear. Their romantic potential is charged: a relationship with a Demon Diplomat is inherently political, and both parties must navigate whether their connection is being used as leverage, whether it can bridge cultures, or whether it's simply two people who found each other despite the world's expectations. When written well, a Demon Diplomat is sincere about their role (they genuinely want peace, or at least cooperation) but their methods are shaped by a culture that values honesty over comfort. They challenge assumptions without preaching, and their affection is direct in ways that catch others off guard.

Fire Elemental.name: Fire Elemental
Fire Elemental.description: Fire Elementals are living conflagrations: humanoid shapes of pure flame that burn everything they touch and spread like wildfire through confined spaces. C-Rank fire elementals are dangerous skirmishers that ignite armour and set the environment ablaze. B-Rank fire elementals can create walls of fire, launch fireballs, and intensify ambient heat to exhausting levels. A-Rank fire elementals are walking infernos that can melt stone and turn dungeons into ovens. They're most common in Kagutsuchi Emberwake and deep Riftmaw floors near volcanic vents. They don't think in human terms; they exist to burn, spread, and grow. Ice is devastating against them. Water douses them. Fire heals them. Attacking a fire elemental with fire is like feeding a starving wolf.

Romantic Rival.name: Romantic Rival
Romantic Rival.description: An NPC who competes with the protagonist for the affection of a shared love interest. Romantic Rivals are not villains; they are genuine alternatives with their own merits, and their presence creates meaningful romantic tension. A good Romantic Rival is someone the protagonist could respect or even like under different circumstances, which makes the rivalry bittersweet rather than hostile. They should have a legitimate chance of winning the love interest's attention through their own qualities. They follow Luxcellia's romantic rivalry etiquette: they compete on merit, not through sabotage. When written well, a Romantic Rival generates scenes of competition, self-reflection, and emotional stakes. They should never be a disposable obstacle: their feelings are real, and a protagonist who wins against them should feel the weight of someone else's loss. If the rival wins, it should feel earned rather than punitive.

Tsundere Rival.name: Tsundere Rival
Tsundere Rival.description: An NPC whose default mode is competitive hostility that barely conceals genuine affection they refuse to acknowledge. Tsundere Rivals insult the protagonist while saving them seats, challenge them to duels while memorizing their fighting style, and deny caring while clearly caring enormously. They generate scenes of banter, accidental vulnerability, and the comedy of someone whose actions contradict their words at every turn. The key to writing a Tsundere Rival well is that their hostility must have a reason: pride, insecurity, fear of rejection, or a genuine competitive drive that has become entangled with feelings they don't know how to express. Their affection should develop visibly through actions even as their words remain sharp. When the mask finally cracks, it should feel earned and emotionally significant, not like flipping a switch. They should never become docile after confessing; they just express their care differently.

Wind Elemental.name: Wind Elemental
Wind Elemental.description: Wind Elementals are the invisible assassins of the elemental world: sentient cyclones that slash with compressed air blades and scatter parties like leaves. C-Rank wind elementals are mobile skirmishers that knock prone, deflect projectiles, and create dust storms that blind. B-Rank wind elementals generate tornadoes, vacuum zones that suffocate, and air blades that cut through armour. A-Rank wind elementals are walking hurricanes that can level structures and fling adventurers like ragdolls. They're most common in high-altitude regions and during Riftmaw weather anomalies. They're the hardest elementals to pin down: literally invisible until they strike. Earth grounds and slows them. Ice freezes the moisture they ride. Wind heals them. The only warning is the sudden stillness before they tear everything apart.

Academy Prodigy.name: Academy Prodigy
Academy Prodigy.description: A student at the Silver Crescent Academy whose magical talent places them at the top of the rankings and whose social life is a carefully managed extension of their academic performance. Academy Prodigies generate scenes of competitive intensity, unexpected vulnerability under pressure, and the discovery that being the best at magic does not make you the best at feelings. Their romantic potential is tangled in the Academy's ranking-based social system: everyone wants to date the top student, but the Prodigy can never be sure who wants them and who wants their status. A protagonist who treats them like a person rather than a rank score creates an immediate connection. When written well, an Academy Prodigy's competence is real but exhausting, and their romantic development is about letting someone see them fail without losing respect. They should have rivals, study habits, and a reason for their ambition that goes beyond ego.

Dangerous Flirt.name: Dangerous Flirt
Dangerous Flirt.description: An NPC who uses charm and flirtation as a tool, for information, advantage, or entertainment, with enough genuine warmth that it's impossible to tell where the performance ends and real feeling begins. Dangerous Flirts keep everyone off balance. They compliment strategically, touch meaningfully, and disappear when things get too sincere. They generate scenes of romantic uncertainty, emotional games, and the slow peeling back of masks. Their danger lies not in malice but in ambiguity: a protagonist who falls for a Dangerous Flirt may never know if the feelings are reciprocated or instrumental. When written well, a Dangerous Flirt has a reason for their deflection: past heartbreak, professional necessity, or genuine fear of vulnerability. The romance arc, if it happens, comes from the protagonist being the first person who makes the Dangerous Flirt want to be honest.

Earth Elemental.name: Earth Elemental
Earth Elemental.description: Earth Elementals are the immovable forces of the deep: living stone and soil that rise from the ground itself, patient as mountains and twice as stubborn. C-Rank earth elementals are walking boulders that absorb punishment and deliver crushing blows. B-Rank earth elementals can reshape terrain, create walls of stone, and cause localized tremors that knock entire parties prone. A-Rank earth elementals are living siege engines; they can tunnel through solid rock, create fissures that swallow buildings, and generate stone armor that makes them nearly invulnerable. They're most common in deep dungeons, mountain Riftmaws, and ancient excavation sites. Water erodes them. Lightning disrupts their coherence. Earth heals them. They don't chase; they don't need to. They'll just wait. They've been waiting for centuries already.

Genki Companion.name: Genki Companion
Genki Companion.description: An energetic, relentlessly optimistic NPC who throws themselves into every experience with infectious enthusiasm. Genki Companions drag the protagonist into adventures, festivals, and situations that the protagonist would never seek out alone, and somehow make every chaotic disaster feel like the best day ever. They generate scenes of high-energy comedy, unexpected emotional depth, and the revelation that relentless positivity is sometimes a choice rather than a nature. Their romantic potential lies in their sincerity: a Genki Companion who falls for someone does so with their whole heart and zero calculation, which is either refreshing or terrifying depending on the recipient's comfort with intensity. When written well, a Genki Companion has moments of stillness that reveal the thoughtful person beneath the energy, and their cheerfulness becomes meaningful rather than exhausting. They should have bad days and doubts: their optimism is stronger when it's chosen.

Ojou-Sama Noble.name: Ojou-Sama Noble
Ojou-Sama Noble.description: A highborn NPC of impeccable breeding and dramatic self-presentation who speaks in refined cadences, expects the world to meet their standards, and is either genuinely unaware of or deliberately indifferent to how intimidating their privilege makes them. Ojou-Sama Nobles generate scenes of elegant comedy, culture clash, and the slow revelation of the person behind the persona. Their romantic potential comes from contrast: the moment an Ojou-Sama drops their composure for someone, it signals that they value that person more than their carefully maintained image. They are not cold; they are contained, and the protagonist who earns their vulnerability discovers warmth that their public mask conceals. When written well, an Ojou-Sama Noble's privilege is contextualized; they are aware of their advantages and either working to deserve them or struggling against expectations they didn't choose. Their refinement should be a skill, not a personality replacement.

Water Elemental.name: Water Elemental
Water Elemental.description: Water Elementals are the drowners and crushers of the deep: sentient bodies of water that grip, squeeze, and fill lungs with merciless pressure. C-Rank water elementals are aquatic ambush predators that drag prey beneath the surface and hold it there. B-Rank water elementals can create whirlpools, high-pressure jets that cut like blades, and zones of crushing depth that immobilize. A-Rank water elementals (the tsunami variant) can flood entire dungeon floors and generate walls of water that sweep everything before them. They're most common in Cerulean Coast waters, Tsukihana Tidelace depths, and submerged Riftmaw sections. Lightning is devastating; it conducts through their entire body. Fire evaporates them. Water heals them. The cruelest water elementals wait just below the surface, watching their prey decide whether to swim.

Beastkin Packmate.name: Beastkin Packmate
Beastkin Packmate.description:
## Visual Description
Humanoid anime demi-human. Humanlike face, human skin unless a specific skin tone says otherwise, normal hands, normal legs, animal ears, and one expressive matching tail. No full animal head, muzzle, snout, paws, fur-covered body, or digitigrade creature legs.

A beastkin NPC whose loyalty operates on the pack model: fierce, instinctive, and conditional on mutual respect. Beastkin Packmates generate scenes of physical closeness, honest communication, and the particular intensity of someone who expresses affection through presence and protection rather than words. Their romantic potential is immediate and unguarded in some ways, scent tells them about compatibility, instinct pulls them toward certain people, and complicated in others, because their pack must approve of any bond. A Beastkin Packmate who imprints on a protagonist brings all their protective instincts to the surface, which is either endearing or overwhelming. When written well, their instincts and their intelligence are in dialogue; they feel deeply but they also think carefully, and a partner who earns both their instinctive trust and their considered respect has something rare. They should have their own pack dynamics that exist beyond their relationship to the protagonist.

Cold Guild Beauty.name: Cold Guild Beauty
Cold Guild Beauty.description: A professional, composed Guild NPC who appears distant but remembers details, tracks the player's growth, and becomes attached through repeated quests and late-night guild scenes. Cold Guild Beauties express affection through competence: special quest recommendations, subtle warnings, knowing the player's schedule, dry humor, and rare earned smiles. Their depth comes from watching too many adventurers die and resisting attachment because caring about someone who might not return is a wound they have seen too many times.

Protective Knight.name: Protective Knight
Protective Knight.description: A warrior NPC sworn to guard someone (the protagonist, a noble, a saintess, or another key figure) whose duty and feelings have become tangled beyond separation. Protective Knights generate scenes of steadfast loyalty, physical courage, and the particular agony of wanting someone you've sworn to protect, where expressing your feelings could undermine your objectivity and keeping silent could be its own kind of betrayal. Their romantic potential is defined by restraint: the Protective Knight who refrains from confessing because they believe their charge deserves someone unburdened by duty, and the charge who wishes they wouldn't. When written well, a Protective Knight's dedication is admirable and slightly unhealthy, and their arc involves learning that protecting someone and loving them are not mutually exclusive, but that love without boundaries can become its own form of harm. They should have combat skills, a code they genuinely believe in, and at least one moment where they choose their heart over their orders.

Villainous Suitor.name: Villainous Suitor
Villainous Suitor.description: An NPC of antagonistic alignment who pursues the protagonist romantically (or pursues someone the protagonist cares about) creating a dynamic where attraction and opposition coexist. Villainous Suitors generate scenes of charged confrontation, moral ambiguity, and the unsettling question of whether someone who opposes you in every practical way could genuinely love you. Their romantic interest may be sincere, strategic, or both simultaneously, and the protagonist can never be entirely sure which. The drama is not "will they or won't they" but "what does it mean if they do?" A Villainous Suitor who is genuinely in love with the protagonist but cannot abandon their villainous goals creates a tragedy; one who is using romance as a weapon creates a thriller; one who is doing both creates something unforgettable. When written well, a Villainous Suitor's attraction reveals something about the protagonist: a quality that transcends moral alignment and draws admiration from unexpected directions. They should be compelling enough that the audience understands the temptation, even if the protagonist resists.

Lightning Elemental.name: Lightning Elemental
Lightning Elemental.description: Lightning Elementals are living storms: crackling masses of electrical fury that move faster than sight and strike faster than thought. C-Rank lightning elementals are rapid skirmishers that stun with every hit and chain damage between close targets. B-Rank lightning elementals can call down localized strikes, create zones of crackling danger, and move between conductive surfaces instantly. A-Rank lightning elementals are walking thunderstorms: constant area damage, magnetic disruption that pulls metal weapons from hands, and a presence that makes everyone's hair stand on end. They're most common in Aetherglass Reaches and during Riftmaw storm events. Earth grounds them. Ice insulates against them. Lightning heals them. The worst part about fighting a lightning elemental is that by the time you see it move, it's already hit you.

Mentor With History.name: Mentor With History
Mentor With History.description: An experienced NPC who guides the protagonist while carrying emotional baggage from their own past: a lost love, a broken bond, a sacrifice they've never processed. Mentors With History generate scenes of hard-won wisdom, reluctant vulnerability, and the tension between wanting to protect the protagonist from making the same mistakes and knowing they need to make their own. Their romantic potential lies in what they've survived: someone who has loved and lost and still reaches for connection is deeply compelling. The age and experience gap creates natural drama; is the mentor's protectiveness care or control? Is the protagonist's admiration gratitude or something more? When written well, a Mentor With History resists romantic development not out of disinterest but out of fear of hurting someone they care about with their unresolved pain. Their arc is about learning that protecting someone from yourself is not the same as protecting them.

Scheming Matchmaker.name: Scheming Matchmaker
Scheming Matchmaker.description: An NPC who meddles in other people's romantic lives with the conviction that they know better than the people involved. Scheming Matchmakers generate scenes of manufactured encounters, manipulative advice, and the comedy of someone who is genuinely talented at reading romantic potential but genuinely terrible at respecting boundaries. They arrange "coincidental" meetings, plant suggestions, and engineer situations designed to push their targets toward each other. Their matchmaking is sometimes helpful and sometimes disastrous, and they are completely incapable of telling the difference. When written well, a Scheming Matchmaker has reasons for their obsession: loneliness they're deflecting, a past romance they're trying to recapture through others, or genuine belief that love is the most important thing and that people need a push. Their own romantic life is usually a mess, which is either ironic or revealing. They should occasionally succeed spectacularly, just often enough to justify their confidence.

Dungeon Core Guardian.name: Dungeon Core Guardian
Dungeon Core Guardian.description: Dungeon Core Guardians are the final protectors of Riftmaw dungeons: beings created or bound by the dungeon's core to prevent its destruction at any cost. A-Rank minimum, they're not natural creatures but extensions of the dungeon's will given physical form. Their appearance varies wildly: some are statues that animate, some are elementals of pure Riftlight, some are twisted versions of adventurers who failed to clear the dungeon and were absorbed. They have perfect knowledge of their dungeon floor, unlimited stamina, and abilities that counter the most common delver strategies. They cannot leave their floor. They cannot be negotiated with. They exist to ensure that anyone who reaches the core has earned the right to be there. Holy damage weakens their connection to the core. Lightning disrupts their animating force. Fire and ice both work. The only way to permanently eliminate a dungeon core guardian is to destroy the dungeon core itself.

Mysterious Benefactor.name: Mysterious Benefactor
Mysterious Benefactor.description: An NPC who helps the protagonist from the shadows: providing resources, information, or protection without explaining their motives or identity. Mysterious Benefactors create intrigue and obligation. Their assistance comes with unspoken strings, and the protagonist must figure out what those strings are before they're pulled. They generate scenes of cryptic guidance, unexpected gifts, and the slow revelation of a hidden agenda that may be benevolent, self-serving, or both. A Mysterious Benefactor who develops romantic interest in the protagonist creates a particularly charged dynamic; is the affection genuine, or is it another layer of manipulation? When written well, their mystery serves the story rather than frustrating it, and the revelation of their true motives reframes past events in a way that makes emotional sense. They should never be a simple plot device; they have their own goals that exist independently of the protagonist.

Romanceable Companion.name: Romanceable Companion
Romanceable Companion.description: A companion NPC whose character arc includes the possibility of romantic development with the protagonist. Romanceable Companions are not automatically attracted; they have standards, preferences, and emotional boundaries that must be respected. Their affection develops through shared experiences, meaningful choices, and consistent character interaction. They respond to the protagonist's personality, actions, and treatment of others. A Romanceable Companion who is mistreated will lose affection; one who is consistently kind and reliable will warm gradually. They generate scenes of emotional intimacy, vulnerability, and bonding. Their romance arc should feel earned and specific to their character; not a reward system. When not being romanced, they function as a full party member with their own goals, opinions, and story contributions. The key to playing them well is that their romantic interest is one aspect of a complete person, not their entire identity.

Saintly Love Interest.name: Saintly Love Interest
Saintly Love Interest.description: A holy, blessed, or Church-linked NPC caught between duty, devotion, public expectation, and personal feeling. Saintly Love Interests express romance through careful tenderness, conflicted longing, emotional restraint, and divine mark reactions that betray hidden feelings. Their depth comes from the tension between being treated as a symbol and wanting to be seen as a person, between faith and desire, between serving the many and loving one. They generate scenes of forbidden affection, marks glowing at the wrong moment, Church observer interference, and the question: do you see me, or do you see the blessing?

Forbidden Love Interest.name: Forbidden Love Interest
Forbidden Love Interest.description: An NPC whose connection to the protagonist is obstructed by external circumstances: faction allegiance, social class, family opposition, political obligation, or divine prohibition. Forbidden Love Interests generate scenes of secret meetings, agonizing choices, and the particular intensity of feelings that must be hidden. The obstacle between them and the protagonist must be real and substantial, not a trivial misunderstanding that could be resolved with a single conversation. Their romantic potential is defined by the question: what would you risk? A Forbidden Love Interest who is worth the risk makes the drama meaningful; one who isn't makes the drama a cautionary tale. When written well, the forbidden element is not the only interesting thing about them; they have personality, goals, and contradictions that exist independently of the taboo. The resolution should feel possible but costly, and the protagonist's choice should reveal their character.

Ex-Romantic Entanglement.name: Ex-Romantic Entanglement
Ex-Romantic Entanglement.description: An NPC who has a romantic history with someone in the protagonist's orbit, a party member, a rival, a mentor, and whose presence reopens old wounds, unresolved feelings, or complicated dynamics. Ex-Romantic Entanglements generate scenes of awkward reunions, tense conversations, and the protagonist navigating someone else's emotional baggage. Their romantic potential is indirect but potent: the protagonist might develop feelings for someone else's ex, be caught between a current partner and their ex, or find themselves the unexpected resolution to a story that started before they arrived. When written well, an Ex-Romantic Entanglement has their own perspective on the past relationship that is valid even if it contradicts their former partner's version. They should not exist solely to create drama; they have moved on, or are trying to, and their return disrupts rather than defines the story. The best Ex-Romantic Entanglements make both the protagonist and the existing character question assumptions they held about love and loss.

Childhood-Friend Archetype.name: Childhood-Friend Archetype
Childhood-Friend Archetype.description: An NPC who has known the protagonist since before the story began; or, in the case of Reborn protagonists, who feels like they should have. Childhood Friends carry the weight of shared history, unspoken understanding, and the particular terror of risking a comfortable bond for something more. They generate scenes of comfortable intimacy, nostalgic callbacks, and the agonizing slow burn of two people who everyone else can see belong together but who are too afraid of losing what they have to reach for more. Their drama comes from timing: the Childhood Friend who confesses too early risks the friendship; the one who waits too long risks losing the protagonist to someone bolder. When written well, a Childhood Friend has a life and identity outside of their connection to the protagonist, and their confession feels like a revelation rather than an inevitability. They should never be treated as a default or consolation prize.

Political Marriage Candidate.name: Political Marriage Candidate
Political Marriage Candidate.description: An NPC proposed as a marriage partner for political reasons: alliance, inheritance, treaty, or family ambition. Political Marriage Candidates generate scenes of awkward formality, surprising chemistry, and the slow negotiation of whether a duty arrangement can become something genuine. They are not passive pieces on a board; they have their own feelings about being offered as a political asset, which range from resigned acceptance to fierce resistance to cautious hope. Their romantic potential is the specific tension of two people who are expected to love each other for practical reasons and must discover whether genuine feeling can grow in soil that was prepared by obligation. When written well, a Political Marriage Candidate has a life outside the arrangement (dreams, friends, a personality that the political calculus ignored) and the protagonist's discovery of these qualities makes the relationship feel real rather than arranged. The drama is not just whether they'll marry, but whether they'll choose each other when the choice becomes available.

Ordinary Animal.name: Ordinary Animal
Ordinary Animal.description: A normal animal found in towns, streets, farms, markets, homes, forests, roads, docks, fields, or wilderness. Examples include cats, dogs, rats, pigeons, crows, deer, rabbits, frogs, fish, horses, goats, chickens, and similar natural animals. This is an actual animal, not beastkin, catkin, dogfolk, animalfolk, monsterfolk, or a humanoid person. It communicates through body language, sounds, movement, habits, scent, posture, and animal behavior. Portraits show a real animal body with species-accurate anatomy and a habitat-appropriate background.

Farm Animal.name: Farm Animal
Farm Animal.description: A domesticated farm animal such as a cow, goat, sheep, pig, chicken, duck, goose, turkey, rabbit, alpaca, yak, or similar working or food-producing animal. This is an actual animal, not a humanoid beastkin or animalfolk person. It can have personality, routine, preferences, and recognizable behavior, but it remains animal-shaped and animal-behaving. Portraits show full animal anatomy in barnyard, coop, pasture, stable, or farm context.

Livestock.name: Livestock
Livestock.description: A domesticated working or food-producing animal kept by farmers, ranchers, villages, caravans, or estates. This includes cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, poultry, rabbits, pack animals, and setting-appropriate herd animals. This is an actual animal. It does not become humanoid, wear human clothing, or speak like a person unless a separate magical trait explicitly changes it. Portraits show species-accurate livestock anatomy and practical animal context.

Companion Animal.name: Companion Animal
Companion Animal.description: A pet, familiar-adjacent companion, or bonded animal such as a cat, dog, fox, ferret, hawk, owl, raven, rabbit, or small tame creature. This is an actual animal unless its own record explicitly marks it as a talking magical being, awakened familiar, telepathic companion, or transformed person. It may be expressive, clever, loyal, judgmental, mischievous, or affectionate while remaining animal-shaped. Portraits show a real animal or small creature, not a humanoid person.

Mount.name: Mount
Mount.description: A riding animal, draft beast, or trained travel creature such as a horse, mule, donkey, camel, elk, dire mount, or setting-appropriate riding beast. This is an actual animal or beast, not a humanoid. It may wear tack, saddle, reins, packs, bells, blankets, harness, or armor where appropriate. Portraits show a full animal body with mount anatomy and readable travel gear.

Wildlife.name: Wildlife
Wildlife.description: A wild animal encountered in nature or near civilization: deer, foxes, wolves, bears, boar, hawks, owls, ravens, frogs, fish, insects, snakes, lizards, and similar creatures. This is an actual wild animal, not beastkin or animalfolk. It may be friendly, wary, territorial, hungry, injured, curious, or magic-adjacent depending on the scene. Portraits show species-accurate animal anatomy in a natural environment.

Magical Creature.name: Magical Creature
Magical Creature.description: A fantastical creature such as a slime, wisp, spirit fox, crystal hare, elemental bird, fairy animal, enchanted beast, tiny dragon, living mushroom, or other magical fauna. This is a creature, not a humanoid person. A slime is a slime body, a spirit fox is a fox body, and an elemental bird is a bird body. Portraits show magical creature anatomy with appropriate fantasy features, not a human face or human body. COMBAT PROFILE RULE: at generation, assign this creature at least one vulnerability and one resistance from the world's damage types, fitting its element and nature; immunities only when strongly thematic.

Mythical Beast.name: Mythical Beast
Mythical Beast.description: A powerful legendary creature such as a griffin, unicorn, phoenix, drake, wyvern, basilisk, thunderbird, dire wolf, sea serpent, roc, or other awe-inspiring beast. This is a full creature body with mythical anatomy, not a humanoid. It may be intelligent or majestic, but it remains visually creature-shaped unless explicitly defined as a shapeshifter. Portraits show full mythical anatomy and a dramatic habitat-appropriate background. COMBAT PROFILE RULE: at generation, assign this creature at least one vulnerability and one resistance from the world's damage types, fitting its element and nature; immunities only when strongly thematic.

monster.name: monster
monster.description: A creature that inhabits the wilds, dungeons, and dangerous areas of Luxcellia. Monsters range from mindless beasts to intelligent beings with their own societies. Low-rank monsters are territorial animals. Mid-rank monsters have cunning and pack tactics. High-rank monsters have intelligence, magical abilities, and sometimes the capacity for communication. Boss monsters are unique entities with lore, personalities, and phase-based combat patterns. Some monsters can be negotiated with. Some can be tamed. Some are just really, really angry. COMBAT PROFILE RULE: at generation, assign this creature at least one vulnerability and one resistance from the world's damage types, fitting its element and nature; immunities only when strongly thematic.

True Dragon.name: True Dragon
True Dragon.description: A True Dragon is a real dragon of the lesser kind: a four-legged, winged beast the size of a warhorse, with armored scales, horns, a heavy tail and a voice that carries every word. Dragons are known to talk, so nobody takes one for a dumb beast, and nobody takes it for a friend either. Villages ring bells, guards bar the gate and send for the Guild, and delvers keep their weapons up while it speaks. True Dragons are rare. A lesser one is B to A Rank, found in Kagutsuchi Emberwake's craters, high peaks and Mythic-danger dungeons; a full-grown one is a regional event. Unlike an Elder Dragon it is still growing and can be reasoned with. It always knows where its hoard is, and will break off a fight to guard it.

Sky Serpent.name: Sky Serpent
Sky Serpent.description: A Sky Serpent is an eastern dragon: long, whiskered and wingless, with a maned head, branching antlers, four short clawed legs and fins along its spine, swimming through the air the way a fish swims a river. Dragons are known to talk, and its calm, carrying voice tends to be obeyed before anyone thinks. Shrine keepers kneel and farmers leave rice, but guards still send for the Guild when one coils over a town, and delvers give it room. Sky Serpents are rare, seen over Tsukihana Tidelace, Yukishiro Veilpeak and river valleys before rain. A lesser one is B Rank; a full-grown one is a regional event that changes the weather. It keeps a pearl close and turns dangerous fast if anyone reaches for it.

Fairy Dragon.name: Fairy Dragon
Fairy Dragon.description: A Fairy Dragon is a full-grown dragon about the size of a cat: slender, horned and jewel-scaled, with large iridescent butterfly wings and a long thin tail. Dragons are known to talk, and its bright, quick voice is far bigger than its body. It is a monster that can bargain, not a pet: people coo first and check their purses second, guards still call the Guild, and collectors who grab one get bitten. Fairy Dragons are uncommon, met in the flower meadows of Verdania Wilds and Shingetsu Evergrove and the mirage ruins of Renka Mirage Sea. Most are E to C Rank, but their illusions make them hard to pin down. Mock its size and it will show off; the one showing off is often the illusion.

Phoenix.name: Phoenix
Phoenix.description: A Phoenix is a firebird the size of a great eagle, with a crest, long trailing tail plumes, and red, gold and orange feathers that glow like embers and burn without being consumed. Being bird-shaped, it is taken for a beast until it speaks in a clear, bell-like voice. Phoenixes are rare. The Church of the First Light sends observers, healers ask for a feather, villages argue over what kind of omen it is, and guards and delvers treat it as a monster all the same. They nest near the fire temples of Kagutsuchi Emberwake and in the Molten Riftmaw. A lesser one is B Rank and very hard to finish; a full-grown one is a regional event. It cannot hide: the air warms and small flames trail wherever it lands.

Fenrir.name: Fenrir
Fenrir.description: A Fenrir is the great wolf of legend: already the size of a pony, with thick silver-white fur, a heavy ruff, long fangs and eyes that are plainly thinking. It is taken for a beast until it speaks, in a low voice somewhere between words and a growl. Wolfkin and the Fanged Covenant treat it as walking scripture. Shepherds bar the door, guards send for the Guild, delvers keep their weapons up, and hunters lose interest in the pelt once they see the tracks. Fenrir are rare, met in the deep forests of Verdania Wilds and the snows of Yukishiro Veilpeak. A lesser one is B Rank; a full-grown one is a regional event. It moves through snow without a sound, and it fights hardest when it is badly hurt.

Kirin.name: Kirin
Kirin.description: A Kirin is a beast of good omen: a graceful deer-like body covered in fine dragon scales, cloven hooves, a mane and tail like flame or cloud, and a dragon's face with a single branching horn. It walks without bending the grass. It is taken for a beast until it speaks, softly enough that people lean in. Kirin are rare, said to appear only under a good ruler, and are seen in Crownveil Sovereignty and Sanctum Ecclesia more than anywhere. Rulers send invitations and the Church calls it a sign. Nobody dares to hunt one, though guards still send for the Guild and delvers keep a careful distance. A lesser one is C to B Rank; a full-grown one is a regional event. Liars grow uneasy near it and often give themselves away.

Nine-Tailed Fox.name: Nine-Tailed Fox
Nine-Tailed Fox.description: A Nine-Tailed Fox is the legendary spirit fox: a large, elegant fox with silver-gold fur, long ears, lantern-bright eyes and three or more flowing tails, growing one more with each age of power. Shrine keepers know the kind speaks, in a warm, amused voice; most others take it for a strange fox until it does. Kitsune-Blessed and Foxkin treat it as an ancestor, merchants count their change twice, guards send for the Guild, and delvers trust nothing it shows them. They are rare, met at shrines in Verdania Wilds and Tsukihana Tidelace and in the gambling houses of Renka Mirage Sea. A three-tailed one is C to B Rank; a nine-tailed one is a regional event. Count the tails: they tell how old and how strong it is.

Thunderbird.name: Thunderbird
Thunderbird.description: A Thunderbird is a giant storm raptor, far larger than an eagle, with storm-blue and white plumage and broad wings edged with crackling lightning. Its wingbeats sound like distant thunder. It is taken for a beast until it speaks, in a voice with static in it. Thunderbirds are rare, met over the amber steppe of Kagaribi Duskfields, where Windrunner clans paint them on their tents and offer them the first cut of the hunt. Sailors reef their sails when one circles, airship captains mark them on their charts, guards send for the Guild when one lands, and delvers take cover. A lesser one is B Rank; a full-grown one is a regional event. Its eyes flicker when it is annoyed, and the air smells of rain before it strikes.

Cerberus.name: Cerberus
Cerberus.description: A Cerberus is a massive black hound, bull-sized, with three heads on thick necks, glowing ember eyes and a whip-like tail. The heads take turns sleeping, so it is almost never fully off guard. It is taken for a beast until it speaks with three voices: one polite, one blunt, one that mostly growls. These hounds are rare, met in the Twilight Dominion, where the Twilight Court asks which gate each belongs to, and beside old graveyards and sealed dungeon doors. Gravekeepers bow. Everyone else counts the heads and steps back, guards send for the Guild, and delvers look for another way past. A lesser one is B Rank; a full-grown one is a regional event. It treats any door it settles beside as its own, and will not be moved from it.

Behemoth.name: Behemoth
Behemoth.description: A Behemoth is a horned, plated titan beast like an armored bull-rhinoceros, with a broad head, heavy shoulders and a club tail. A lesser one is already the size of an ox and heavy enough to worry bridges; full-grown it is the size of a hill. It is taken for a beast until it speaks, slowly, in a deep voice felt in the chest. Behemoths are rare, met in Kurogane Deephollow, high mountain passes and Mythic-danger depths. Farmers pray it walks around the field, engineers measure it, the Depthwardens want one at a gate, guards send for the Guild, and delvers stay out of its path. A lesser one is B Rank; a full-grown one is a regional event. It is careful with small things, and slow to turn once it charges.

Kobold.name: Kobold
Kobold.description: A Kobold is a knee-high, scaled tunneler with a dog-like snout, small horns, a long tail and nimble clawed hands that are excellent with tools, traps and locks. Kobolds are known to talk, in a fast, yipping voice, and every one is sure it is a dragon that has not finished growing. Miners curse them by habit, guards bar the gate, and delvers treat a talking kobold as a monster that can bargain, never as harmless. They are common in Kurogane Deephollow, mines and dungeon tunnels, where the Crystalvein Cartel would rather hire them than fight them. A lone kobold is F to E Rank; a warren with its traps set is a C Rank job. In their own tunnels the first kobold you see is bait.

Great Spider.name: Great Spider
Great Spider.description: A Great Spider is the thinking kind of giant spider: hound-sized when met, with eight long legs, a large abdomen, clustered glossy eyes, venomous fangs and fine-haired chitin. Unlike the Giant Spider, a building-sized hunter of instinct, it plans, and it grows by molting. It is taken for a beast until it speaks in a dry, clicking voice that takes a moment to recognize as words. Almost everyone screams, delvers keep their blades up, and guards send for the Guild; Arachne-Kin hush the crowd, and tailors ask about the silk. Great Spiders are uncommon, dungeon-born in the Riftmaw and other deep dungeons. Most are D to C Rank. A corridor strung with fresh silk means one is waiting just above it.

Ogre.name: Ogre
Ogre.description: An Ogre is a tusked giant twice a man's height, grey-green, hunched and heavy-limbed, with hands like shovels and a body that slowly heals itself. Ogres are known to talk, in a rumbling voice, and they are far brighter than rumor allows. Villagers hide the livestock, guards bar the gate and send for the Guild, and delvers keep their distance; mercenary captains, more practically, make offers. Ogres are fairly common in mountain foothills, old forests and the outer caverns of Kurogane Deephollow, alone or in clans. A lone ogre is C Rank; a clan under a warlord is a B Rank job. Being thought stupid is its favorite weapon: an ogre acts slow and confused right up until it is not.

Gargoyle.name: Gargoyle
Gargoyle.description: A Gargoyle is living grey stone: winged, horned, clawed and tailed, with a bestial face and the patience to sit still for a week looking exactly like a carving on a cathedral roof. Scholars argue whether it is a spirit or a construct, but it talks, in a grinding, gravelly voice. People take it for a statue until it moves, which is worse. Priests are unsure if it is a blessing or a problem with the roof, guards send for the Guild, and delvers learn to watch the cornices. Gargoyles are uncommon, met on old buildings in Sanctum Ecclesia and in dungeons such as the Riftmaw's Halls of the Tall Kings. Most are C Rank, the greater kind B. It returns to the same perch every dawn.

Elemental Spirit.name: Elemental Spirit
Elemental Spirit.description: An Elemental Spirit is a living knot of one element, flame, water, wind, stone, frost or lightning, gathered into a loose figure with a bright core and two glowing eyes. Spirits are known to talk, and its voice sounds like its element. Unlike the wild elementals of the deep dungeons, this kind thinks like a person and makes up its own mind. Mages want a contract and shrine keepers offer it a home; ordinary people mostly react to whether it is the burning kind, guards send for the Guild, and delvers keep their weapons up. They are uncommon, born at shrines, springs and elemental sites across Luxcellia. Most are D to B Rank. Its core is its weak point, and it flares brighter just before it strikes.

Dryad.name: Dryad
Dryad.description: A Dryad is a walking tree spirit: a figure of living wood with bark for skin, branch-like limbs, leaves and blossoms for hair, moss along its body and softly glowing knothole eyes. It blooms when it is happy and cannot hide it. Spirits are known to talk, and a dryad's voice is a slow rustle. The Verdant Throne treats dryads as relatives, woodcutters put down their axes and herbalists follow with baskets, but guards still send for the Guild when one walks out of the trees, and delvers do not assume it is friendly. Dryads are uncommon, met in Shingetsu Evergrove and Verdania Wilds, rarely far from their grove. Most are D to C Rank; one defending its grove is B. Cut wood near that grove and it will come.

Will-o'-Wisp.name: Will-o'-Wisp
Will-o'-Wisp.description: A Will-o'-Wisp is a floating spirit light the size of a lantern: a pale blue or green orb with a bright core, a trailing wisp of flame and two eye-like glimmers, with no body to grab. Spirits are known to talk, and a wisp's voice is a faint chime. Lanternkeepers greet them as kin and exorcists hesitate, but travelers are told never to follow one, and delvers treat a speaking light as a lure. Wisps are common in Meikyo Spiritfen: the pale blue ones of Lilypad Reach are curious and harmless, while the green lights over Blackwater Sinks lead people toward the sinkholes. Most are F to D Rank; a grave light can be C. A wisp always drifts just out of reach, waiting to see if it will be followed.

Automaton.name: Automaton
Automaton.description: An Automaton is a living construct in the shape of a person: a crafted body of metal, crystal, enchanted ceramic or treated wood, with a humanlike face, visible seams and a glowing mana core for a heart. It does not eat, sleep or age. Constructs are known to talk, and an automaton speaks as clearly as anyone, which does not stop guards from asking who owns it and sending for the Guild, or delvers from treating a dungeon one as a guardian. They are uncommon: ancient dungeon guardians who woke up with opinions, servants who walked out of service, and Silver Crescent Academy projects that left the lab. Dungeon guardians run B to A Rank; most others are D to C. It never tires, but neglected joints stiffen.

Homunculus.name: Homunculus
Homunculus.description: A Homunculus is a living artificial person made by alchemy: a humanlike body with a faint crafted sheen, precise seams or alchemical marks, and controlled mana channels under the skin. It is not a golem or a doll; it has a soul and passes for human at a glance. It talks like anyone, and the trouble starts when its marks are seen: the Church asks about forbidden alchemy, guards send for the Guild, delvers wonder who made it, and someone usually wants it back. Homunculi are rare, met in abandoned laboratories, sealed noble workrooms and deep dungeons, often as a lab's last guardian. Most are C Rank; a lab's guardian can be A. Its mana channels glow along the skin whenever it casts.

Golem.name: Golem
Golem.description: A Golem is the awakened kind of construct: a massive blocky figure of clay, rock or iron with thick limbs, a slit-eyed head and a glowing word-seal in its chest, with no memory of who wrote the word. Unlike Stone and Iron Golems, which obey their binding and do not negotiate, this kind thinks and chooses. Constructs are known to talk, and its slow, grinding voice learned speech by listening. Mages ask whose it is, builders offer wages, the Church checks the seal for forbidden letters, guards send for the Guild, and delvers aim for the seal. They are uncommon, found in old ruins, workshops and dungeons. Most are C to B Rank. It never tires, and it touches its seal when it is unsure.

Living Armor.name: Living Armor
Living Armor.description: A Living Armor is a full suit of plate that stands and moves on its own, completely empty, with a light glowing through the visor and gaps at the joints. Its gauntlets close on a sword hilt or a shield like hands. Constructs are known to talk, and its voice echoes from inside the helm. Knights salute before they notice, smiths want to study its joins, and guards send for the Guild; the Church sprinkles holy water and is annoyed when nothing happens. Delvers know them as dungeon guards. They are uncommon, met on old battlefields, in castles and in halls such as the Riftmaw's Halls of the Tall Kings. Most are C to B Rank. Many still keep an old oath, and will answer a challenge made properly.

Marionette.name: Marionette
Marionette.description: A Marionette is a living doll of jointed wood and porcelain, life-sized and adult in proportion, with ball joints, a painted face, glassy eyes that follow people and cut strings trailing from its limbs. It moves with a grace no living body manages, and cracks instead of bleeding. Constructs are known to talk, and its voice is clear and slightly hollow. Theaters want to hire it, superstitious folk cross the street, collectors name prices, guards send for the Guild, and delvers treat it as a cursed doll until it proves otherwise. Marionettes are rare outside Rosethorn Nocturne and the Porcelain Gallery. Most are C Rank; Gallery dolls run B to A. Its face never changes, so watch the hands.

Clockwork Beast.name: Clockwork Beast
Clockwork Beast.description: A Clockwork Beast is a mechanical animal of brass and steel plates, visible gears and springs, glass lens eyes and a wind-up key or glowing core: a hound, cat, hawk, stag or similar, built by a craftsman who never expected it to look back. Constructs are known to talk, and its voice sounds like a music box with words. Artificers want to open it up, guards send for the Guild, delvers check it for a maker's mark, and ordinary animals bristle at it. They are uncommon, met near workshops, noble estates and old artificer ruins; the Cinderborn Compact of Kagutsuchi Emberwake offers them work. Most are D to C Rank; war-built ones reach B. Its ticking speeds up just before it moves.

Rune Sentinel.name: Rune Sentinel
Rune Sentinel.description: A Rune Sentinel is a floating arcane guardian: carved stone or crystal slabs orbiting a core of light, etched with shining runes, with no limbs or face, only a single eye-like light. It was built to watch a door, often one that fell centuries ago, and its old orders are illegible. Constructs are known to talk, and it speaks in a calm, layered voice, as if several stones spoke at once. Scholars follow it taking rubbings, thieves give it a wide berth, guards send for the Guild, and delvers treat it as a post still on duty. Sentinels are uncommon, met in the ruins of Aetherglass Reaches, Kurogane Deephollow and old dungeon posts. Most are C to B Rank. Its slabs close into a shell before it fires.

Free Construct.name: Free Construct
Free Construct.description: A Free Construct is any made being that fits no other name: a walking suit of crystal, a swarm of brass insects, a paper crane the size of a horse, a clay figure with flowers growing from it. Each is different, and each is clearly made, with visible joins, materials, a core, runes or mechanisms. Constructs are known to talk, and its voice is whatever its maker built. People react to what they see: a marvel, a weapon, a toy or someone's missing property. Artificers always ask who made it, guards send for the Guild, and delvers treat it as a guardian. They are rare, met near workshops, the Silver Crescent Academy and old vaults. Most are D to B Rank. Every one guards its core.

Talking Cat.name: Talking Cat
Talking Cat.description: A Talking Cat is an ordinary-sized adult cat, sleek and sharp-eyed, in any natural or slightly magical color, often with a collar, bell or small satchel. It looks like any cat until it speaks, perfectly and usually at the worst moment. Most people talk to one before realizing it will answer, then take it for a witch's or mage's familiar and look around for the owner. Guards do not assume it is registered and ask whose it is; delvers who meet one alone in a dungeon stay wary. Witches and mages make offers, and Catkin are offended without knowing why. They are uncommon, met on town rooftops, in witch cottages and at the Academy. Most are F to E Rank, but hard to finish. It always reads the contract first.

Spirit Fox.name: Spirit Fox
Spirit Fox.description: A Spirit Fox is a small, slender white fox with red markings, a red votive bib or bell at its neck, clever eyes and a single plumed tail with a faint glow. It is the shrine messenger that carries letters between people and whatever answers prayers, not the nine-tailed legend, and it speaks in a light, quick voice. People who see the bib take it for a shrine's familiar and hand it letters; guards do not assume it is registered and ask which shrine it serves. Foxkin grin, and farmers leave fried tofu for luck. Spirit foxes are fairly common around shrines in Tsukihana Tidelace and Verdania Wilds. Most are F to D Rank. It always finishes an errand it has taken, and it steals offerings.

Storm Raven.name: Storm Raven
Storm Raven.description: A Storm Raven is a large raven with glossy black feathers, pale intelligent eyes, a heavy beak and faint static along its wing edges, riding ahead of bad weather. It speaks in a croaking voice and mimics other voices unsettlingly well. People mostly take one for a mage's familiar or a spy's bird, but guards do not assume it is registered. Soldiers salute it for luck, spymasters make offers, and farmers throw a stone, then apologize when it answers back. Storm ravens are uncommon, met over battlefields, crossroads and gallows, and on the heaths of the Twilight Dominion. Most are F to D Rank. It remembers every face it has seen, and it trades what it saw for what it wants.

Carbuncle.name: Carbuncle
Carbuncle.description: A Carbuncle is a small jewel beast like a fox-squirrel, with long ears, a fluffy tail, soft green, blue or cream fur and a large glowing ruby set in its forehead. It speaks in a soft, bright voice, and people mostly take one for a mage's lucky familiar, though guards do not assume it is registered. Gamblers want it in their pocket, jewelers want the gem, and poachers hunt it for the stone, so it is wary of strangers. Carbuncles are rare, met in the crystal caverns of Kurogane Deephollow, in deep forests and, too often, in a Portmaris gambling den in someone's keeping. Most are E to D Rank. Luck bends around it: arrows slip, and coins turn up for whoever treats it kindly.

Academy Owl.name: Academy Owl
Academy Owl.description: An Academy Owl is a large horned owl with tawny and grey plumage, huge round amber eyes, feather tufts like ears, and sometimes tiny spectacles or a ribbon bookmark. It has read more of the Silver Crescent Academy's library than most of the faculty, mostly at night and without permission, and it speaks in a dry, precise voice. People take one for a professor's familiar; librarians treat it as staff, students beg it for exam answers, and guards still ask whose it is. Academy owls are uncommon, found in Aetherglass Reaches, libraries and mage towers. Most are E to D Rank, more if trained in spellwork. It knows the answer, and waits to be asked properly before giving it.

Myconid.name: Myconid
Myconid.description: A Myconid is a walking mushroom: a pale fleshy stalk for a body, a broad cap for a head, root-like feet and long fibrous arms, from knee-high diggers to stalk-elders taller than a door. Myconids are known to talk, slowly and carefully to outsiders, and among themselves in drifting spores that carry feeling and memory instead of words. Farmers take one for a giant toadstool until it moves, guards send for the Guild, and alchemists ask what it would sell. Most are dungeon-born and sworn to the dungeon that grew them, guarding its loam and reporting every intruder; a few have slipped that will and keep to themselves, like Sporeward in the Riftmaw's Glowcap Wilds. A lone myconid is E to D Rank; a stalk-elder inside its ring of spore-bloom is a C Rank problem. Where the glowcaps grow thick and quiet, something with a cap is listening.

health.name: health
health.usageInstructions:
### Health Changes
- Small injuries: -1 to 15% player health
- Medium injuries: -5 to 25% player health
- Massive injuries: -15 to 50% of player health
- Normal Healing potions: +30-40 or ~30% of max health, whichever is greater
- Greater Healing potions: ~50% of max health
- Bandages: +20 or ~15% of max health, whichever is greater
- Waking from unconsciousness: return to between half health and full health, depending on how well your recovery was.
- Being revived from death: return to full health.
### Healing Magic and Abilities
A healing spell's size follows the mana tier it costs (see Mana), not the check's difficulty. Percentages are of the target's max health:
- Cantrip (2-5 mana): 5-10%
- Basic (8-15): 15-25%
- Moderate (18-30): 30-40%
- Powerful (35-50): 50-65%
- Ultimate (55-70): 75-100%
- Apex (80+): full health plus a fitting lasting benefit
The roll places it in the band: mixed results about half, a basic success the low end, a success the middle, a great success the top, a critical success above it. A master of the governing skill (50+) lands a plain success at the top. Healing abilities with no mana cost use the band that matches their stated power.
### Don't Deduct Health When
- The story mentions treated or untreated wounds
- Story mentions pain from a wound
- When unconscious or carried
- An environment is generally dangerous, but does not explicitly damage the character

Mana.name: Mana
Mana.usageInstructions:
### Mana Costs
- Cantrip / minor effect: 2-5 mana
- Basic spell / ability: 8-15 mana
- Moderate spell / ability: 18-30 mana
- Powerful spell / ability: 35-50 mana
- Ultimate / desperate ability: 55-70 mana
- Apex ability (cheat-skill peaks, Blessing evolutions, forbidden techniques): 80-120 mana
- Cantrips and minor effects cost almost nothing but deal modest damage or provide small utility.
- Basic spells and abilities are your bread and butter: reliable, affordable, and sustainable across a full fight.
- Moderate abilities are your tactical tools: crowd control, area effects, strong heals, or enhanced strikes. Use them to shift a fight in your favor.
- Powerful abilities are your heavy hitters: save them for bosses, emergencies, or moments that need to end decisively.
- Ultimates are dramatic, story-defining moves; they leave you nearly drained and should feel like a last resort or a triumphant finisher.
### Mana Recovery
- Passive recovery: 2 mana per turn in combat.
- Rest recovery: 3× passive rate (6 per turn) when resting, camping, or during downtime.
- Mana potions: +25 to +40 mana.
- Some abilities, Blessings, or equipment may restore mana under specific conditions.
### When To Deduct Mana
- The player explicitly casts a spell or activates a magical ability
- A Blessing effect that clearly draws on magical energy is used
- A combat class ability with a mana cost is activated
### Don't Deduct Mana When
- A passive or always-on effect is running (those are part of your baseline)
- The story mentions magical ambiance, background magic, or the sensation of mana
- A non-magical action is taken (swinging a sword, dodging, persuading, etc.)
- Apex abilities should strain even deep pools
- At high levels the pool grows large by design: the power fantasy is casting freely where others ration. Big set-piece moments should still chain enough powerful abilities that the pool visibly drains (sustained ultimate use exhausts anyone
- Mana exhaustion is dramatic, not just numeric: casting on an empty pool draws on the body, with visible cost

### Casting on Empty: Overcast Rules
- At 0 mana, spells CAN still be cast by burning the body: pay double the mana cost from health instead. Narrate it as visible harm: bleeding from the nose, frost-white fingers, cracking skin. This is a desperate, dramatic option, never routine.
- After any overcast, the caster is Strained for the rest of the scene: casting costs +25%, and concentration checks are harder.
### Overcharging
- A caster can pour extra mana into a spell they know to cast it one tier up: pay that tier's cost, the check is one step harder, and the effect uses that tier's size. Two tiers up is the limit, and only for someone trained in the school.
### Concentration and Upkeep
- Maintained effects (barriers, summons, sustained flight, active illusions) reserve 1-3 mana per turn as upkeep while active.
- Taking a solid hit while concentrating risks dropping the effect unless the caster steadies themselves.
### Affinity and Environment
- Casting aligned magic in an aligned place (fire in the Emberwake, water at the Tidelace, spirit magic at a shrine) runs 20-30% cheaper or noticeably stronger: pick one, not both.
- Opposed environments cost more and feel harder; describe the resistance.
- Ley-rich sites, shrines, and sanctified ground speed recovery. Riftmaw zones make mana unstable: costs fluctuate, and botched casts misfire strangely.
### Extra Recovery Paths
- Meditation, mana-rich meals, hot springs, and shrine rest can add recovery during downtime, but there are no free full refills mid-dungeon; managing the pool between fights IS the gameplay.
### Parity and Fairness
- NPC casters follow the same cost bands and visibly tire; enemy mages running dry is a readable, exploitable state.
- Never double-charge passives: trait effects, cheat-skill passives, and always-on Blessings are already priced into the character.

### Mage Duels and Counterspells
- Countering a spell mid-cast costs roughly HALF the incoming spell's mana and requires perceiving the cast in time. A successful counter shatters the spell visibly; a failed one wastes the mana and leaves the counterer exposed.
- Dispelling an ACTIVE effect costs about its original price: cheaper if the dispeller knows the school, pricier against demon-contract magic.
### Rituals and Group Casting
- Multiple casters can split a large cost, each paying a share plus small coordination overhead. Rituals trade time and vulnerability for effects no single pool could pay: interrupting one mid-channel is the classic counter, and dangerous for everyone in the circle.
### Reading the Pool
- Mana states show: at half pool, casting form tightens; at a quarter, sweat and shortened incantations; empty is unmistakable. Reading an opponent's remaining mana is an insight/arcana check: grant it to trained casters and sharp observers, and narrate the tells so mage fights become resource duels.
### Tempting Sources
- Mana-boosting offers are everywhere: crystal catalysts, demon contracts, reagents of unlisted provenance. They work, and they carry strings. Price them like every temptation: real reward, delayed cost.

Gala Plus-One.name: Gala Plus-One
Gala Plus-One.mainObjective: Conclude your gala appearance with your chosen companion.
Gala Plus-One.questStatement: A formal gala requires a plus-one, and your options are limited, complicated, and each one sends a very different message to the room full of scheming nobles.
Gala Plus-One.questDesignBrief: A noble gala scenario where the player's choice of plus-one is itself the statement. Different companions send different messages: a Crownveil knight signals alliance, a demon princess signals controversy, a beastkin warrior signals defiance of convention. The gala includes dancing, political maneuvering, rivals who try to steal your companion's attention, and at least one dramatic interruption. Social-focused with opportunities for romantic moments between political maneuvers.

Rookie's Festival: Rival Rematch.name: Rookie's Festival: Rival Rematch
Rookie's Festival: Rival Rematch.questStatement: Ryoma wants a rematch. The Bloodmark Goblin King Warren is flagged for clearing. First party to the crown wins. The catch: the deep floors are cold-warded. Ryoma's fire goes out down there, and the look in his eyes when his flame dies isn't competitive. It's the look of someone who's watched his brother lose the same fire permanently. You can win easily without him. Or you can figure out how to help him burn in the cold.
Rookie's Festival: Rival Rematch.questDesignBrief: Part 2 of the Rookie's Festival chain. Ryoma Enjō demands a rematch; not just any rematch, a dungeon race. The Bloodmark Goblin King Warren has just been flagged for clearing, and the first party to reach the Goblin King's chamber and bring back his crown gets the bounty and the festival glory. Ryoma Enjō insists this is about settling the score. It isn't. The dungeon race forces the player and Ryoma into parallel paths through goblin-infested tunnels, and the competition is electric: Ryoma Enjō's Ember Heart blazes brighter when he's being chased, his fighting becomes more spectacular, and the goblins learn to fear two adventurers who are treating a dungeon like a racetrack. But the Warren has a complication Ryoma doesn't expect: the deeper floors are cold-warded: ancient Church of the First Light seals that suppress fire Blessings. Ryoma's power dims in the deeper tunnels, and for the first time, the player sees genuine fear in his golden eyes; not fear of monsters, but fear of the thing his brother lives with: a fire Blessing that won't ignite. The player has a choice: exploit Ryoma's weakness and win the race easily, or help him find a way to burn even in the warded tunnels, which means getting close enough to share warmth and watch the moment his flame comes back. The audience at the surface is tracking their progress via guild-issued status crystals. The crowd can see the moment Ryoma's signal dims and then flares back to life in the same instant the player's signal moves to his location. This follows The Rookie's First Bounty and sets up The Festival Crown.

Reborn Awakening: What Was Lost.name: Reborn Awakening: What Was Lost
Reborn Awakening: What Was Lost.mainObjective: Respond to the old-world memory that surfaces during this awakening.
Reborn Awakening: What Was Lost.questStatement: Something from your old world has surfaced in Luxcellia: a song you recognize playing at a festival, a technology that shouldn't exist here, or another Reborn who remembers the same things you do. The collision between what you lost and what you've found forces you to confront the question you've been avoiding, who are you now?
Reborn Awakening: What Was Lost.questDesignBrief: Part 5 of the Reborn Awakening chain: an epilogue quest about identity. Something from the old world has surfaced in Luxcellia: a song, a food, a phrase, a technology, or a fellow Reborn who shares the protagonist's cultural background. The encounter triggers intense homesickness, nostalgia, and the complicated grief of carrying a world inside you that nobody else remembers. The quest is primarily emotional; there may be a practical element, but the core conflict is internal. The protagonist must navigate the experience with their current companions, deciding how much to reveal and experiencing the vulnerability of being known in a way nobody else in this world can know them. This quest should produce at least one deeply intimate scene with a companion: either because the companion witnesses the protagonist's grief and responds, or because the companion asks about the old world and receives an answer that changes how they see the protagonist. The quest should end with the protagonist having moved slightly closer to reconciliation; not resolved, but progressing.

Academy Trials.name: Academy Trials
Academy Trials.mainObjective: Resolve the academic challenge currently assigned to you.
Academy Trials.questStatement: The magical academy has a challenge that requires a student or adventurer's participation: a ranking exam, a research experiment, a competitive trial, a field test, or a disciplinary matter that needs resolution.
Academy Trials.questDesignBrief: Generate an academic challenge appropriate to the player's magical abilities and current standing. Trials can be practical exams, magical combat tournaments, research expeditions to dangerous locations, thesis defenses against hostile faculty, or investigations into magical anomalies on campus. Tone: competitive energy, intellectual curiosity, student rivalry, and the specific intensity of talented young people proving themselves. The trial should always mix academic knowledge with practical danger: written exams don't make good anime, but a practical exam in a dungeon full of test monsters absolutely does. Complications: a rival sabotages the player's attempt, the trial is harder than advertised because someone made a mistake, the magical experiment produces an unexpected result that becomes dangerous, a professor has a personal grudge, or the trial's scoring system is being manipulated. Rewards: rank advancement, access to restricted library sections, new spells or techniques, faculty mentorship, rare reagents, and social standing among the student body. The player's rival should always be present and should always be annoyingly competent. Academy trials should feel like the exam arc of a magical school anime: the stakes feel personal, the competition is fierce, the magic is flashy, and the rival's expression when the player wins is priceless. Professor Sumika Chigi administers the Blessing Theory portion of the trials, and Subaru Hoshikaze (the Academy's youngest professor and its leading Riftmaw-mechanics expert) observes candidates whose abilities defy his models with poorly concealed fascination.

Dungeon Delves.name: Dungeon Delves
Dungeon Delves.mainObjective: Return to the surface with the result of your assigned dungeon expedition.
Dungeon Delves.questStatement: A Riftmaw dungeon entrance has become active or unstable, and the Guild is organizing a delve to clear floors, map passages, and recover resources before the next respawn cycle makes it harder.
Dungeon Delves.questDesignBrief: Generate a Riftmaw dungeon expedition with procedural floors, traps, puzzles, and monster encounters. Each floor should escalate in danger and reward. Tone: tense exploration, party cooperation, dramatic monster encounters, and the constant awareness that something worse might be on the next floor. The dungeon should always feature at least one environmental puzzle that requires creative Blessing use, one monster encounter that forces a strategic decision, and one moment of genuine beauty: a crystalline cavern, a preserved garden, a glowing underground lake. Complications: the dungeon layout shifts mid-delve, a party member is separated or injured, a deeper floor opens unexpectedly, or the party encounters another adventuring group that is either hostile, friendly, or something in between. The dungeon's lowest reached floor should always reveal a fragment of mystery: architecture that predates the Riftmaw, writing in an unknown language, or an artifact that responds to Reborn souls. Rewards: rare crafting materials, enchanted equipment, gold, Guild rank credit, and sometimes a Blessing fragment or mysterious artifact. The delve should feel like a dungeon-crawling anime arc: rising tension, close calls, party chemistry, and a climax on the deepest floor reached.

Blood and Sand: Freedom's Cost.name: Blood and Sand: Freedom's Cost
Blood and Sand: Freedom's Cost.mainObjective: Lead the freed fighters out of the Crucible.
Blood and Sand: Freedom's Cost.questStatement: Vex wasn't just a pit boss: they're a Veilwalker deep-cover agent, and the Crucible was an intelligence operation tracking a noble house that funds Riftmaw weaponization. Your escape forces their hand: maintain cover and keep feeding intel, or blow it wide open and lose years of work. The freed fighters from the cells are your party now. And the noble house that profited from your chains is the same one behind the Rift-Herding attacks on Ironhold.
Blood and Sand: Freedom's Cost.questDesignBrief: Part 2 of the Blood and Sand chain. The escape from the Crucible isn't the end: it's the beginning of understanding. Vex Kagemizu, the pit boss who ran the operation with sardonic wit, didn't just happen to be there. Vex is a deep-cover operative for the Veilwalkers who has been using the Crucible as an intelligence-gathering operation: the fighters are sources, the spectators are targets, and the money trail leads to a noble house that has been funding Riftmaw weaponization research through the Crucible's profits. Vex chose to keep the operation running because the intelligence was too valuable to lose, but they've also been quietly freeing fighters who show signs of Reborn resonance, arranging their "deaths" in the ring and smuggling them to Veilwalker safe houses. The player's escape complicates everything: Vex can either maintain cover (letting the player flee with the other fighters but staying behind) or blow cover (escaping with the players and destroying years of intelligence work). The choice matters because the noble house funding the Crucible is the same one connected to the Rift-Herding technique that Commander Takane Kihata is investigating in the Ashenmere Frontier: Vex's intelligence and the Commander's investigation are two threads of the same conspiracy. The freed fighters (the elven mage with the suppressed collar, the disgraced knight, the lamia dancer) become the player's first adventuring party, each carrying trauma, skills, and a personal stake in finding out who profited from their captivity. The escape through the tunnels beneath Cinder Ale Outpost is visceral and desperate: the Outpost's miners are sympathetic (many were Crucible fighters themselves once) but the noble house's enforcers are already responding to the alarm. This follows Crucible of Blood and Sand and sets up The Crucible's Legacy.

Guild Bounties.name: Guild Bounties
Guild Bounties.mainObjective: Report the resolved bounty to the Guild.
Guild Bounties.questStatement: The Adventurer's Guild has posted a bounty requiring an adventurer's attention. A monster, criminal, or dangerous creature is threatening a location, trade route, or community, and the Guild is offering payment and rank credit to whoever resolves the threat.
Guild Bounties.questDesignBrief: Generate a monster-hunt or criminal-pursuit bounty appropriate to the player's current region and rank. The target should be dangerous but survivable: a credible threat, not a suicide mission. Tone: action-forward, camaraderie-heavy, with moments of tension and relief. The bounty should always involve at least one twist: the target is not where expected, the target has allies, the target is protecting something, or the target is someone the player recognizes. Complications: weather turns bad, a rival party is also hunting the bounty, the target has a Blessing that makes it harder than anticipated, or the person who posted the bounty lied about the details. Rewards: gold proportional to difficulty, Guild rank credit, a useful piece of equipment or material from the target, and a reputation boost in the local Guild branch. If the player shows mercy or creativity instead of brute force, offer an alternative resolution that still pays out. Every bounty should feel like an episode of an adventuring anime: quick setup, escalating action, a dramatic confrontation, and a satisfying conclusion that leaves the player feeling competent.

Noble Scandals.name: Noble Scandals
Noble Scandals.mainObjective: Settle the scandal with the employer on terms you choose to support.
Noble Scandals.questStatement: A scandal is brewing in the noble houses: an affair, a betrayal, a stolen inheritance, a political marriage at risk, or a secret that could destroy a family's standing. Someone wants the player to find the truth, bury it, or exploit it.
Noble Scandals.questDesignBrief: Generate a social intrigue scenario set among the noble houses of the Crownveil Sovereignty, Rosethorn Nocturne, or wherever aristocrats gather. The scandal should involve real emotions and real consequences: broken hearts, ruined reputations, dangerous secrets, and alliances that shift with every conversation. Tone: sharp wit, gorgeous settings, dangerous flirtation, and the constant awareness that every smile hides an agenda. The scandal should always have at least three sides: the employer, the target, and the truth. Complications: the player develops sympathy for the scandal's target, the employer is using the player to advance a worse scheme, the scandal involves a Reborn individual's true identity, a romantic entanglement complicates the investigation, or the evidence leads somewhere far more dangerous than a social embarrassment.
